dyad.what_is_scored: The seam between two adjacent paragraphs inside one chapter, judged as a Third Thing the pair should become.

criteria.name: Third Thing Emerges
criteria.question: Does the pair together say or enable something (a consequence, contrast, test, cost, payoff) that neither paragraph says alone?
criteria.yes_when: A reader can state something from the pair that neither paragraph states alone, cutting either paragraph weakens the other, and the pair does not merely stack two agreeing claims: at least one paragraph supplies the test, limit, counter-case, or cost the other lacks.
criteria.no_when: The paragraphs could be swapped, merged, or one dropped with nothing lost but length; the pair restates itself or stacks reinforcing claims; or it persuades only through rhythm or parallel phrasing, so that no claim survives once the cadence is removed.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (3 approved the draft as written; 2 proposed the stacking and cadence additions, both adopted).

criteria.name: Handoff Carried
criteria.question: Does the second paragraph pick up something the first actually established (an example, fact, step, or open tension), so the reader can name what was handed across?
criteria.yes_when: The second paragraph uses or answers something the first set up on the page, and would read differently if the first were removed.
criteria.no_when: The second paragraph starts cold, re-defines a term just used, leans on a bare connective ('Furthermore', 'Next'), or invokes a capitalized or coined label that the first paragraph only asserted and never earned. Such a label is a stage prop, not a handoff.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (3 approved as written; 1 proposed the stage-prop clause, adopted).

criteria.name: Link Is Honest
criteria.question: Can the reader name the relation (cause, example, objection, step, reversal, zoom), and is every connective or jump in scope or confidence backed by something on the page?
criteria.yes_when: The relation is stated or plainly implied; any 'therefore' or 'which is why', any jump from case to rule, and any mechanism claimed (feedback, growth, decay) is backed on the page, with the paragraph showing how sure it is; and the seam does not slide from a described pattern or event to a claim about who the reader is.
criteria.no_when: A tidy or fluent connective covers a non sequitur, so the link feels earned only because it reads smoothly. Also: an anecdote is promoted to a law, an assumption in the first paragraph is stated as settled fact in the second, the seam is dressed in wordplay or hedging instead of stated, or it moves from what the reader does to what the reader is (pattern to identity, lapse to defect).
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (3 approved as written; 4 proposed changes to it, merged into this wording).

criteria.name: Turn Is Even or Earned
criteria.question: Does the seam hold register, vocabulary, and altitude, or change them visibly and on purpose, while introducing at most one new term or concept across the join?
criteria.yes_when: Register, term, example, and level of abstraction stay continuous, or the change (story to claim, cosmic to concrete) is prepared by the first paragraph; at most one new idea arrives before the previous one has been used; and a move from pain or personal difficulty to cosmic or systemic framing first acknowledges the hurt.
criteria.no_when: The reader notices an unexplained jump of term or scale, a second new concept lands before the first has been used (a smooth seam that dumps two concepts fails), or a lofty leap lands on a hurting moment without naming the hurt (spiritual bypass).
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (3 approved as written; 4 proposed changes to it, two adopted in full and two folded elsewhere or not adopted).

dyad.dissent: Not adopted: voter 1's wording that makes a named stock, flow, limit, or delay mandatory at every seam (kept only as 'mechanism claimed must be backed'), since most seams claim no mechanism; voter 5's separate plain-join rule (folded into the wordplay clause of Link Is Honest); voter 10's rule that a story-to-claim shift must carry a person or object across, which is too narrow because most seams are not story-to-claim.

skein.what_is_scored: One chapter: a group of paragraphs bound by a shared aim, the way a Skein is bound by a shared practice.

criteria.name: One Stated Aim
criteria.question: Can a careful reader state in one sentence what this chapter is for, and does the chapter signal that aim near its opening and keep to it?
criteria.yes_when: Independent readers give essentially the same one-sentence aim, without needing 'and also' or a list of topics.
criteria.no_when: Readers give different aims, the aim only becomes visible at the end, or the title promises something the body does not deliver.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (no one proposed a change).

criteria.name: Every Paragraph Earns
criteria.question: Does each paragraph visibly serve the aim and add something, so that removing or relocating any one would leave a noticeable gap?
criteria.yes_when: No paragraph could be lifted into another chapter unchanged, repeat an earlier point at equal strength, or be deleted without loss; where the chapter's claim depends on an idea, someone (a case, face, or cost) stands in it.
criteria.no_when: The chapter has padding, tangents, orphans, or pairs doing the same job twice, including a pile of stacked rhetorical questions or qualifiers where one sentence would carry it, a claim-bearing idea with nobody standing in it, or a paragraph whose only function is to blame or diagnose the reader. The remedy is rework (reduce to the essential sentence, give it a person, describe the pattern the reader is caught in), never silent cutting.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (0 approved as written; 4 proposed additions, all adopted in merged form).

criteria.name: Order Builds to Arrival
criteria.question: Does the sequence build, each step preparing the next, and end in a landing the body has paid for?
criteria.yes_when: Shuffling the paragraphs would damage the argument; no concept is used before it is taught; new concepts arrive at a learnable pace (never three at once in one paragraph); and the final paragraph lands on a changed understanding, ideally returning to an image, person, or situation planted near the opening, now carrying more weight.
criteria.no_when: The paragraphs could be shuffled with the argument intact, forward references go unexplained, a difficulty spike or an idle stretch of pure reception appears, the ending restates the opening or stops, or it closes on a confident payoff larger than the body supports (a landing that feels earned from cadence, not from what was shown).
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (0 approved as written; 4 proposed additions, adopted except voter 1's local-rule clause).

criteria.name: Delivers Something Usable
criteria.question: By the end, can the reader do, notice, or test something specific and small, with a causal account behind it and a sign of whether it worked?
criteria.yes_when: The reader can name one action, observation, or test small enough to try today in ordinary life, even on a bad day; the chapter supports its claim with a causal account, a worked example with a name or number, or a checkable step (an image alone does not count); and it says what would show the practice is not working or how sure it is, keeping story distinct from evidence.
criteria.no_when: The chapter informs without equipping; gives advice no outcome could contradict ('be present', 'find your loop'); leaves the claim as assertion or metaphor; treats a vivid anecdote as proof; or its main payload is more self-scrutiny or rumination rather than a step.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (0 approved as written; 9 proposed changes to this one, the most contested criterion; the shared core is adopted).

skein.dissent: Not adopted: voter 4's mandatory named trigger and two-minute version (too rigid for every chapter; kept at World, where the first step is judged); voter 8's requirement that every chapter name whose rules shape the behavior (one voter, and judged at Culture and World where it fits); voter 5's body-only practice (excludes legitimate thought tests); voter 1's local-rule-before-generalization clause (overlaps the causal-account requirement in Delivers Something Usable).

culture.what_is_scored: One Part of the book (Front Matter, Parts One to Seven, or the Appendix): a set of chapters with its own character and ways, inherited upward from its chapters.

criteria.name: Distinct Inherited Character
criteria.question: Does this Part have a recognizable job, voice, and way of working that differs from its neighbors and visibly comes from what its chapters actually do, rather than from an opener or title imposed on them?
criteria.yes_when: A reader dropped into a random chapter could guess which Part it belongs to, and the Part's stated promises are matched by what its chapters deliver (no gaps, no orphans).
criteria.no_when: Chapters could be reshuffled into a neighboring Part unnoticed, or the Part opener promises terms and ways the chapters never use.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (2 approved the draft as written; no one proposed a change to this criterion).

criteria.name: Chapters Build Each Other
criteria.question: Do later chapters lean on, extend, or test earlier ones, so the Part shows a result no single chapter reaches alone, with progress the reader can feel inside the Part?
criteria.yes_when: Removing or reordering a chapter leaves a visible gap and the closing chapter could not be read first without loss; a usable move or payoff arrives before the Part's last chapter; and at least one recurring image, case, or person returns in later chapters with changed weight. Chapters may also qualify or correct one another.
criteria.no_when: The Part is a shelf of standalone essays, chapters repeat the same point with new anecdotes, the order is arbitrary, or all the payoff is deferred to a later Part so the Part reads as setup only.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (2 approved as written; 3 proposed additions, voters 7 and 10 adopted, voter 1 not).

criteria.name: Ways Held Consistently
criteria.question: Do the chapters share the same terms, definitions, and standard of evidence, with each use of fractal, loop, or scale earning its meaning, and keep faith with the book's core operation?
criteria.yes_when: Key terms mean one thing throughout the Part and across Parts; each use of fractal, loop, scale, or repeats names what repeats and what limits it; bolder claims get stronger support than weaker ones; and at least one claim in the Part is exposed to a case or counterexample that could have gone against it, with a report of how it fared.
criteria.no_when: A term shifts meaning between chapters or Parts, or 'fractal' only means deep or pretty; one chapter undercuts another; the largest claims rest on the thinnest support; every cited case confirms the thesis; or a term coined earlier is cited as authority or precedent without having been earned by an example or measurement.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (2 approved as written; 5 proposed additions, the most of any Culture criterion; voters 1, 6, and 9 adopted).

criteria.name: Honest Entry and Handoff
criteria.question: Does the Part open by saying what it inherits, close by saying what it did and did not establish, and hand the reader forward with something the next Part uses, without harming a fragile reader?
criteria.yes_when: The closing claim does not exceed what the chapters supported; limits and costs are named, including who the Part could hurt (rumination, self-blame, use against others) with a way for a fragile reader to pause or step back; the Part speaks to what a person does or is caught in, never to what a person is; and it leaves one repeatable action, not just understanding, which the next Part builds on.
criteria.no_when: The Part ends in a crescendo larger than any chapter supported, trails off or cliff-edges, or is bloated or starved for its role; it asks for deep self-examination or hard truths with no pacing, off-ramp, or acknowledgment of pain; a chapter slides from guilt-type to shame-type framing; or it hands forward ideas only, leaving the reader nothing to run on Monday.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (2 approved as written; voters 3 and 4 proposed additions, both adopted).

culture.dissent: Not adopted: voter 1's requirement that the scale claim be tested at the next level up and down in every Part (covered by the 'what repeats and what limits it' clause, and too heavy for the Front Matter and Appendix); voter 8's rule that structural causes need a named mechanism, owner, or lever (one voter here; adopted at World, where the whole book's reach is judged); voter 3's stance rule was moved from Ways Held Consistently to Honest Entry and Handoff, where it is a safety matter.

world.what_is_scored: The whole book as one thing that lives in a reader's life and meets the world outside its pages.

criteria.name: Whole Exceeds Parts and Enacts Itself
criteria.question: Does the complete book enable something no single Part delivers, with its one operation stated as a mechanism and visibly enacted in its own structure at every scale?
criteria.yes_when: A reader can name the spine and what the whole adds beyond any Part; the operation is stated as a mechanism (a local rule, what repeats, at what ratio, what limits it) so the structure follows from the thesis; the self-enactment can be checked against the text, not merely claimed by analogy; early images and promises return near the end carrying more weight; and the reader can name at least one person or image they will still remember tomorrow.
criteria.no_when: The thesis is complete in any one Part, the book is a binder of good chapters or of metaphors, the structure would be the same if the thesis were false, enactment is claimed by analogy only so any structure would count, a promise is dropped, or the book ends on a crescendo of abstraction with no human face to pay it off.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (2 approved as written; 3 proposed additions, voters 1, 6, and 10, all adopted).

criteria.name: Lives In A Life
criteria.question: Could a reader carry the book into an ordinary week, including a bad one, taking a small first step they can repeat and check, and re-enter the book later without the author or the full worldview?
criteria.yes_when: A reader can name one practice that takes only a few minutes, the cue that starts it (a trigger, moment, or mental state), what they would do on a bad day when they manage only the smallest version, and how they would know it worked; the step is something the body or attention does and needs no teacher, notebook, or ideal conditions; a lapse is treated as information, not as failure or a character verdict; and there is a way back in.
criteria.no_when: The reader agrees with everything and changes nothing; the first step is large, has no cue, demands energy or self-scrutiny, or works only as a resolution to try harder; a lapse implies the reader is the failing pattern; or the book can be absorbed only linearly, once.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (2 approved as written; 4 proposed changes to it, voters 3, 4, and 5 adopted, voter 8 moved to Survives Contact).

criteria.name: Survives Contact
criteria.question: Does the book hold up against a skeptic, a counterexample, a failure of the practice, or a misuse, with stated limits and at least one claim a hostile but fair reader could in principle show wrong?
criteria.yes_when: The book states where its central claim stops helping and what evidence would count against it; names at least one case where the loop does not hold or does not scale up or down; states which problems personal practice cannot fix because incentives, institutions, or environments produce them, and does not let inner work stand in for shared action; and gives the strongest opposing view in the voice of someone who holds it for good reasons.
criteria.no_when: Every counterexample is absorbed as another instance of the pattern; the framework explains everything and so predicts nothing; opponents appear as straw men; inner work is offered as the remedy for something designed into the environment, or fatalism excuses the reader from acting; or the book is a closed system only believers can use.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (2 approved as written; 3 proposed additions, voters 1, 8, and 10, all adopted).

criteria.name: Trustworthy and Safe in the Hands
criteria.question: Does the book keep its voice honest about what it knows and stay safe for the most vulnerable reader and for use on other people, working as an offer of help rather than a verdict or label?
criteria.yes_when: The book's total confidence ends no higher than its support; key terms stay stable; it says plainly which claims are measured or checkable and which are metaphor or useful fiction; it tells a reader in acute distress to seek human or professional help; every route through it leaves a fragile reader no worse off; and its vocabulary resists being used as an accusation or diagnosis.
criteria.no_when: The book finishes more certain than it began; it drifts on central terms; it wears its ritual costume with a straight face and no wink toward the reader; it implies a reader's suffering is caused by their own beliefs or loops, or bypasses pain with oneness or acceptance language before acknowledging it; or it offers blame or diagnosis of who the reader is or hands out language easy to weaponize against self or others.
criteria.support: 10 of 10 backed it (2 approved as written; 3 proposed additions, voters 3 and 9 adopted, voter 5 not).

world.dissent: Not adopted: voter 5's 'calm to read aloud' and 'wordier than its content needs' tests for Trustworthy and Safe (too subjective for a yes/no answer, and wordiness is judged at the Skein scale); voter 8's requirement that the first step feed shared action (merged into Survives Contact, where the limits of personal practice are judged, to keep Lives In A Life about the first step); voter 4's fixed two-minute limit and 'one question to carry' (replaced with 'a few minutes' and left optional).

P0001>P0002.label: How to Read a Recursive Book
P0001>P0002.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0001] to paragraph [P0002] (chapter "How to Read a Recursive Book")

modeler: Epigraph feeds the river line, but the pair restates one image. No stock or flow; show what accumulates between readings.
skeptic: Epigraph is a decoration; the river is picked up honestly, but together they add little beyond a pleasing echo. Fine, not a Third Thing.
clinician: River quote becomes the reader who changes, not the page. Gentle and usable; a reader can state the pair's claim.
habit: River quote is picked up cleanly, but it's decoration. Nothing here I can do tomorrow. Give the second reading a cue.
contemplative: The river is carried across and turns into the claim: the page stays, the reader changes. Quiet and plain.
stress: River epigraph is used in the last line. Modest, usable. But 'second reading working' is hard to falsify; name a sign that it isn't.
gamedesigner: Epigraph pays off in the river line, but the pair just agrees. Nothing is tested. Give me a first move before the quote closes.
structural: Epigraph supplies the river, paragraph spends it. Honest handoff, but an epigraph seam adds no Third Thing. Fine as ornament.
satirist: Heraclitus is cashed in at once: the river becomes the reader. Rare epigraph that works for a living. Keep it.
mythmaker: The river returns with weight, lovely. But the quote only decorates the warning. Give me a reader who rereads and finds the page changed.

P0002>P0003.label: How to Read a Recursive Book
P0002>P0003.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0002] to paragraph [P0003] (chapter "How to Read a Recursive Book")

modeler: Circle-versus-line claim gets its limit and cases next door. Good build, though 'most of what matters loops' still wants a stock named.
skeptic: Line-versus-circle gives the warning a reason, but 'most of what matters to you' loops is asserted. How would you know? Show one case.
clinician: Circle-versus-line is explained by the next paragraph. Plain examples, no blame, nothing asked of a struggling reader.
habit: Line-versus-circle is asserted, then earned with examples. Good pair. Still no action; add 'next time, mark where you got stuck'.
contemplative: The line-versus-circle point is made twice. Examples are good, but the second paragraph mostly restates the first. Trim one.
stress: Line vs circle carries over well. But three examples become 'most of what matters to you' loops. Case to rule with no check.
gamedesigner: Circle versus line gets its reason: language loses loops. Good set-up, then the cost lands. Still no move for me yet.
structural: Circle-versus-line is stated, then argued with examples. Reader can say why one reading fails. Real work done across the seam.
satirist: The circle-versus-line warning gets its reason and three plain examples. Passes the bar test. Bricks and tires help.
mythmaker: Circle versus line becomes a real cost of ordinary language, with habit, belief and school as cases. Still no person inside it.

P0003>P0004.label: How to Read a Recursive Book
P0003>P0004.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0003] to paragraph [P0004] (chapter "How to Read a Recursive Book")

modeler: Line can't draw a circle, so the book is written in arcs. Design follows from the limit. Looping-as-felt-circling is still unmodeled.
skeptic: Problem then design response, and 'worth knowing too' admits the claim can fail. Only worry: 'what a Loop feels like' is asserted, not shown.
clinician: Arcs pick up the line/circle problem. 'Notice the feeling' is mild and bounded; say what to do next after noticing.
habit: Problem then design response. 'Notice the feeling' is the nearest thing to a rep. Name when to notice it.
contemplative: Arcs answer the limit of lines honestly. The 'didn't we cover this?' feeling is a small, usable practice.
stress: Arcs follow from the line problem. Then any rereading result confirms the thesis, and 'Loop' arrives capitalised and unearned. Name a failing outcome.
gamedesigner: Arcs become a structure with a feedback cue: 'didn't we cover this?' Nice. Lost me slightly on the Part names.
structural: The line/arc diagnosis becomes a design choice, and the 'didn't we cover this' feeling is a test. Earned.
satirist: Arc image becomes an actual book structure, with the 'if it reads the same, that's worth knowing' escape hatch. Honest and useful.
mythmaker: Arcs answer the circle problem, and the 'didn't we cover this?' feeling gives the reader a live test. Good handoff.

P0004>P0005.label: How to Read a Recursive Book
P0004>P0005.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0004] to paragraph [P0005] (chapter "How to Read a Recursive Book")

modeler: Signpost after an argument. Nothing handed across; fold it into the reading routes.
skeptic: Pure signpost. P0005 starts cold and the pair adds nothing; fold the line into the paragraph before or after.
clinician: A transitional line. Merge it into the next paragraph; it carries nothing a reader could use alone.
habit: A pivot line, not a pair. Cut it or fold it into the list. Starts cold.
contemplative: The book was just called circular, then 'you needn't read front to back.' A bare pivot. Say how the two fit.
stress: Pure signpost. Nothing is tested or risked across this join. Merge it into the list intro.
gamedesigner: Pivot to a menu. Nothing from the arc paragraph is used. A bare signpost between tutorial and map.
structural: Having sold arcs, the book says skip around. No tension is named. This is a bare transition; merge with the list.
satirist: Having just insisted on arcs, the book says skip around. A throat-clear. Cut it or fold it into the next list.
mythmaker: A bare pivot to instructions. Nothing from the arcs paragraph is used. Tie the reading path to the felt circling.

modeler: Arcs carry into entry points, but P0005 is a lead-in. No stock or test here; merge it into P0004's close.
skeptic: 'Arcs' hands over cleanly to entering anywhere, but P0005 is a lead-in colon; the pair adds no claim beyond a stated consequence.
clinician: Arcs hand off cleanly to entry points, but it's procedural: the pair adds no test or cost. Fine as navigation.
habit: Arcs hand off to 'enter anywhere' cleanly, but it's a transition. Where do I start tomorrow? Say it.
contemplative: Arcs lead gently to entering anywhere. Plain, but the pair adds no test or cost. One could carry the other.
stress: Arcs imply multiple entry points. Modest, honest consequence. But 'can be entered anywhere' sits oddly beside P4's claim that return visits reveal change.
gamedesigner: Good handoff from arcs to entry points, but 'arcs, therefore enter anywhere' is a leap; P0004 itself prescribes an order. State the reason.
structural: Arcs justify entering anywhere; the revised opener carries the term across. Modest consequence, but earned.
satirist: Fine signpost, arcs to entry points. It earns a handoff but no third thing; a sign that points to other signs.
mythmaker: Arcs hand across cleanly, but the pair only ushers us to a list. Lovely signpost; nobody's standing in it yet.

P0005>P0006.label: How to Read a Recursive Book
P0005>P0006.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0005] to paragraph [P0006] (chapter "How to Read a Recursive Book")

modeler: Lead-in to a list. Honest relation, but no content crosses the seam.
skeptic: Lead-in then first item. Honest and clear, but no claim emerges. Dropping the lead-in loses only length.
clinician: Intro line leads into the first instruction. Fine signposting, but nothing is created by the pair.
habit: Lead-in to a list. Fine as signage, but nothing emerges. Merge into the first route.
contemplative: Announcement then first instruction. Plain and fine, but nothing new is made by the pair.
stress: Intro line to first item. Clean but adds nothing. Fold the intro into the item.
gamedesigner: Header line, first list item. Works as a list, but together they add nothing a heading wouldn't.
structural: Lead-in to a list. Handoff is real, but the pair adds nothing; fold the lead-in into the first item.
satirist: Signpost then first bullet. Works as a menu, but a lead-in line is not a Third Thing. Merge into the list.
mythmaker: A lead-in line and its first step. Sequence is clear but adds nothing together. Fold the intro into step one.

P0006>P0007.label: How to Read a Recursive Book
P0006>P0007.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0006] to paragraph [P0007] (chapter "How to Read a Recursive Book")

modeler: Part Two reappears, but the pair is stacked instructions. Say what delay separates reading from doing.
skeptic: Sequential steps in a list. P0007 picks up Part Two, but the pair stacks instructions. 'Doing is where ideas land' is unevidenced.
clinician: Sequential steps. 'Doing is where ideas land' leads to Part Two, but the pair only stacks instructions.
habit: Sequence step, good. But 'real days' has no cue or length. Say which days and what to do.
contemplative: Step follows step; Part Two is named in both. Neither tests the other. Clear, and a list item.
stress: Step two leans on Part Two from step one. Sequential advice, no test. 'Many ideas' hedges but never says when it fails.
gamedesigner: 'Doing is where ideas land' hands off to 'live in Part Two.' The second adds the cost of skipping. Good level progression.
structural: Sequence of instructions. Doing-lands-ideas is picked up, but item two just stacks a stronger version of item one.
satirist: Step two follows step one, but two instructions side by side add nothing. 'Actual point of the whole project' is chest-thumping.
mythmaker: Step two starts cold. Doing is where ideas land, but the first step never says who's doing. Show one reader living it.

P0007>P0008.label: How to Read a Recursive Book
P0007>P0008.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0007] to paragraph [P0008] (chapter "How to Read a Recursive Book")

modeler: Parallel list items, swappable. Where's the delay between living a practice and needing the language?
skeptic: Parallel list items. P0008 opens cold with the Loop Tongue, a new coined term, before Part Two's practice has been used.
clinician: Another list item that starts cold. Loop Tongue arrives as a label with no tie to the 'live in Part Two' step.
habit: 'Use not study' carries across. Best cue in the section: third time in the same argument. Move that trigger up front.
contemplative: Another step in a list. Part Three starts cold. Clear, but you could swap the order and lose nothing.
stress: Parallel list items. Either could be swapped. No condition says when 'live in Part Two' fails.
gamedesigner: Another list item, cold start. Part Three arrives with a trigger condition, but nothing carried over from Part Two.
structural: Reading-order bullets; the second starts cold with the Loop Tongue. Parallel structure carries it. No test, limit or cost.
satirist: Another list item with a cold start. Fine as a reading order, but nothing arises from the pair.
mythmaker: Another list item. 'Auditioning a belief' is a nice image, dropped at once. Carry it into the Loop Tongue step.

modeler: Practice first, then a language for it. The 'real loop' trigger is a decent gate. Still no stock named, but the sequencing is earned.
skeptic: Live in Part Two, then Part Three once it supplies a real loop: a sensible condition. 'Loop Tongue' arrives unearned, but only once.
clinician: Condition is carried well, and 'this keeps happening' without 'you keep doing it' is clinically right. Still sequencing, not a Third Thing.
habit: Live in practice first, then theory arrives on a cue: the third repeat of the same argument. That's a real trigger. Keep.
contemplative: Part Two's real days become the loop Part Three needs. A clear step, yet only sequence, nothing new from the pair.
stress: Clean sequencing, but it's list stacking. Drop either and nothing breaks. No test or cost emerges, just two instructions in order.
gamedesigner: Clean level progression: live in Part Two, then Part Three unlocks once you have a real loop. The player earns the next tool.
structural: Practice-first sequencing becomes a condition for opening Part Three. Reason and consequence both on the page.
satirist: Practice first, then the language: Part Two supplies the loop Part Three needs words for. Honest dependency, one new term.
mythmaker: Practice first, then language arrives when a real argument demands it. The Part Two loop becomes the reason to open Three. Good sequencing.

P0008>P0009.label: How to Read a Recursive Book
P0008>P0009.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0008] to paragraph [P0009] (chapter "How to Read a Recursive Book")

modeler: Another parallel instruction; the Part Four shelf starts cold. Reorderable with nothing lost.
skeptic: Another item in the reading list. 'Why does the dice game draw triangles?' leans on something not yet on the page. Swappable.
clinician: Parallel reading instructions. Either could be dropped without loss. A bad-day reader needs a clearer 'start here' marker.
habit: Parallel list items; each stands alone. The nagging-question trigger works. Add a Monday-morning first move.
contemplative: Items in a row, each fine alone. The shelf image is kind. No handoff between them.
stress: Bullet stack, no handoff. Reading advice with no cost if wrong.
gamedesigner: Parallel bullet. Swappable. Needs one line saying how shelf-reading differs from the loop-talk use before it.
structural: Parallel bullets, swappable. Nothing from the Loop Tongue item is used by the shelf item.
satirist: Reading advice stacked on reading advice. The dice-game question is the only concrete hook. Lead with it.
mythmaker: The third-argument scene has a face in it, then the next step moves on. Stacked instructions, no payoff across the join.

modeler: Learned-by-use against looked-up-by-need makes a clean contrast. Each defines the other by what it isn't.
skeptic: 'Learned by use' versus 'looked up by need' is a real contrast, stated openly. The seam does its job.
clinician: Learned by use versus looked up by need is a real contrast, and the 'where Part Three' hinge is explicit.
habit: 'Learned by use' versus 'looked up by need' is a real contrast, and the nagging question works as a cue.
contemplative: Learned by use, then looked up by need. The contrast is real and usable. Quiet and clear.
stress: 'Learned by use' versus 'looked up by need' is a real contrast the pair makes together. Modest, checkable, calm sea.
gamedesigner: 'Learned by use' versus 'looked up by need' is a real contrast. Reader can state the difference. Nice hook with the dice game.
structural: 'Where Part Three is learned by use' sets up a clean contrast with lookup by need. Seam is stated.

modeler: Opener lines stacked; the fast-track pointer is separate navigation.
skeptic: Opener blurbs side by side; the routing line is independent of the preceding one. No joint claim; fine as signage.
clinician: Outcome line then route advice. Practical, but a pointer paragraph, not an emergent pair.
habit: Third line is the useful one: chapter list. Put it first, since it tells me what to do.
contemplative: Third summary line; a pointer to chapters. Useful signpost, no joint work.
stress: Navigation stack. Promise of 'see the loop' has no stated cost if it fails.
gamedesigner: Goal, outcome, route. Routing line is useful but independent. Third Thing mentioned before it's earned.
structural: Three-line opener format. Parallel, swappable, signage. No relation beyond order.
satirist: Blurb, then a signpost. The signpost is the useful one. Housekeeping, not a seam.
mythmaker: A promise, then a routing line. The marriage as Third Thing is asserted, never earned here. Routing needs no handoff.

modeler: 'Since this is seeing, not practice' makes the routing conditional on the page. A clean handoff.
skeptic: 'Not yet a practice' directly licenses the shortcut for changers. The conditional is stated and does real work.
clinician: Good: 'a shift in seeing, not yet a practice' is the limit that justifies the fast route. Honest about what Part One won't do.
habit: 'Not yet a practice' hands straight to a route for people who want to act this week. Exactly the escape hatch I want.
contemplative: Not yet a practice, so here is where to go if you want one. A real handoff, honestly stated.
stress: Honest: 'shift in seeing, not yet a practice' hands the practice-seeker a concrete detour. A modest limit stated up front. Good.
gamedesigner: 'Not yet a practice' sets up a skip-ahead route for the impatient player. Dependency is clear and the cost is stated.
structural: 'Not yet a practice' converts directly into a shortcut for the impatient reader. A real handoff.
satirist: 'Not yet a practice' is the limit that justifies the detour to Part Two. Honest and actionable; the reroute earns its place.
mythmaker: Not yet a practice becomes the reason to jump to Part Two. A limit and its consequence, honestly joined.

P0024>P0025.label: 1. What You Already Know
P0024>P0025.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0024] to paragraph [P0025] (chapter "1. What You Already Know")

modeler: 'See this' has no referent after an epigraph. The lawn path is a lovely seed with no stock.
skeptic: 'This' points at nothing; the Dillard epigraph does not establish a referent. Either could vanish. Give the 'this' a content.
clinician: Dillard epigraph and a shortcut across the lawn only loosely touch. 'See this' has no referent in the quote.
habit: Epigraph then 'this' with no antecedent beyond the quote. Name the thing being seen.
contemplative: Dillard's days become a lawn path and a family joke. Gentle and concrete. 'This' is slightly loose.
stress: Dillard's days do not lead to the lawn path. 'This' points at nothing on the page.
gamedesigner: Epigraph then 'this' with no antecedent. 'You may already have seen this' has nothing to point to.
structural: Epigraph then example stack agreeing gestures; nothing emerges. 'This' has no referent on the page. Name the accumulation idea first, then offer the lawn as its case.
satirist: 'This' has no antecedent; Dillard says nothing about lawns. The shortcut and the family joke are nice but unmoored.
mythmaker: Dillard's line and the lawn shortcut don't touch. A worn path is a good image, but it isn't tied to the quote.

modeler: Epigraph plus two agreeing examples. Lovely images, but no stock, flow or limit. Say what accumulates on the lawn path.
skeptic: Epigraph then illustration, hedged with 'may'. Lawn path and family joke fit loosely; the pair adds no claim over the quote.
clinician: Lawn path and family joke are fair instances of 'days added up'. Gentle, but it's an epigraph plus illustration, nothing new.
habit: Lawn and family joke ground the epigraph, but they illustrate rather than test it. Nice cue, no action. Add a lap-around question.
contemplative: The epigraph is answered with the lawn path and family joke. Lovely and plain, but they simply agree.
stress: Epigraph feeds the lawn-path example directly. Small, plain, checkable against the reader's own park. Vague 'it' could be tightened.
gamedesigner: Dillard's line gets two concrete instances, the lawn path and the family joke, so the reader can test it. Good first beat.
structural: Dillard's claim gets concrete instances: lawn path, family joke. Plain example relation, hedged with 'may'.
satirist: Dillard's days-add-up becomes a trodden lawn path and an orphaned family joke. Concrete, checkable, no hush required.
mythmaker: Dillard's days become a lawn path and a family joke: the quote stretched from one life to a group. Still no one standing on that lawn.

P0025>P0026.label: 1. What You Already Know
P0025>P0026.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0025] to paragraph [P0026] (chapter "1. What You Already Know")

modeler: More instances stacked on the lawn and joke. Phone check, fern, past self: draw the accumulation, not another example.
skeptic: Same appeal, more examples. P0026 picks up 'felt it', but the pair stacks agreeing anecdotes. 'Nobody built that person on purpose' is unsupported.
clinician: 'Seen' becomes 'felt', with more examples. Warm and recognizable, but it only stacks agreeing instances.
habit: Examples stack on the first. Phone-check line is a real cue. Choose one example and develop it.
contemplative: More examples of the same claim. Warm, but the fern and phone stack agreement rather than test it.
stress: More examples stacked on the earlier ones. Reinforcing, with no limit or counter-case.
gamedesigner: More examples stacked on the lawn and the joke. Good player-recognition cues, but cut either and the other still works.
structural: Both paragraphs are lists of felt instances. They reinforce; neither tests the other.
satirist: More examples piled on examples. Phone, fern and past self are mood, not evidence. Pick one and measure it.
mythmaker: 'Felt it' picks up 'already seen', but it's more examples stacked. Pick the best one and stay inside it.

P0026>P0027.label: 1. What You Already Know
P0026>P0027.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0026] to paragraph [P0027] (chapter "1. What You Already Know")

modeler: Instances rise to the book's observation, but fern to society is a rhyme. Say what repeats and at what ratio.
skeptic: Examples lead to a general rule, but 'genuinely just an observation, not a leap' is overconfident. Habits, self and society from anecdotes? Compared to what?
clinician: Four felt examples earn the general observation. Calling it 'just an observation' is slightly generous, but the support is on the page.
habit: Three vignettes become a universal law, billed as 'just an observation'. Say how sure you are; anecdotes aren't proof.
contemplative: Four small instances become 'the biggest things in your life.' 'Not a leap of faith' hedges the leap instead of showing it.
stress: Examples feed the book's core claim. But 'just an observation, not a leap' is overclaimed; the jump to society is unearned.
gamedesigner: Examples lead to the thesis. But 'just an observation, not a leap of faith' oversells how far four anecdotes carry. Hedge it.
structural: Four soft anecdotes become 'the shape of your society' with 'just an observation.' Case-to-rule leap; society and a phone check differ.
satirist: Examples become a thesis, then swear it is 'not a leap of faith.' It is. Phone-checking to society's shape is a big hop.
mythmaker: Cases become the thesis, and it's honestly flagged as an observation. Phone, fern and past self supply the setup. Needs one face.

P0027>P0028.label: 1. What You Already Know
P0027>P0028.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0027] to paragraph [P0028] (chapter "1. What You Already Know")

modeler: Restates the bolded observation in shorter words. One could go.
skeptic: Restates the bold claim shorter. 'Nothing large was built large' is an absolute that persuades by cadence. Merge or drop.
clinician: The second paragraph restates the first in short form. Drop one, or give the second a cost or counter-case.
habit: Restates the bold claim in plainer words. Drop one.
contemplative: The bold claim is repeated in six words. Beautiful and unneeded. One of them can go.
stress: Restates the bolded claim in shorter words. Cut one.
gamedesigner: Restates the bold claim in plain words. Reader gets nothing new; drop one.
structural: The second restates the first in shorter words. Rhythm only. Cut one.
satirist: Restates the bolded thesis in shorter words. Drop one of them.
mythmaker: The second paragraph restates the first in short beats. Cadence, not claim. Cut it or give it a cost.

P0028>P0029.label: 1. What You Already Know
P0028>P0029.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0028] to paragraph [P0029] (chapter "1. What You Already Know")

modeler: 'Can happen differently' follows from weather-like persistence. But 'exists because something keeps happening' is a mechanism claim with no stock behind it.
skeptic: Weather image adds a consequence, 'can happen differently', but that change-is-possible step is asserted for character and culture alike. How would you know?
clinician: Small and repeated becomes 'weather', and 'can happen differently' offers hope without blame. Good bad-day landing.
habit: 'Weather' metaphor does the work; 'what keeps happening can happen differently' is asserted, not backed. Show the mechanism.
contemplative: Weather turns 'built small' into 'still happening,' and so can change. A new idea, held lightly and used at once.
stress: Adds impermanence: 'can happen differently'. Comfort asserted via weather imagery; what if a keeping-it-going loop is imposed from outside? Show a counter-case.
gamedesigner: Small-built-large becomes 'weather, not objects,' and that gives change a handle: what keeps happening can happen differently. Good lift.
structural: Adds 'what keeps happening can happen differently.' Useful turn, but changeability is asserted, and nobody keeps the thing happening or profits.
satirist: The weather image lands, but 'what keeps happening can happen differently' is a hopeful leap from metaphor, not a mechanism.
mythmaker: Weather image turns 'built small' into 'must keep happening, so it can change'. A real consequence and a memorable picture.

P0029>P0030.label: 1. What You Already Know
P0029>P0030.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0029] to paragraph [P0030] (chapter "1. What You Already Know")

modeler: Exercise follows the claim fairly. It tests it but adds no new knowledge to the pair.
skeptic: A test the reader can run on their own life. Pair is claim then check. 'Rest of the book falls out' is puffery, minor.
clinician: Claim becomes a concrete, small question to ask today. Exactly the next step I look for. Keep it.
habit: Best seam so far: claim becomes one question to carry all day. Add a cue, such as tonight at the fridge.
contemplative: The claim becomes a question I can ask over breakfast. Practice that tests the paragraph above. Exactly right.
stress: Claim then a self-test the reader can run. Fair. Add what a failed test would look like.
gamedesigner: Claim turns into a move I make: pick something solid, ask what holds it. Agency at last. The best seam so far.
structural: Weather claim becomes a test the reader can run. 'Rest of the book falls out' oversells. Ask also who holds it there.
satirist: Claim becomes a one-question test the reader can run today. Stephenson test passed. 'Rest of the book falls out' is cape-swishing.
mythmaker: Weather claim becomes a task: find what holds the solid thing. The reader becomes the one at stake. Clean.

P0031>P0032.label: 2. The Third Thing
P0031>P0032.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0031] to paragraph [P0032] (chapter "2. The Third Thing")

modeler: Epigraph then coastline; the Richardson example stands without it.
skeptic: Epigraph about coastlines, then coastline measured. Honest pickup; the pair is quote then illustration, nothing emergent.
clinician: Epigraph to coastline demonstration. Clear and concrete, but the quote and image are one claim stated twice.
habit: Epigraph feeds the coastline. Clear. But the zoom is a lecture; nothing to do. Offer a ruler test.
contemplative: Mandelbrot's line is shown by a walk down a coast. Clear. 'Largely one process' is an odd phrase.
stress: Coastline epigraph feeds the ruler demo. Concrete and checkable, but the pair says no more than the demo.
gamedesigner: Epigraph flows into coastline. Good hook, but quote and scene agree; the pair adds no test.
structural: Epigraph then coastline. Handoff clean; ornament seam.
satirist: Richardson and the shorter ruler is a real number-and-name moment, Bryson-grade. 'Largely one process' is hand-waved but forgivable.
mythmaker: Mandelbrot sets the coastline, which then proves it. Fine, but the epigraph is just restated. Let the epigraph lose.

P0032>P0033.label: 2. The Third Thing
P0032>P0033.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0032] to paragraph [P0033] (chapter "2. The Third Thing")

modeler: Shifts from coastline to a do-it-yourself build. Good move toward local rule, but only a transition.
skeptic: Bridge to the die exercise. Reasonable handoff ('these shapes'), but P0033 is a lead-in; drop it and nothing is lost.
clinician: Bridge sentence. Inviting, with a doable step tonight; fold it into the next paragraph.
habit: Bridge sentence. Invites action, good. Fold it into the next paragraph.
contemplative: Short invitation to try it tonight. Plain and welcoming, but a lead-in only.
stress: Transition line. 'Largely one process' hedge is honest but unexamined.
gamedesigner: Coast measuring turns into 'make one tonight.' Observation becomes an invitation to play. Good pivot.
structural: Coastline then 'make one yourself.' Bridge sentence only. Merge into the die experiment.
satirist: A pure hand-off: 'make one yourself tonight.' Good invitation, but a lead-in sentence, not a pair.
mythmaker: A bridge sentence. It promises the die, and the coast gives it the shape-from-process idea. Nothing new emerges.

P0033>P0034.label: 2. The Third Thing
P0033>P0034.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0033] to paragraph [P0034] (chapter "2. The Third Thing")

modeler: Setup then procedure. Exactly the build-from-local-rule I like, but the seam is only a handoff.
skeptic: Invitation then procedure. Clear, honest, but a lead-in line contributes no claim of its own.
clinician: Instructions follow the invitation. Concrete small step, low stakes. Fine, but no emergence between the two.
habit: Promise then procedure. Excellent: pen, die, tonight. That is a rep. Procedure is the real content.
contemplative: Promise, then the steps. The pen-and-die instructions are doable. Seam is a hinge.
stress: Intro to the procedure. Good that it is testable at home; merge the two.
gamedesigner: Promise, then rules I can actually run, with the feedback signal of noise turning into a triangle. A real tutorial.
structural: Announcement then the procedure. Honest, but fold the announcement away.
satirist: Lead-in plus recipe. The recipe is great; the pair adds nothing beyond the one sentence.
mythmaker: Invitation and instructions. The dice game is physical and kind to the reader. A lead-in line isn't a seam.

P0034>P0035.label: 2. The Third Thing
P0034>P0035.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0034] to paragraph [P0035] (chapter "2. The Third Thing")

modeler: Triangle to wetness to marriage is a jump. Chaos game is a mechanism; marriage is just an analogy riding it.
skeptic: Leaps from a die game to wetness and marriage as 'real' things. One example becomes a law, and two new ideas arrive together. Show the bridge.
clinician: Sierpinski jumps to wetness and marriage as 'genuine independent things' in one move. Two new analogies; the jump is not backed.
habit: Dice triangle jumps to wetness and marriages as 'real' independent things. Overreach, two domains. Earn the leap or hedge.
contemplative: From dots on paper to wetness and marriage as 'real' things. The leap is asserted, not shown, and 'hardest idea' is posturing.
stress: Dice demo leaps to wetness and marriage as 'real'. Case to rule, and two big new ideas land. Slow down.
gamedesigner: Experiment jumps to wetness, marriage and 'real.' Chance-plus-rule to independent marriage-thing is a leap, and three concepts arrive at once.
structural: A die game becomes wetness and marriages being 'real.' Wetness and marriage jump arrives with no bridge, and two concepts at once. Stage them.
satirist: Triangle game to wetness and marriage in one leap. Order from a rule is not 'a genuine independent thing' that can be sick. Metaphor promoted.
mythmaker: Dice order leaps to wetness and marriage as 'real, independent, with integrity'. The jump from math to marriage is smooth, not shown.

P0035>P0036.label: 2. The Third Thing
P0035>P0036.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0035] to paragraph [P0036] (chapter "2. The Third Thing")

modeler: Names the Third Thing after the marriage example, then three applications. Label for 'appears from parts'; nothing new.
skeptic: Label then use. Fine pickup, but the 'real' marriage claim from P0035 is carried over unexamined; P0036 is instruction, not new content.
clinician: Names the Third Thing and gives sight-lines for home, work, fridge. Mostly application of the previous claim.
habit: Naming the Third Thing, then three seeing moves with cues: argument, work, midnight fridge. Good.
contemplative: The name arrives, then three small seeing-instructions. Good practice, but mostly a label on what came before.
stress: Names the label then gives instructions. Reinforces rather than tests. Give a case where seeing the Third Thing misleads.
gamedesigner: Names it Third Thing and then gives three concrete sightings to try: marriage, culture, habit. One term, used straight away.
structural: Naming what was just described, then three applications. Label is earned, and the fridge example places it. Still restatement.
satirist: Names the thing and applies it to fridge and marriage. A label plus uses; plain, but nothing is tested.
mythmaker: Names the Third Thing and gives three applications. A label plus examples restates the marriage. Give one scene, one face.

P0036>P0037.label: 2. The Third Thing
P0036>P0037.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0036] to paragraph [P0037] (chapter "2. The Third Thing")

modeler: 'Real like a coastline' asserted, not shown. A habit's reality needs stock and loop, not the claim.
skeptic: Restates the thesis under 'if you take one thing'. 'Same sense a coastline is real' is asserted, not shown. Pure emphasis.
clinician: 'A complete stop if you need one' is kind to a tired reader. The realness claim is asserted, not added to.
habit: Restates the claim as a 'complete stop'. Flatters rather than adds. Cut the reassurance.
contemplative: 'If you only take one thing' and 'complete stop' perform for the reader. The claim repeats and grows firmer without new support.
stress: Restates the claim as 'real like a coastline' and calls it complete. Likeness asserted as proof. Break-it condition missing.
gamedesigner: Restates 'it is real' with a coastline and triangle comparison but no new test. Assertion by repetition.
structural: 'Real like a coastline' restates the claim without new support. A bare assertion with a bold flag.
satirist: 'Complete stop if you need one' then 'stranger territory.' The coastline-is-real claim is asserted, not shown. Foma without a label.
mythmaker: A summary stop that re-states 'real like a coastline'. The pair stacks agreeing claims. Cut one.

modeler: P0037 names its own argument as likeness and promises to test the limit. That's the cost label the claim needed.
skeptic: Naming 'argument by likeness' and promising to test it is the calibration I want. Coastline-realness is still a loose analogue.
clinician: Strong. 'A complete stop if you need one' respects the tired reader, and 'argument by likeness' states the claim's real limit.
habit: Naming the Third Thing, then admitting it's an argument by likeness, supplies a real limit. Fridge-at-midnight is a usable cue.
contemplative: Naming the Third Thing, then restating it as real. The honest 'argument by likeness' helps, but the pair mostly repeats itself.
stress: Best seam here: P37 admits the claim is 'an argument by likeness' and promises a test. A claim that names its own weak point.
gamedesigner: Strong. The save-point paragraph names the claim as argument by likeness and promises a test. Honest, gives the reader a signal to track.
structural: P0037 re-asserts reality using coastline and triangle, not what P0036 just named. Candid about likeness, but restates. Tie it to the marriage/fridge cases.
satirist: Names the Third Thing, then owns up: 'an argument by likeness.' The confession is the third thing. 'Complete stop' is oddly pompous.
mythmaker: Naming the Third Thing, then admitting the realness claim is an argument by likeness. That honesty is the turn. Needs a person at the fridge.

P0037>P0038.label: 2. The Third Thing
P0037>P0038.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0037] to paragraph [P0038] (chapter "2. The Third Thing")

modeler: Kitchen warmth plus the new word symphysical, with the stakes of 'real' still unspent. One concept at a time.
skeptic: Kitchen analogy and 'symphysical' coinage. One new term, fairly handed over; analogy adds illustration, not evidence.
clinician: The kitchen answers 'is it real' without mysticism. But 'metaphysical' and 'symphysical' arrive together. Use one new term.
habit: Kitchen warmth is vivid, but metaphysical and symphysical arrive together. Pick one new word.
contemplative: The kitchen warmth gives the claim a body, and 'not metaphysical' sets its limit. Lovely. Still, the coined word is heavy.
stress: Kitchen warmth is a good concrete case. But 'symphysical' and 'metaphysical' arrive together; use one coined term at a time.
gamedesigner: Kitchen warmth is a good image, but metaphysical and symphysical arrive together. Difficulty spike; take one at a time.
structural: Kitchen analogy plus coined 'symphysical' lands when the claim is already made. Label arrives before it is used.
satirist: Holiday-kitchen warmth is a good, testable image: it leaves when they do. Then 'symphysical' lands as a coinage for a thing already shown.
mythmaker: The holiday kitchen is a lovely image. The warmth leaves when the cooks do. It earns 'symphysical', but I wish a cook had a name.

P0038>P0039.label: 2. The Third Thing
P0038>P0039.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0038] to paragraph [P0039] (chapter "2. The Third Thing")

modeler: Threshold adds a real limit to emergence; I like the ice. But emergence and threshold arrive together.
skeptic: Two new concepts (emergence, threshold) and the freezer image replaces the kitchen without a join. 'Worth remembering when stuck' is a comfort, not a claim.
clinician: Emergence plus threshold plus freezing point at once. The 'nothing seems to happen' payoff is useful. Split the two concepts.
habit: Emergence and threshold both land in one beat. Give emergence its own rep before threshold.
contemplative: The threshold idea is useful, but 'emergence' and 'threshold' land together. Give emergence a paragraph first.
stress: Threshold is a real limit on emergence. But 'emergence' and 'threshold' land in one paragraph. Split them.
gamedesigner: Freezing threshold adds something real: sudden change. But emergence is named on top of symphysical. Two new terms.
structural: The threshold limit is useful, but emergence and threshold both arrive back-to-back. Introduce one first.
satirist: Emergence and threshold arrive together. Ice is a real phenomenon but the symphysical gets a second name. One new word per seam.
mythmaker: Emergence plus a threshold in one turn. Freezing water works as a cost and a delay. Two new ideas land together.

P0039>P0040.label: 2. The Third Thing
P0039>P0040.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0039] to paragraph [P0040] (chapter "2. The Third Thing")

modeler: Threshold turned into advice about waiting; hedged with 'can be'. Best seam so far, though the delay is not quantified.
skeptic: Freezer threshold becomes 'you're on the wrong side of a threshold' for marriage and habit. Unfalsifiable comfort: nothing says how you would know.
clinician: Offers reassurance that a stuck marriage may be near a threshold. Unbacked; could keep someone in a failing situation. Add a limit.
habit: Ice threshold becomes 'why isn't this working yet' for marriages and habits; unbacked. Useful patience cue; name evidence.
contemplative: Kind and practical, but 'you are on the wrong side of a threshold' is asserted. It might equally be the wrong effort.
stress: Freezing becomes an excuse for no visible progress. Unfalsifiable: effort with no results still 'counts'. State how to tell accumulating from wasted.
gamedesigner: Threshold becomes the answer to 'why isn't this working.' Nice payoff, but ice to marriage claims invisible accumulation without support.
structural: Ice threshold to marriages 'about to flip' is a physics analogy stated as mechanism. Comfort without evidence. Say how a team would show it.
satirist: Freezing threshold becomes 'why isn't this working yet.' Kind, useful, but ice does not show a marriage is on the wrong side of anything.
mythmaker: Ice threshold becomes 'why isn't this working'. Real comfort, but a marriage's threshold is asserted from water. Say it's a hope.

P0040>P0041.label: 2. The Third Thing
P0040>P0041.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0040] to paragraph [P0041] (chapter "2. The Third Thing")

modeler: Chair arrives cold from a threshold. 'Likeness is not proof' is honest, but the scale jump is unprepared.
skeptic: Abrupt switch to chair solidity. P0041 hedges well ('likeness is not proof') but starts cold from the threshold point.
clinician: Palm-and-chair appears from nowhere, not from thresholds. The 'likeness is not proof' caveat is honest. Needs a bridge.
habit: Cold swap from patience to chairs. 'Likeness is not proof' is honest. Needs a bridge.
contemplative: From 'why isn't this working yet,' a hurting question, to palms on a chair. No acknowledgment. The argument jumps cold.
stress: Chair argument starts cold. Honest 'likeness is not proof', but then shifts the burden to the skeptic.
gamedesigner: Chair argument starts cold after the threshold comfort. It does hedge: likeness is not proof. Needs a hook back.
structural: Threshold talk jumps to palm-on-chair. Admitting 'likeness is not proof' is the best line, but the seam starts cold.
satirist: Hard turn from thresholds to chairs. The 'likeness is not proof' concession is excellent, but nothing is handed across.
mythmaker: The chair starts cold, a new proof with new terms. 'Likeness is not proof' is honest. Link it to the threshold hope.

modeler: Threshold waiting is accumulation; the chair is interaction force. 'Unseen' is the only bridge. Different mechanisms. Connect hidden stock to the chair, or split.
skeptic: Compassionate opener, but threshold-waiting does not lead to a chair's electrons. A new domain and new concept arrive on a fluent bridge. Fix: separate.
clinician: It acknowledges the waiting, but a chair's solidity doesn't show a marriage is accumulating unseen. The 'unseen' link slips. Bridge threshold to chair.
habit: Acknowledges the wait, then lurches to a chair. 'Most stubborn case' of what? The threshold never reaches the chair. Bridge it.
contemplative: It names the hurt of waiting, then jumps to the chair. How the chair's solidity eases the wait is never said.
stress: Thresholds and waiting jump to chair-solidity. 'Unseen thing' is wordplay; the chair is felt. Two ideas, smooth bridge, no logic. Cut or rebuild.
gamedesigner: Names the hurt of waiting, then offers the chair as proof of unseen solidity. Also flags that likeness is not proof. Good.
structural: Nice hurt acknowledgment, but threshold invisibility to chair solidity is a slide: waiting is not the same as relational reality. Name the bridge.
satirist: 'Waiting is hard, so consider your chair' is a smooth swerve. Threshold patience and electron repulsion are unrelated claims; the connective is the foma.
mythmaker: The hurt of waiting is acknowledged, and the palm on the chair is a fine image. But a chair isn't an unseen threshold; the bridge fakes the link.

modeler: Nice: threshold waiting meets chair as unseen load-bearing product, and likeness-is-not-proof is stated. Still missing the accumulating stock and delay.
skeptic: Names the waiting, then offers the chair, and concedes likeness is not proof or accumulation. The 'need a reason to withhold it' move still shifts the burden of proof.
clinician: Names the hurt of waiting first, then hedges: likeness is not proof effort is accumulating. 'Most stubborn case' is vague about what it is stubborn against.
habit: Names the hurt of waiting, then gives a chair you can press on, with 'likeness is not proof' as the limit. Good. Add one-minute palm test.
contemplative: Opens by naming the pain of waiting, then offers the chair as proof of unseen load-bearing, and admits likeness isn't proof. Calm and honest.
stress: Names the hurt of waiting, then offers the chair and concedes likeness isn't proof. Honest. Still a long step from chair to my effort.
gamedesigner: Best seam here: acknowledges the wait, then the chair gives a concrete test and a limit ('likeness is not proof'). Reader can predict and check.
structural: Acknowledges the wait, then gives a real counter-limit ('likeness is not proof'). But the chair analogy plus 'you'd need a reason to withhold' shifts the burden of proof.
satirist: Bryson move: palm on chair, electrons, then the dry admission that likeness isn't proof. Hurt named first. The last sentence survives the bar test.
mythmaker: Lovely. Names the hurt of waiting, then hands you a palm on a chair. Image sticks, and it admits likeness is not proof.

P0041>P0042.label: 2. The Third Thing
P0041>P0042.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0041] to paragraph [P0042] (chapter "2. The Third Thing")

modeler: Paired forces deepen the chair claim. But 'you cannot affect without being affected' leaps from physics to relationships.
skeptic: Newton's third law stretched to 'you cannot affect without being affected' in all relationships. Physics to interpersonal life is claimed, not argued.
clinician: Paired forces to 'you cannot affect without being affected, in exact proportion'. A physics-to-relationship leap, and risky for a reader who blames themselves.
habit: Physics pairs become 'you cannot affect without being affected'. Law slides to relationships. Two new ideas; give it a check.
contemplative: Chair becomes paired forces. Good. But 'you cannot affect without being affected' slides from physics to every relationship.
stress: Forces in pairs sharpens the chair case. But 'no one-way push anywhere, in exact proportion' is physics stretched to people.
gamedesigner: Third-law jump: forces come in pairs, so no one-way push in any relationship. Physics stretched to claim everything, with new terms stacking.
structural: Third law of motion becomes 'you cannot affect without being affected.' Forces in physics aren't power in an office; ignores asymmetry of who holds the lever.

skeptic: 'Nothing required' against 'one claim' is a good tension, with hedged examples. But Banner, Self, Dyad, Skein and nested loop arrive in one paragraph.
clinician: Contrast with 'requires nothing' is neat, but Self, Dyad, Skein, Banner and nested loop all arrive together. Trim terms.
habit: 'Nothing requires Part One' versus 'one claim it rests on' is a real limit. But Self, Dyad, Skein and Banner all land together. Defer two.
contemplative: The contrast is good: no belief required, one claim needed. But Banner, Dyad, Skein and nested loop all land together. Too much.
stress: 'Does rest on one claim' answers 'nothing required.' But Banner, Self, Dyad, Skein and nested loop pile in at once. Defer terms.
gamedesigner: 'Nothing required' vs 'one claim' is a good contrast. Then Banner, three scales and a nested loop arrive together. Rulebook dump.
structural: No prerequisites, then one prerequisite claim: a good contrast. But Banner, Self, Dyad, Skein and nested loop land together. Cut to one term.
satirist: 'Rests on nothing' to 'rests on one claim' is a clean turn. Then Banner, Dyad, Skein and nested loop arrive in one gulp. Pace it.
mythmaker: 'Needn't settle Part One' becomes 'rests on one claim'. Good turn, but Banner, Self, Dyad, Skein and nested loop all pour in at once.

P0187>P0188.label: PART TWO — HOW TO PRACTICE (opener)
P0187>P0188.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0187] to paragraph [P0188] (chapter "PART TWO — HOW TO PRACTICE (opener)")

modeler: Scales cross four moves into a grid, which is useful. But five coined terms in one paragraph. Introduce the moves one at a time.
