clinician: Four moves plus Hold land at once on top of Banner, Self, Dyad and Skein. Too many terms; introduce one set at a time.
habit: Four moves plus Hold land at once, right after three scales. Useful list, but a second concept before the first is used.
contemplative: Four moves plus Hold land in one go, right after the scales. The scroll-and-walk example helps. Introduce the moves one by one.
stress: Four moves plus Hold dumped on top of three scales. Too many new terms across one join. Stagger them.
gamedesigner: Five new move names, then 'any move works at any scale' asserted. Difficulty spike. Teach one move, play it, then add.
structural: Five moves arrive immediately after three scales. Plant, tend, thin, hold all named before any is used.
satirist: Four moves plus Hold, each capitalized, right after three scales. Vocabulary dump. The scroll-to-walk example is the only part that lives.
mythmaker: Five new move names right after three scales. The scroll-to-walk example helps, but this is a glossary. Stage the moves across the week.

modeler: Scales times moves is a real structure. But four moves plus Hold land at once, before the scales have been used.
skeptic: The scales are made of moves, which is a real link. But Look, Plant, Tend, Thin and Hold arrive on top of three scale terms. Stagger them.
clinician: Scales times moves is real structure, but Look, Plant, Tend, Thin and Hold arrive at once. Introduce moves one at a time.
habit: Scales times moves is a useful grid, and 'those scales' carries over. Five new terms at once (Look, Plant, Tend, Thin, Hold). Stage them.
contemplative: The scales hold the four moves, and the link is clear. But four moves plus Hold in one breath is heavy. Offer them one at a time.
stress: Scales times moves is useful. But Look, Plant, Tend, Thin and Hold arrive straight after three scales. Five terms before any is used.
gamedesigner: Scales hand off to the four moves. But Look, Plant, Tend, Thin and Hold land in one paragraph. Too many new verbs at once.
structural: Scales times moves is a real grid, but five new terms (four moves plus Hold) arrive before the scale terms are used.
satirist: Scales times moves is a real grid. But Look, Plant, Tend, Thin and Hold in one paragraph is a vocabulary dump. Introduce moves one at a time.
mythmaker: Scales times moves makes a real grid. But Look, Plant, Tend, Thin and Hold arrive hot on the heels of three scale names. Too many props.

P0189>P0190.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0189>P0190.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0189] to paragraph [P0190] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Epigraph then a safety notice. No relation on the page; the shift is abrupt, even if the notice is needed.
skeptic: Epigraph on seven days, then a safety note. Unrelated. Each stands alone; no relation is named.
clinician: Epigraph to care disclaimer. I like the disclaimer's early placement and plain wording. Relation to the quote is loose.
habit: Epigraph then a care disclaimer; tonal jump with no link. Move the disclaimer, keep the quote near Day 1.
contemplative: A quotation, then a safety note. Both are kind; neither uses the other.
stress: Epigraph, then safety note. Disclaimer is right but disconnected from the quote. Fine as boilerplate.
gamedesigner: Epigraph on watching, then a care disclaimer. Right content, wrong spot; no link between them.
structural: Epigraph on watching, then a treatment disclaimer. No relation. The hurt is acknowledged, but the join is arbitrary.
satirist: A cute epigraph, then a care disclaimer. The tonal swerve is abrupt. The disclaimer is right; the placement is clumsy.
mythmaker: Epigraph about watching, then a care disclaimer. The disclaimer rightly names the hurt but doesn't connect to the quote.

modeler: Epigraph to treatment warning is a cold jump in register. Safety note is right but unprepared by the quote.
skeptic: 'Watching is not helping' answers the epigraph's 'watch' directly. The safety turn is announced, not sneaked in.
clinician: 'Watch' hands to 'watching is not helping.' Safest seam here: names the limit and points to a trained person.
habit: 'Watch' in the epigraph gets its limit: 'Watching is not helping.' Names the hurt plainly, with no bypass. Strong seam.
contemplative: 'Watching is not helping' states a true limit simply. It is a small aphorism, but it earns its place.
stress: 'Watching is not helping' limits the epigraph's promise. Names the struggling reader. Slightly aphoristic, but it carries a real boundary.
gamedesigner: 'Watch' in the epigraph becomes 'watching is not helping'. Limit set before day one. Honest and well placed.
structural: 'Watching is not helping' is a genuine limit on the epigraph, and it names the struggling reader. Best seam in the opener.
satirist: 'Watch' in the epigraph meets 'Watching is not helping'. The limit arrives before the first day and names the struggle. Rare honest fence.
mythmaker: 'Watching is not helping' caps the epigraph's promise with its limit. Warm, and it names the struggling reader. That's the Beard in the room.

P0190>P0191.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0190>P0191.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0190] to paragraph [P0191] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Safety note, then 'do not adopt everything.' Unrelated. The second begins cold with 'that would be the exact mistake.'
skeptic: Safety note, then 'do not adopt everything.' Both fine, but separate. No handoff.
clinician: Sensible pacing warning after the safety note. Two separate cautions; the second does not depend on the first.
habit: Safety note then a pacing note. Both fine, neither builds on the other. Put pacing before the warning.
contemplative: Care note, then 'do not adopt everything'. Reasonable, but the two sit side by side.
stress: Safety note, then 'don't do everything.' Independent items stacked; either could drop. Reorder so the cautions sit together.
gamedesigner: Care disclaimer followed by 'don't adopt everything'. Cold turn; 'exact mistake the book warns against' is unbacked here.
structural: Disclaimer to 'don't adopt everything'. 'Exact mistake the whole book warns against' is asserted, not shown.
satirist: Disclaimer, then 'don't adopt everything.' Different subjects. A reader couldn't say what was handed across.
mythmaker: Disclaimer to 'don't adopt everything' with no join. The disclaimer is right; place it at the end of the opening instead.

modeler: 'Same care applies to pace' carries the caution frame, but it stacks two cautions. Pace claim is unsupported by the first.
skeptic: 'The same care applies to pace' bridges two unlike warnings with a connective and nothing else. 'The mistake the whole book warns against' is an unearned absolute.
clinician: 'Same care applies' is a bare connective stacking a second caution. Pace advice is fine but a clinician wants a concrete step.
habit: Two cautions stacked under 'the same care'. Smooth, but the pace warning could be dropped without loss to the safety note. Make pace a concrete daily limit.
contemplative: 'The same care applies' is a bare bridge from treatment to pace. Two unrelated cautions. Separate them or find the true link.
stress: 'Same care' is a bare connective gluing a crisis warning to a pacing tip. Different registers, no shared relation. Separate them.
gamedesigner: Two cautions stacked. 'The same care' is a thin hinge. Pace warning could stand alone or fold into the week's rules.
structural: 'The same care applies to pace' bolts pacing onto a safety warning. Two stacked cautions with a connective doing the work.
satirist: Two cautions in a row, joined by 'same care'. Pace is not obviously the same kind of care as treatment. Stacked, not combined.
mythmaker: Two cautions side by side; swap them and nothing breaks. 'The same care' is a thin bridge. Make the pace warning cost someone something.

modeler: 'Because this is a practice not treatment' fakes a cause for 'keep it small'. Nothing on the page links the two. Show the energy-and-attention budget that makes sprinting fail.
skeptic: Disclaimer then 'Because this is a practice and not treatment' reuses it, but the pair stacks caution on caution. 'Likely tired' is hedged, honest; cut one.
clinician: Treatment disclaimer then 'keep it small' is a real limit-then-pacing pair; 'because' is earned. Safe for a bad day, small step named. Good.
habit: 'Because this is a practice and not treatment' carries the warning into a limit: keep it small. Still no concrete first step, but the link is honest.
contemplative: 'Because this is a practice and not treatment' picks up the note honestly. Small steps follow gently. The pair is plain and livable; slightly stacked.
stress: 'Because this is a practice and not treatment, keep it small' is a smooth non sequitur. Treatment status implies nothing about pace. State the real reason for going small.
gamedesigner: Treatment disclaimer hands 'practice not treatment' to the keep-it-small rule; a plausible link. But the two don't test each other. Pacing advice could stand alone.
structural: 'Not treatment' justifies 'keep it small'; the second uses the first's practice-versus-treatment frame. Clear cause, even register. Still, 'likely tired' is asserted, not shown.
satirist: 'Because this is a practice and not treatment, keep it small' is a tidy non sequitur. Disclaimer and pacing advice are separate; drop the 'because'.
mythmaker: 'Because this is a practice and not treatment' doesn't cause 'keep it small'; the connective carries a non sequitur. Give a reader who overdid it, with a cost.

P0191>P0192.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0191>P0192.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0191] to paragraph [P0192] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Warning against one big stroke, then the seven small ones as the remedy. Prescription answers the problem.
skeptic: Don't do everything, so seven days. But 'you will have done all of it' contradicts 191 and promises 'everything you need,' unearned.
clinician: Do-not-do-it-all turns into a concrete small plan. Gentle and bounded. Warning and plan agree rather than test each other.
habit: Don't adopt everything, so here is seven days, one thing a day. Good handoff, clear pace. Nice and small.
contemplative: Don't do everything, so do seven days of small things. A smooth, honest handoff, mostly a restatement.
stress: Warning against everything at once, then 'so: seven days.' Clear step, but plain consequence, no new content.
gamedesigner: Don't do it all, so do seven small days. Warning becomes a concrete plan. Good tutorial pacing.
structural: 'So: seven days' follows from 'not all at once'. Clear step, and the same point twice.
satirist: Don't do it all; here's the small version. A constraint producing a plan. Plain and checkable.
mythmaker: The warning against one deliberate stroke becomes the seven small days. Problem and answer each need the other. 'You will have done all of it' overpromises slightly.

P0192>P0193.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0192>P0193.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0192] to paragraph [P0193] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Plan then criterion. The week is for seeing, not changing. A success test makes it measurable.
skeptic: The week is for seeing, not changing a habit. Tempers 192's promise and says how to tell if it worked. 'Selling something' is a dig, but honest.
clinician: Plan hands to what the week is for and what it cannot do. Honest limit protects a discouraged reader. Good.
habit: Says what the week is for and what it can't do. Honest limit, and 'whether you can see a pattern' is a testable aim.
contemplative: The week states its limit: it will not change a habit, only show whether you can see one. Plain and trustworthy.
stress: Candid: a week cannot change a habit, only test whether you can see. Names the success criterion. Willing to be wrong.
gamedesigner: Plan, then what the week is for and isn't. States the win condition: can you see a loop. Great.
structural: Plan then purpose: the week tests seeing, not habit change. A usable success criterion. Honest about limits.
satirist: 'Any book promising otherwise is selling something' is the right bar-talk. The week's purpose is limited honestly. Good.
mythmaker: Sets out what the week is for, honest about what it can't do. This is the test the days will be judged against. Good.

P0193>P0194.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0193>P0194.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0193] to paragraph [P0194] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Purpose, then the first measurable step: catch it three times. Capacity to see becomes an operation.
skeptic: Purpose then Day 1 enacts it. 'Intervening early produces guilt' is hedged but unsupported. Instruction follows rationale; nothing emerges.
clinician: Purpose, seeing a pattern, becomes Day 1 with a countable goal: three catches. No judging. Strong for a bad day.
habit: Day 1 is the capacity to see made concrete: notice three times. Beautiful. Doesn't add much beyond doing it.
contemplative: Purpose, then the first act. Notice one loop, change nothing, three times. This I could do today in my kitchen.
stress: Purpose then first task. Clean step. 'Intervening early tends to produce guilt' is unbacked, but hedged.
gamedesigner: Goal becomes Day 1 with a countable feedback signal: catch it three times. Textbook onboarding.
structural: Purpose to Day 1 task: noticing is the capacity. Instruction follows rationale. Expected, not emergent.
satirist: Purpose, then the first day's task. Normal instruction flow. Day 1 delivers what the purpose paragraph promised and no more.
mythmaker: Purpose then procedure. Day 1 does serve 'can you see', but stays instruction. Caught-three-times is a fine concrete bar.

P0194>P0195.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0194>P0195.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0194] to paragraph [P0195] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Day 1 to Day 2: habits to trees, with no handoff. The jump of subject has no stated link until the next paragraph.
skeptic: Habit-noticing to trees with no tie. 'Each resting on the one before' is claimed, not shown. 'Every day of your life' presumes the reader.
clinician: Day 1 habit to trees is a topic switch with no stated reason yet. A new object arrives cold. Add a line on why.
habit: Jump from habits to trees with no bridge from Day 1. Say why a fern helps. Cue is fine: out the window.
contemplative: Day 2 starts fresh, with no link to Day 1's habit. Add one line saying what Day 1 left unsaid.
stress: Habit to branching trees with no bridge on the page. Day 2 starts cold; the reason waits for the next paragraph.
gamedesigner: Habit-watching to tree-gazing with no bridge. Reason only arrives a paragraph later. Put a one-line why up front.
structural: Habit to trees with no bridge. Day 2 starts cold; the link comes only in 0196. Reorder.
satirist: Habit-watching to fern-gazing with no stated link yet. The reader hangs until the next paragraph explains the day.
mythmaker: From a personal habit to trees and rivers with a cold start. 'You've walked past this pattern' is lovely but doesn't carry Day 1.

modeler: Watching a loop in yourself, then the same watching where nothing's at stake. Contrast does the work; the yesterday handoff is explicit.
skeptic: 'Same watching on something with nothing at stake' hands Day 1's skill across and says what changes. A clean, stated step.
clinician: Inward watching with stakes, then outward watching with none. Good rehearsal logic, small step, no guilt.
habit: 'Yesterday you watched a loop in yourself; today, something with nothing at stake' is a clean contrast. Cue, duration and trace-a-branch are all there. Ship it.
contemplative: 'Yesterday you watched... today something with nothing at stake.' A plain, kind handoff you could live today.
stress: 'Same watching on something with nothing at stake' is a stated rehearsal logic. Clear step, even register, one new idea.
gamedesigner: Yesterday's watching moves to a no-stakes target. Clean level two. I know what I did and what's next.
structural: Yesterday's watching becomes today's nothing-at-stake rehearsal; the reason is on the page. Clean step.
satirist: Self-watching, then watching something with nothing at stake. The contrast gives day two a reason. 'Almost certainly' is properly hedged.
mythmaker: Yesterday's loop in you, today's tree with nothing at stake: low-stakes rehearsal. A clean step. Day 1's habit gets a face, Day 2's tree is just wood.

P0195>P0196.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0195>P0196.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0195] to paragraph [P0196] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Explains why branching practice matters: pattern before object. The eye training bridges to the inner loop.
skeptic: Explains why the easy day matters. But branching practice training habit-seeing is asserted, not shown. Lovely, and I have no reason to believe it.
clinician: Explains why the easy day matters and ties outward seeing to inward seeing. Needed, and gentle: the one bad night versus its shape.
habit: Explains why the easy tree day isn't filler: pattern before object. Ties the day to the inward use. Good.
contemplative: The branching exercise, then why it matters: pattern before object. Honest about being the easy day.
stress: Exercise then rationale: pattern before object, one bad night versus a month's shape. Each justifies the other.
gamedesigner: Explains why the easy day isn't filler: pattern before object. Pays off the odd exercise.
structural: Rationale arrives and changes the exercise: pattern-before-object is the point. 'Not filler' preempts the objection.
satirist: The tree exercise explains itself: it trains pattern-before-object. 'Only a handful' of splits keeps the wonder honest.
mythmaker: Explains why the easy day isn't filler: pattern before object, turned inward. The one bad night versus a month of them is the cost.

P0196>P0197.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0196>P0197.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0196] to paragraph [P0197] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Step forward to naming beats on Day 1's habit. Handoff is clean, but it is a sequence, not an emergence.
skeptic: Day 3 returns to Day 1's habit and names beats. Four terms at once but announced. Step in a sequence, nothing emergent.
clinician: Trained eye returns to Day 1's habit with four beats to name. Builds on the earlier step; keeps it non-interventionist.
habit: Returns to Day 1's habit and adds four beats. Clear step, one new idea. Pure sequence, but runnable tomorrow.
contemplative: Returns to Day 1's habit, but four named beats arrive at once. Give one beat a day, or one example.
stress: Returns to Day 1's habit; four beats are the one new idea. Sequence is clear, but it is instruction.
gamedesigner: Eye trained on trees, turned back on Day 1's habit with four beats. Good level-two escalation.
structural: Loop-vs-event idea carried into Day 3. One new term set (four beats). Good, but still instructional sequence.
satirist: Return to Day 1's habit with four beats added. Fine sequencing; one new term. A step, not a synthesis.
mythmaker: Returns to Day 1's habit with the four beats, a good loop closing. But it is sequence, not a new thing between them.

P0197>P0198.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0197>P0198.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0197] to paragraph [P0198] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Watch during versus meet afterward: afterward nothing is left to steer. Supplies the why and the timing, which is where delays hide.
skeptic: 198 restates 'not stopping, only watching.' Merge into 197. 'Nothing left to steer' afterward is a vivid unsupported line.
clinician: Says why watching beats meeting it afterward. Brief and backed. Not a self-blame pivot.
habit: Not stopping it; watching a live loop versus meeting the aftermath. The contrast gives the reason. Short and good.
contemplative: Watching a loop run versus meeting its aftermath: the empty bag, the hour gone. Short and true.
stress: Explains why not stopping yet: afterward nothing is left to steer. Mostly restatement; the empty-bag example helps.
gamedesigner: Why you don't stop it yet: afterward nothing is left to steer. Clear, short, earned.
structural: Second paragraph gives the cost of the unwatched loop: afterward nothing is left to steer. Small but earned.
satirist: Why watch without stopping: afterward there is nothing left to steer. Small, clear payoff for the instruction.
mythmaker: Watching versus meeting afterward: empty bag, hour gone. A cost named in two images. Clear and earned.

P0198>P0199.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0198>P0199.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0198] to paragraph [P0199] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Not stopping it, then interrupt it: a reversal that the first paragraph never prepared. Order is a plan, not a build.
skeptic: From 'not stopping it' to interrupting once is a stated progression. Adds a breath mantra. Sequence, no emergence.
clinician: From not stopping to ten breaths is an escalation with a concrete step. Sequence, not a Third Thing.
habit: After 'don't stop it' comes 'interrupt once'. Deliberate reversal, ten breaths with a cue. Very doable.
contemplative: From 'not stopping it' to 'interrupt it'. The turn is quiet but the link isn't spoken. Say why now.
stress: Watching, then interrupting. Sensible progression, but a step rather than a Third Thing.
gamedesigner: Watching, then first intervention. Good rising difficulty. Breath mantra is cryptic but one new thing.
structural: 'Still not stopping' sets up Day 4's stop. Step relation clear, but just next-in-list.
satirist: Day 3 said don't stop it; Day 4 says interrupt it. The breath mantra goes mystic. Mild step, no new meaning.
mythmaker: Moves from 'not stopping it' to interrupt with ten breaths. Fair step, but nothing yet explains the switch; the next paragraph does.

P0199>P0200.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0199>P0200.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0199] to paragraph [P0200] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Instruction plus mechanism: attention is a limited stock the loop draws on. Napkin-worthy. Add the delay.
skeptic: Gives a mechanism, but 'competes for the machinery the loop was using' is fluent claim without evidence. Say 'plausibly' and cite or test it.
clinician: Gives the mechanism for why breath-counting works and says a small irritation is enough. Good: low bar for a bad day.
habit: Gives the mechanism for why breath works: attention is limited. Backed, modest, small-irritation advice. Excellent.
contemplative: 'Mechanical, not mystical' claims a competition for attention as settled. Hedge it or cite it; the small-irritation advice is wise.
stress: Gives a mechanism for the breath, with 'small one teaches better.' But 'competes for the machinery' is asserted. Soften or cite.
gamedesigner: Gives the mechanism, attention is limited, and a small trigger is a better teacher. Testable on yourself.
structural: Mechanism claim ('competing for the machinery') stated confidently with nothing behind it. Hedge or cite.
satirist: 'Mechanical, not mystical' is the right instinct, but the attention-competition claim is asserted without one study, number or name.
mythmaker: Instruction then honest mechanism, and 'mechanical, not mystical' is stated plainly. The queue twitch is a small, real face.

P0200>P0201.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0200>P0201.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0200] to paragraph [P0201] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Day 5 starts a new subject with no handoff. Day headings carry the structure; the seam does not.
skeptic: From irritation in a queue to a month-old stuck project with no bridge. Scale and topic jump. Cold open.
clinician: Interrupting loops to stuck-for-a-month is a fresh topic. Stuck for a month may feed rumination; add a bound.
habit: New day, new task, no handoff from breath. Fine as a day break. Pick the stuck thing today, before breakfast.
contemplative: A new day begins with no tie to the breath. Each day is a stand-alone card.
stress: Day 5 starts cold on a month-long stuck thing. Jump from breath to diagnosis, new frame, no bridge.
gamedesigner: Breath day ends; stuck-for-a-month day starts cold. Different scale and subject. Needs a hinge.
structural: Spiral breathing to a month-stuck thing. Cold jump of scale and term. Needs a bridge sentence.
satirist: From the breath to 'stuck for a month' with no bridge. Starts a new exercise cold.
mythmaker: Breath to a month-long stuck thing: a big scale and subject jump with no handoff. Name what the breath showed about being stuck.

modeler: Seconds-long loop, then months-long loop: a delay contrast I like. The breath's mechanism gives the scale shift a footing.
skeptic: Seconds-long loop versus month-long loop is a real scale contrast, and Day 5 uses Day 4's breath. Good seam.
clinician: Seconds-long loop to months-long one is a clear zoom. Day 5 stuckness is gently framed.
habit: Seconds-long loop to months-long loop is a real contrast and a clear step. Add a cue: when in the day do they pick the stuck thing?
contemplative: Seconds then months is a clear change of scale, and the opening line says so. The turn is prepared and light.
stress: Seconds versus months sets up why a different diagnosis is needed. Brief, plain. Could say what that change implies.
gamedesigner: Seconds-long loop vs months-long loop. Good difficulty ramp, and the contrast is the third thing. Hook for day five.
structural: Seconds versus months is a visible change of timescale, stated up front. Works, though it is still all private.
satirist: Seconds-long loop to month-long loop; the handoff is plain and the scale change is stated. Clean step.
mythmaker: Seconds-long loop, then months-long loop: the contrast tells you the tool must change. A pleasing callback. The stuck person is still unnamed.

P0201>P0202.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding
P0201>P0202.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0201] to paragraph [P0202] (chapter "1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding")

modeler: Question then its three-way answer. Fine mechanics, but an instruction followed by its list is stacking, not a third thing.
skeptic: Heading then list. Capacity, Understanding, Want come directly. Mechanical handoff; nothing emerges.
clinician: Three terms land bolded at once with nothing used yet. Stacked list. Give a one-line example of each.
habit: Three absent things listed as promised. Two coined labels in bold. It's list delivery, not a third thing.
contemplative: The three absent things come as one stack of bold labels. Capacity, Understanding and Want need an example each.
stress: Three diagnoses land at once with no worked case. Capacity, Understanding, Want need one example each.
gamedesigner: Prompt then list. Three new terms land in a line: capacity, understanding, want. Spike.
structural: Prompt then the three options. Pure list setup; fine, fused would be tighter.
satirist: Three bold labels at once: Capacity, Understanding, Want. Defined in a line each. Okay as list, but three concepts before one gets used.
mythmaker: Question then the three answers. Neat list, but the pair is setup plus definitions; no stake yet.

modeler: The colon sets up the list and the list answers. Just one continued item; merge into one paragraph.
skeptic: A lead-in to a list, not a seam. Three new terms (Capacity, Understanding, Want) arrive at once, before any is used.
clinician: A colon unpacked into a list; the second is dependent on the first but adds nothing emergent. Fine as structure.
habit: A lead-in and its list. Neither says more than the other; just merge them. Fine as a 'which is missing' one-question rep.
contemplative: One thought split by a colon across two paragraphs. Nothing emerges beyond the list. Join them.
stress: A list split across two paragraphs; merge them. Three coined definitions land together, and 'it isn't yours to want' is cryptic.
gamedesigner: Colon, then list: one unit split in two. Capacity, Understanding, Want arrive bare, no worked example. Spike; show one case.
structural: A colon-split setup and list. Merge them; nothing is said across the break.
satirist: A colon, then the list of three terms. Merge them. Capacity, Understanding and Want land at once in bold; that's three props.
mythmaker: The second paragraph just finishes the first's colon. Merge them; nothing is lost but a line break. Give the stuck person a name.

P0202>P0203.label: 1. Start Here: The One-Week Onboarding

modeler: When then how. Pairing is functional. Nothing beyond the sum.

contemplative: Moment of use, then naming the four beats. 'The only place a loop can be changed from' is stated as fact. Soften.

gamedesigner: Catch-yourself moment then the four-beat move. Playable. Ties back to Day 3.

clinician: Real limit: beats aren't equally reachable. But 'craving comes from the meaning you assign' is asserted without support.
habit: Names the beats, then says which beat is reachable. Good limit. But craving's interpretive step and 'meaning you assign' land together.
contemplative: Where you can reach in the loop is a useful idea. But 'craving is produced by the meaning you assign' is unsupported.
stress: Adds a counter-point: beats are not equally reachable. But 'craving is produced by the meaning you assign' is stated as settled.
gamedesigner: Beats aren't equally reachable; good limit. But 'craving is produced by the meaning you assign' is asserted as fact.
structural: 0223 limits 0222's 'naming is enough': beats are not equally reachable, and the interpretive beat is the one. Real addition.

mythmaker: Names which beats you can reach and which you can't, and why craving is where naming bites. A real limit.

modeler: Gives the success picture: a cue arrives and nothing follows. A concrete end-state the reach claim implies.

clinician: Gives a picture of success: a cue arrives and nothing follows. Realistic and undramatic. Helps the reader know what done looks like.
habit: Says what success looks like: a cue arrives, nothing follows. Rare and useful. Tied to the craving beat.
contemplative: What success looks like: a cue arrives and nothing follows. Quiet, specific, true to experience. A good picture.
stress: Says what success looks like (a cue arrives, nothing follows). Concrete and checkable-ish. Tightest pair in the chapter.
gamedesigner: Gives the win state: a cue arrives and nothing follows. A real feedback signal.
structural: Gives the practice a success picture: a cue arrives and nothing follows. Builds on the reachable beat.
satirist: Reachable beat, then what success looks like: a cue arrives and nothing follows. Concrete, undramatic, honest.
mythmaker: Success as 'nothing follows' completes the interpretive-beat point. Quiet, honest, and it names why people miss it.

P0224>P0225.label: 2. The Daily Practices
P0224>P0225.desc: the seam from paragraph [P0224] to paragraph [P0225] (chapter "2. The Daily Practices")

modeler: Kahneman's two systems as mechanism. But 'naming brings the slow system in' is asserted, not shown; no delay or limit.
skeptic: Success description to a Kahneman mechanism with no link. 'Naming brings the slow system in' is an authority-borrowed assertion.
clinician: Kahneman's two systems arrive as a fresh explanation not tied to the success picture. Reasonable, but the handoff is thin.
habit: Success state then Kahneman's two systems as mechanism. Reasonable, but a new framework enters a seam that was concrete.
contemplative: Kahneman and two systems enter right after the quiet success state. Explanation arrives before it is wanted. Trim.
stress: Kahneman's two systems land cold after a success description. 'Naming brings in slow thinking' is claimed, not shown. A borrowed prop.
gamedesigner: Kahneman's two systems arrive on 'what it's doing'. Tied to naming, not the success state just given.
structural: Kahneman's two systems arrive as the mechanism with no tie to the quiet-success state. 'Naming demands slow system' is asserted.
satirist: Success-as-nothing jumps to Kahneman's two systems. Name-dropped authority for an asserted mechanism. Bryson would show the study.
mythmaker: Success-as-nothing and the Kahneman system split never meet. The 'small tax on autopilot' is a fine line without a bridge.

modeler: 'Nothing follows' success isn't what Kahneman's slow system explains. Second starts a fresh mechanism cold; tie it to the quiet-state test.
skeptic: Kahneman's two systems start cold after a success criterion. Mapping 'naming' onto System 2 is asserted. Tie it to the 'nothing follows' state.
clinician: Success-as-nothing-follows gets a mechanism, but 'naming brings the slow system in' is stated as fact. Hedge it.
habit: Success-as-nothing-follows never gets picked up; Kahneman starts fresh. Tie the slow-system second back to 'nothing follows' or swap the order.
contemplative: Success as quiet registering, then the why. But 'brings the slow system in' is asserted flatly, with 'tax' and 'currency' wordplay. State it plainly.
stress: Mechanism for the success state. But 'naming brings in the slow system' is stated as fact, not hedged. Where it fails: fast habits.
gamedesigner: Success-state described, then a mechanism. But 'naming brings the slow system in' is asserted, not shown. Hedge it or give a test.
structural: Success-as-nothing-following gets a Kahneman explanation. Template header restarts cold, two metaphors and a famous name pile up, and the cause is asserted. Tie it back.
satirist: Registering a cue without moving gets a mechanism. But Kahneman's two systems is stated as settled cause, and 'tax on autopilot' is wordplay doing the lifting.
mythmaker: Success as nothing-follows, then Kahneman's two systems from a cold start. Neither needs the other. Open the mechanism with the quiet moment.

modeler: Good: target state, then the mechanism, hedged ('seems'). But System 1/2, attention as currency and the choice window all land at once, and no loop or delay is drawn.
skeptic: Success-state then mechanism is a real handoff, but 'seems to bring slow system in' rests on a popularized dichotomy; Kahneman, tax and choice-gap land together.
clinician: Quiet state is handed over, but Kahneman's slow system arrives as an unproven mechanism ('seems to') plus a new concept. Explaining reasons may invite over-analysis; keep it practical.
habit: Quiet state gets a mechanism, good, but Kahneman, two systems and attention-tax land together. Too many new ideas; and still no instruction on what to do.
contemplative: The quiet state is picked up, but 'seems to' hedges a mechanism borrowed from Kahneman. Say you do not know it, and the tax image decorates.
stress: Mechanism for the quiet state is a real payoff. But Kahneman's split is borrowed pop-science, and 'this is how' then 'seems' is confidence not backed. Cite or test.
gamedesigner: Quiet state is the goal; mechanism explains how naming reaches it. Nice pairing, but Kahneman's two systems arrive cold, and 'seems to' hedges a hard-claimed mechanism.
structural: Quiet state is explained by Kahneman's two systems, a real handoff. But 'seems to' hedges a mechanism the page never backs; Kahneman plus attention-tax adds two concepts.
satirist: Quiet state, then how it's reached, with Kahneman named and 'seems to' hedged. Bryson test passed. Naming-as-slow-system is still one study short of proof.
mythmaker: Quiet state answered by its mechanism, hedged honestly with 'seems'. But Kahneman's two systems and the phone buzz land together. Hold the buzz back.

contemplative: A new practice cue after the Kahneman account. Clean edge, nothing carried.

skeptic: 'The same second into your own voice' carries the handoff. Otherwise it is a new practice, not a payoff, so nothing new emerges from the pair.
clinician: 'Same second' carries over; harsh-with-yourself moment acknowledged. A new practice, not an emergent claim.
habit: 'That same second' carries the pause into your own voice. Two named moments (hard conversation, harsh self-talk) give cues. Good next rep.
contemplative: 'That same second into your own voice' hands over the second. Then a new practice begins; nothing joint emerges.
stress: 'That same second' extends the idea to speech. A new practice, not a new result. Neither paragraph gains from the other.
gamedesigner: 'That same second' links practices, but it's a new section header more than a seam. Nothing emerges beyond sequence.
structural: 'That same second' carries across to a new practice. Plain handoff, one new term, no new claim.
satirist: 'Same second' into 'your own voice' is a decent hinge, but this is the next practice in a menu. Pair adds no joint claim.
mythmaker: 'That same second' carries over, but Seeding is a new practice, not a consequence. Stacked tools. The buzz-and-hand image doesn't come back.

clinician: When-line to the one question. Asking about the thought's growth rather than truth avoids a rumination trap. Concrete.
habit: Two moments become one question: seed of fear or care? One question to carry all day. Love it.
contemplative: When to use it, then the question: 'seed of fear or care?' Simple, warm, and I could ask it at breakfast.
stress: Use-moments then the question. Clear step, but it's a recipe pair with no test or cost.
gamedesigner: Two moments to use it, then the question: fear or care? Clear trigger-and-move pair.
structural: Use-when then the question. Smooth sequence; seeds-not-true-or-false is a nice small move.
satirist: Use-case then the question. The seed-of-fear versus seed-of-care line is clean. Plain instruction.
mythmaker: Use-moments then the question. 'Seed of fear or care' is a sticky image, but the pair is trigger then instruction.

gamedesigner: Question then optional spoken lines. Lines echo seed/field, but it's just instruction stacking; no test or cost emerges. Add a signal for whether it worked.

modeler: Mechanism arrives as 'simply what repetition does'. Pathway claim is unbacked; no delay, no limit on the loop. Draw the stock.
skeptic: Mechanism does explain the lines, but 'simply what repetition does to a mental pathway' is asserted with no evidence. Name the source or hedge.
clinician: Lines then mechanism: repetition eases whatever is repeated, good or not. That is the cost the lines lacked. Safe, non-blaming framing.
habit: The script says what to repeat; the mechanism explains why repeating matters regardless of content. Mechanism is stated plainly and backed. Good rep plus reason.
contemplative: Lines to say, then why they work. Mechanism claim is mild and plain. Good breath. Trim 'simply'.
stress: Mechanism explains the ritual, but 'simply what repetition does' is asserted. Name the condition where repeating does not ease the thought.

structural: Mechanism supplies the cost: repetition doesn't check goodness. Fair link. Still a private fix; no group lever named.
satirist: The mantra gets its plain mechanism: repetition eases whatever it repeats. Passes the bar test. Honest, brief, and it earns the incantation.
mythmaker: The lines become the thing repetition makes effortless. The mechanism lands on the words just spoken. A person's face would help.

modeler: Good counter-case: you plant either way. The misreading sharpens the mechanism. Honest, even, earned.

clinician: Strong. Corrects the misreading that you start planting; you already do. Removes self-blame and leaves only visibility as the change. Safe on a bad day.
habit: Mechanism, then the correction: you're already planting. That reframes the practice from starting to seeing. Clear limit, same register.
contemplative: Names the misreading, then the limit: you plant either way. Honest and clarifying. Lets the reader exhale.
stress: Mechanism implies you are planting regardless; the misreading follows and limits the practice. Solid, modest, testable.
gamedesigner: Misreading paragraph supplies the limit: you're planting regardless. Changes what the practice asks. Real pivot, honestly stated.
structural: Counter-reading limits the practice honestly: you are planting regardless. Rare correction. Environment doing the planting stays unnamed.
satirist: Counter-case lands well: you're planting already. The misreading correction turns a to-do into a seeing. Good, and nobody had to say 'foma.'
mythmaker: Counter-case earns it: you are planting already. The misreading is named and corrected. Good pair.

clinician: Seeing what goes in the ground gets a checkable return step. Small, doable, explicitly not judging the crop. Good clinical pacing.
habit: Seeing the planting, then go back and look: a check that closes the loop. Exactly what I want, a second beat with a cue ('before the day ends').
contemplative: Seeing what goes in the ground leads to looking back. A real step. The 'fed sense of agency' claim wants a plainer word.
stress: Seeing-the-ground leads to looking back. Adds the feedback step the other lacks. Fine, though 'fed sense of agency' is unproven.
gamedesigner: Finally a feedback beat: go back and look. Answers the 'seeing' set up above. This is the signal I want on every practice.
structural: Looking adds a test, go back and check the ground. Honest about slowness. Fine; still all private.
satirist: Seeing the planting needs a return visit, a real step. 'Fast return' is one coined term, used at once. Mild earnestness, tolerable.
mythmaker: Ground under the seeds carries over, and the check-back supplies the cost of waiting. Has a pulse.

modeler: Check step then its failure mode, with a concrete correction. A loop plus its distortion. Works.
skeptic: Names the bias in the very check just prescribed, with a concrete fix: predict first, count misses. This is the Skeptic's seam.
clinician: Check-back step then its own bias, with a concrete fix: state the hope first, count the misses. Honest limit supplied.
habit: The check gets its own failure mode: confirmation bias, with a fix I can run (say what you hope to see first). Best seam in the chapter.
contemplative: The check is tested against its own bias, with a concrete fix. Humble and practicable. Both paragraphs need each other.
stress: Best kind of seam: the check step supplies its own failure mode, with a falsifiable fix. Praise modest, self-limiting claims.
gamedesigner: Check-back gets its failure mode: confirmation bias, with a fix (predict first). Cost and counter-test. Strong playable loop.
structural: Second paragraph supplies the failure mode the first lacked: confirmation bias with a concrete corrective. Earned.
satirist: The check-back gets its own bias warning, with a testable fix: say your hope first. A practice supplying its own skeptic. Rare. Applause.
mythmaker: Looking back becomes the place bias creeps in. The patience example gives it blood.

modeler: Chapter wrap mapped to four moves, asserted. 'Breath is thinning' has no stock behind it; scale jumps to the whole part.
skeptic: Cold swerve to a four-moves recap. The practice-to-move mappings are asserted, not shown, and the confirmation-bias hand-off is dropped.
clinician: Chapter summary riding on this seam. Practice names (Tree-Gazing, Naming the Loop) arrive as labels; the closing question is fine. Earn labels first.

contemplative: Gathers the four practices into the four moves and ends on a living question. Works because it asks for action.
stress: Failure mode is dropped for a tidy four-move summary. 'Everything else is those four moves' is a theory-of-everything flourish. Cut or test it.
gamedesigner: Maps four practices to four moves and ends on a prompt. Rewards recall; practice names land a bit fast but earned earlier.
structural: A tidy recap mapping practices to moves. Nothing new emerges; cut it or pose a test. Who benefits from this pretty symmetry?
satirist: Tidy ledger mapping practices onto four moves, with new labels arriving by the armful. Mostly a table of contents in sermon clothing.
mythmaker: Practices snap onto the four moves, and the closing question puts the reader inside. Works.

modeler: Corrected-for-bias check becomes tending; the four-practice synthesis rests on what was just built. Claims backed earlier.
skeptic: Naming the bias-corrected check as 'tending' makes the four practices into the four moves. It is a synthesis, hedged with 'nearly'. The closing question is fair.
clinician: Bias correction becomes 'tending,' and the four-moves mapping unifies the practices. Closing question is a usable step.
habit: Bias fix becomes 'tending'. Useful mapping, but it mostly summarizes the section. Cut the bias bit from the summary, keep the closing question.
contemplative: The bias check becomes tending, and the four practices become the four moves. A true gathering, ending with a question to live.
stress: Bias correction feeds the tending mapping. Mapping practices to moves is a real synthesis, hedged with 'nearly.' Untested, but plain.
gamedesigner: Bias correction becomes 'tending'; four practices map to four moves. Ends with a self-check question. Best seam so far.
structural: Bias-corrected check slots into tending; practices map onto moves. The mapping is the Third Thing. Hedged 'nearly'.
satirist: Bias correction becomes 'tending', then all four practices map to four moves. A real synthesis; the closing question makes the reader do it.
mythmaker: Bias check corrected, then named as tending: the four practices click into four moves. Earned payoff. The snapping-morning-line example is a good face.

modeler: Money-fudging example promoted to outward law, then Nest, Dyad, Skein pile on. Show the flow between scales.

clinician: Restates the epigraph, then dumps Nest, Dyad, Skein, Local Rule. Money-fudging anecdote becomes a law about travelling outward. Trim to one idea.

contemplative: Epigraph restated, then Nest, Dyad, Skein, Global Form arrive at once. Too many labels. Keep the money example, drop the vocabulary.

structural: One fudged-money anecdote promoted to law about travel up the scales. Nest, Dyad, Skein dumped together. Name one mechanism.
satirist: Epigraph restated as thesis, then Nest, Dyad, Skein dumped at once. Fudged-money anecdote promoted to outward-travelling law. Busy, busy, busy.

modeler: 'Rarely stays alone' is earned by the money example. But Dyad, Skein, Local Rule and Nest all arrive undefined in one paragraph.

habit: The fudged-numbers cost makes 'walks into every room' concrete. But Local Rule, Dyad, Skein and Nest all land in one paragraph. Trim to one.
contemplative: Walking into every room, then the money example, is good and hedged. But Local Rule, Nest, Dyad and Skein arrive unearned. Drop two.

gamedesigner: Epigraph becomes the fudge-the-numbers example, hedged. But Local Rule, Nest, Dyad, Skein pile in unearned. Cut the labels.
structural: Epigraph is elaborated, not tested. 'The reason is a Local Rule... Nest' is a coined label doing mechanism work; five terms at once.
satirist: Fudging money is a fair example, but 'Local Rule', 'Nest', 'Dyad' and 'Skein' are asserted as authorities. 'Travels outward' is a mechanism claimed, not shown.

stress: Chain arithmetic is correct and fun, but unconnected to origins of rules. Drake is a flourish. Bridge or move.

modeler: 'Built or delivered' is a hollow bridge to chain-multiplication odds. Arithmetic is right (0.9^5), but unrelated to origins. Start cold honestly.

clinician: Built-versus-delivered rules to chain arithmetic is a cold start; 'whether' covers a non sequitur. Drake adds a new concept. Maths itself is right.

satirist: 'Whether built or delivered' hides a swerve from origins to chain arithmetic, then Drake lands as a second new idea. Smooth connective, no reason.
mythmaker: 'Whether built or delivered' is a fluent hinge over a non sequitur. Chain arithmetic and Drake have no kin to inherited Local Rules.

modeler: Downward stock inflow, then a cold start on chained odds. Nothing handed across. Drake's equation appears with no tie to delivered versus built rules.
skeptic: Culture-to-Self inflow jumps to Drake-style chain arithmetic with no handoff. Built-versus-delivered rule is dropped. Open 720 on the origin question.
clinician: Culture-scale inflow to a five-step habit with Drake: cold start, no relation. 'Delivered, more common' goes unsupported. Needs a bridging sentence.
habit: Origins of delivered rules, then cold start on chain arithmetic and Drake. No handoff; 'same arithmetic' is a stretch. Say how a delivered rule is a chain.
contemplative: Inherited rules, then suddenly five-step arithmetic and Drake. Nothing is handed across. Two separate teachings.
stress: Delivered versus built rules drop out; a five-step chain arithmetic starts cold. 'Second is more common' is unsupported. These are two paragraphs, not a seam.
gamedesigner: Downward recursion to chain arithmetic and Drake: cold start, no bridge. Reader has nothing to test. Open with the delivered-rule origin.

modeler: Meadows' definition arrives as a new topic after the Drake detour. Strong definition, but nothing is handed across. Put it earlier.

satirist: Five-step habit is picked up and defined as a system. But arithmetic and Meadows' definition don't test each other; swap them freely.
mythmaker: Five-step habit becomes a 'small system'. Definition is tidy and the swapped-player team lives, but it never uses the arithmetic before.

skeptic: 'Bare links' limits the arithmetic and hands over to system-as-whole. The odds check out (0.9^5). Pair has a counter-case; 721's Part Two sweep is slightly broad.
clinician: Bare links then 'also a small system': the second paragraph supplies the missing limit. One new definition, used at once.

mythmaker: 'Treats the five steps as bare links' is a genuine limit on the arithmetic. Sports team swaps a player, and the habit gains a function. Honest turn.

modeler: Epigraph about play and depression is never used by the opening. Cut the quote or connect it to the engagement claim.

clinician: The depression epigraph is glib and never picked up. The chapter opening speaks to a doubting reader but ignores the quote.

mythmaker: The play and depression epigraph is never picked up, and the paragraph jumps to practices. Either echo the epigraph or let it go.

stress: Sutton-Smith's 'play' is quietly redefined as absorbed engagement. Three mechanisms are previewed at once, none used yet.

structural: 'The quote's play is absorbed engagement' makes a stated reading and leads into the three-part preview. Interpretation is explicit, not hidden.
satirist: Quote's 'play' is conveniently defined as engagement, then three research claims are previewed at once. Epigraph plus roadmap.
mythmaker: Epigraph sets stakes, then the doubter's question. But 'the quote's play is absorbed engagement' redefines the quote by fiat. Show the play.

modeler: Quote's bleak claim is bounded, with the hurt named before the mechanism. Play becomes engagement, which has adjustable causes. I'd like the stock behind 'goes flat'.

clinician: Good: 'Depression is not a shortage of technique' names the hurt first. But three research concepts are previewed at once. Offer one, with a small step.
habit: Quote's play gets defined and the hurt is named before the research. Honest, one thread. Next: which practice, when, and what to change when flat.
contemplative: Naming depression plainly before the research is right. But absorption, learning reward and fading finish-line arrive together. Give one first.
stress: Quote is reframed, not just echoed, and depression named with care. Three research hooks are promised, not yet shown. Still honest and even.

structural: Paragraph limits the quote and names depression without bypass. But three mechanisms (difficulty match, learning reward, finish-line fade) are previewed at once. Introduce one.
satirist: Epigraph gets flatly corrected: depression is not a technique shortage. Honest hurt acknowledged before the research turn. Sutton-Smith earns his keep. Best seam here.
mythmaker: Names the hurt before reframing the quote. Sutton-Smith's line gets earned by 'absorbed engagement'. Warm, and doesn't let depression slide. Good.

satirist: Recipe carries over and 'may' hedges honestly; form changes, aim persists is a real claim. Spark Feast plus 'Becoming a Third' arrive cold together. Drop one.

structural: Leans on 'the worry this Part opened with', which isn't on the page. 'Every tradition' is a promoted anecdote.

modeler: Pivots from outliving to a worry never on this page. Survivorship line helps, but 'aim underneath' is a label, not a stock. New concept arrives.

clinician: The 'worry this Part opened with' is not set up in the prior paragraph, so the handoff reaches back a Part. Name the worry first.
habit: Form changes, aim survives; first-try tradition answers the opening worry. Honest, earned. Still abstract: name one feast to hold this year.

satirist: 'Every tradition you've loved was once a first try' is an anecdote promoted to law, and the worry it answers is far back.

stress: Admits the cost: you won't see it. Comfort scoped to 'smaller and sturdier'. Names the hurt before the reframe.

structural: Supplies the cost: you won't see it. Names the lost comfort before offering a smaller one. Earned turn.
satirist: Chapter closer on the comfort of 'the laying'. Pretty rhythm, no claim survives once cadence is removed. At least it admits you won't see it.
mythmaker: Admits you won't see it, then comforts smaller and sturdier. Earned turn and the laying image rhymes. Best seam here.

modeler: Intro promises short repeatable lines and delivers one. Path-worn-by-walking is a nice reinforcing loop, though no limit is named.
skeptic: 'The repeating does the work' is a mechanism claim backed by a simile. Repetition alone may fix a belief as readily as improve it.
clinician: Intro gives the use (kettle, doorway, a breath) and the mantra fits. Safe. A short 'when to say it' cue would help.
habit: Cues named: kettle, doorway, red light. Great. Then a blank to fill. Tell me which cue pairs with which mantra.
contemplative: The kettle, the doorway, the red light: a real invitation to practice. Short enough for one breath. The intro is a little long.
stress: Intro frames use; mantra follows. 'The repeating does the work' is asserted, not tested. Fine as liturgy.
gamedesigner: Intro says short, say in a breath; the first mantra delivers. Usable, but I get no sign whether the repeating works.
structural: Intro frames the mantras. Introduction and item, no test or limit.
satirist: Intro promises something short enough for a breath, and the first mantra with a blank delivers. 'Repeating does the work' is metaphor posing as mechanism.
mythmaker: Kettle, doorway, red light are good places to stand. Intro to a mantra, nothing more.

modeler: Two free-standing mantras. No relation between them. Fine as a list, not a dyad.
skeptic: Two adjacent mantras, no relation. Swappable without loss. Fine as a liturgy; not a pair that says anything together.
clinician: Two mantras side by side, interchangeable. Fine to say aloud, but the pair carries nothing across.
habit: Two mantras side by side, no relation. Fine as a list. 'Which small step' is a good single question.
contemplative: Two separate mantras, each fine alone. They are not a pair; no handoff is needed, only room between.
stress: Two separate mantras, swappable. No handoff; one ends with a blank, the other with a question.
gamedesigner: Two separate mantras with no relation I can name. A list, not a sequence. Order by scale or by when to use each.
structural: Two mantras side by side. Interchangeable; no stated relation.
satirist: 'What I'll repeat' threads into 'let me repeat that one'. Two similar mantras stacked, no test between them. Pick one.
mythmaker: Independent lines in a list; tending a field and a small step don't pass anything across. Fine as liturgy, not a seam.

modeler: Second line picks up the repeat. But it restates the loop; no stock, delay or limit added. Same claim twice.
skeptic: Two liturgical lines, each fine alone. Nothing handed across; field-tending and small-step are parallel. Cadence carries it, not a claim.
clinician: Two separate mantras, each fine alone. A reader in a spiral gets a small step either way, but nothing passes between them.
habit: Plant the day's repeat, then choose which step to keep. Fill-in blank to filter question. A usable pair, cue is the day's pauses.
contemplative: 'What I repeat' passes smoothly to the next line, but two short lines do not build anything together. Fine to say in one breath.
stress: Two restatements of repeat-to-become, one forward, one backward. Neither supplies a test or cost; 'worth it' never says how to judge. Name one failure condition, like repeating a bad step.
gamedesigner: Standalone mantras; neither builds on the other. They could be swapped freely. Fine as a menu, but it's a list, not a sequence. No progression.
structural: 'Repeat' and 'worth' carry across, so it reads as a sequence. But 'what I repeat becomes what I do' is mechanism stated as fact. Liturgy, not argument, yet nobody owns or pulls a lever.
satirist: Two mantra lines, one rhythm. Nothing here survives the cadence. Say the relation: does the second test the first?
mythmaker: The 'repeat' blank gets answered by choosing the step worth repeating. A real handoff, brief but earned.

modeler: The blank gets filled by the step chosen: a small stock-to-flow loop, yesterday's act feeding tomorrow's. Tight handoff, steady register. Could name the correction delay.

clinician: The blank is handed over and answered: 'let that one fill the blank'. Small, doable and gentle. Clean, usable seam.
habit: The blank to fill becomes tomorrow's question: which small step was worth it. Real handoff, one rep. Name the cue, though: which pause?
contemplative: 'Let that one fill the blank' picks up the blank and 'repeat' cleanly. Small, warm, speakable on one breath.
stress: The blank is posed and the next line answers it. Clean call-and-response, nothing overclaimed. Plain and continuous.
gamedesigner: Next mantra in the set picks up 'repeat' from the blank. Smooth, but it's a stacked sequence; no new capability from the pair.
structural: The blank is set up, then a test ('worth it') fills it. Clean handoff. Missing: any check that the step chosen is actually good.
satirist: Blank in one, 'let that one fill the blank' in the other. Small, plain, same voice. A mantra that actually hands something over. Busy, but quiet.
mythmaker: Second picks up 'what I'll repeat' and asks which step is worth it. But these are liturgy lines, not a story; no one has anything to lose.

modeler: Individual step jumps to a woven web. 'Rewoven' arrives with no tie to the step loop before it.

mythmaker: Jumps from my day's step to a family, town, world with no bridge. Two new ideas, thread and reweaving, land at once. Needs a person feeling the tie.

satirist: Trophy versus the step in front: a plain instruction following the tree line. Mild contrast, honest enough.
mythmaker: The trophy is a good counter-temptation to the step. But the voice flips from I to you and the tree is dropped; the image is used once.

modeler: The seed is used at once: reaching past it for the trophy is the failure, and tending the step is the fix. Clear cause and cost, same image, one new term.
skeptic: Seed is picked up and the trophy supplies the counter-pull. Relation is plain, with one new image. Best seam here, though as a mantra it earns little proof.
clinician: The seed image is used at once: reaching for the trophy is the temptation. Light self-catching, no rumination. Works.
habit: Seed to trophy: reaching past the step is the failure the first one implies. Reads as a clean cue-and-redirect. Best seam here.
contemplative: Seed, then the pull to reach past it for the trophy. The failure mode is named and the remedy is doable. Clean and breathable.
stress: The seed is used: reaching past it for the trophy is the failure mode. Same image, one new idea. This is a working seam.
gamedesigner: Seed sets up the failure mode: reaching for the trophy. That's a counter-case plus a move. Plays well.
structural: Seed hands off to the failure mode: reaching past it for the trophy. One new idea, used at once; the pair gives claim and discipline.
satirist: Seed answered by trophy: a real contrast, plainly stated, one new image. The tidiest seam here. Even Bokonon would let it pass.
mythmaker: Seed carries over into tending the step instead of the trophy. Consistent, but it restates the same advice in new words. No cost shown.
