modeler: Trophy to feet-breath-room: unrelated. No handoff, and whole-keeps-balance has no feedback behind it.
skeptic: Short, calm, parallel. Balance appears from nowhere in the second. Fluent, and I'd call it a stack of reminders.
clinician: From step to feet, breath, room. A pleasant grounding cue, but the pair has no link. A body-based step is the right instinct.
habit: Step-versus-trophy shifts to feet, breath, room. A body-scan with no link. Needs a cue and a line of context.
contemplative: Simple, bodily and sayable: feet, breath, room. That is practice. It shares nothing with the line before, which is fine.
stress: Trophy-versus-step shifts to feet, breath, room. Different image, no link. Swappable.
gamedesigner: From steps and trophies to feet, breath, room. New imagery, no link. Reads as a shuffled deck.
structural: Step line then feet-breath-room. Separate prompts, no handoff.
satirist: 'Feet, breath, room' lands cold and 'the whole' has no referent. Balance appears from nowhere.
mythmaker: Step to feet-breath-room: a new register of body attention. Neighbors, not partners.

modeler: 'When reaching won't stop' answers the previous reaching. Adds a body-based remedy, but 'whole keeps balance' is metaphor, no feedback shown.
skeptic: Reaching for trophy then 'feet, breath, room' and balance: new image and new concept with no handoff. Why would this stop the reaching?
clinician: Catching the reaching, then what to do when it won't stop: feet, breath, room. Concrete, non-shaming, usable at 3 a.m. Best seam here.
habit: Best pair here: the cue is the reaching, the rep is feet, breath, room. Doable before breakfast. Keep as is.
contemplative: The reaching is picked up and given a practical remedy: feet, breath, room. Intellect to body. This seam does what a mantra should.
stress: Real handoff: the failure case (reaching won't stop) gets a concrete fallback. A genuine if-then pair; the only mantra seam with a test in it.
gamedesigner: Trigger then escalation: when reaching won't stop, give a body-level move. Clear step relation, concrete controller (feet, breath, room). Works as a fallback tier.
structural: Fallback for when the first instruction fails: 'reaching' is picked up and 'won't stop' admits the difficulty. Body anchors are a modest, honest step. The best seam here.
satirist: Reaching continues into feet, breath, room. Useful as a do-this step, but the second only extends the first.
mythmaker: 'When the reaching won't stop' picks up the reaching directly and gives a body-level answer: feet, breath, room. A real beat of doubt answered.

P1057>P1058.label: A. The Mantras, Prayers, and Meditations — Full Text
P1057>P1058.desc: the seam from paragraph [P1057] to paragraph [P1058] (chapter "A. The Mantras, Prayers, and Meditations — Full Text")

modeler: Balance to loop-bigger-each-time is an abrupt jump. 'Good or not' is the first balancing hint; nothing here sets it up.
skeptic: 'My days feel like a straight line' tells me how I feel, then asserts the loop 'a little bigger' with no check. New concept arrives cold.
clinician: Balance to straight line versus loop is a cold switch. 'Good or not' is honest, but nothing connects the two.
habit: Balance moment then loop-versus-line claim. New concept, no bridge. 'A little bigger, good or not' is fair.
contemplative: Balance in the body gives way to a loop idea with no bridge. The loop is clear but needs its own space.
stress: Balance in the body, then loops in days. Unrelated; second starts cold.
gamedesigner: Balance of the whole jumps to straight line versus loop. Two ideas, no bridge. Nothing to do or check.
structural: Balance in the body jumps to straight line vs loop. New concept with no preparation.
satirist: Balance to straight line versus loop. 'Comes back a little bigger' is a growth mechanism asserted, not shown. New concept mid-list.
mythmaker: Balance to loop, no handoff. Each is fine alone.

modeler: Balance as small corrections names a balancing loop; then straight-line illusion versus loop adds the reinforcing side. Best seam here.
skeptic: Balance as small corrections to straight line versus loop: a different thought. 'Comes back a little bigger' claims growth with no basis on the page.
clinician: Balance becomes a straight line versus a loop that grows 'good or not'. Growth is asserted without support, and a new concept lands. Split them.
habit: Balance is small corrections, then loops. The move from body to a claim about loops is unearned. No cue, no action.
contemplative: Balance as small corrections is good, then the straight line and loop arrive as a new idea. 'A little bigger, good or not' is asserted, not shown.
stress: 'Balance' echoes the prior line, then straight-line versus loop lands as a second new idea. Neat rhythm hides a topic change.
gamedesigner: Balance mantra then the straight-line-versus-loop claim: a cold start, new concept, and 'comes back a little bigger, good or not' asserted as mechanism without backing.
structural: 'Balance' is picked up, then the straight-line-to-loop claim arrives as a second concept. 'Comes back a little bigger' is growth asserted without backing. Split into two mantras.
satirist: Balance turns to small corrections, then straight line and loop. Metaphor promoted to mechanism with no case. Two new ideas.
mythmaker: Balance as small corrections links to loops, but 'comes back a little bigger' is asserted with no mechanism, and the straight-line-versus-loop image is new and unprepared.

modeler: Balance as small corrections, repeating, is the mechanism the body line implied: a loop with a feedback reading. It could name the delay, but it earns the step.
skeptic: Balance becomes a loop through wordplay. A body-balance image carries a claim that repetition 'comes back for me', which nothing shows. Scale shifts without notice.
clinician: Balance is explained as small repeating corrections, a loop. Grounding body first, then the idea. 'Good or not' keeps it unblaming. Solid.
habit: Balance practice jumps to loop claim with no tie. 'Corrections, repeating' is asserted, not shown. Two ideas; drop one or add a cue.
contemplative: Balance becomes a loop, then 'comes back for me' arrives unsupported. Two ideas, and the leap is unearned. Pick one and stay with it.
stress: Balance reframed as repeating correction is a real turn. But 'good or not, comes back' is asserted, and the reaching-won't-stop hurt goes unnamed.
gamedesigner: Balance as small corrections gives the feedback loop a body-level proof. But 'whatever I repeat comes back' is a second, larger claim, unearned.
structural: Balance carries across, but 'small corrections' for a body doesn't show that whatever I repeat comes back. The analogy glides over the gap.
satirist: Balance as small corrections is true of standing; then it leaps to 'whatever I repeat comes back for me'. Posture to destiny, and loop is a second concept.
mythmaker: Balance leaps to loops and straight lines with no handoff. A second new concept arrives before the first is used. Bridge from corrections to the loop.

P1058>P1059.label: A. The Mantras, Prayers, and Meditations — Full Text
P1058>P1059.desc: the seam from paragraph [P1058] to paragraph [P1059] (chapter "A. The Mantras, Prayers, and Meditations — Full Text")

modeler: Loop claim becomes a test: would you repeat this unchanged forever? Gives the balancing check and a small adjustment. Good seam.
skeptic: The second does test the first's loop claim by asking what I'm running. Good. But 'comes back around, a little bigger, good or not' is unearned.
clinician: Claim, then test and next step: ask what loop, then make a small adjustment to today's rule. Warm and actionable. Minor worry: 'indefinitely' could sting.
habit: Loop claim then loop question. Good. 'Would I repeat this indefinitely?' is my one-question test. Keep it.
contemplative: The loop is picked up and turned into a question I can ask. 'Not a bigger future reward' is wise. A little crowded.
stress: Loop claim is followed by a question that tests it: would you repeat this unchanged indefinitely? That is a real stress test.
gamedesigner: Loop claim, then the question to run: what loop am I running, would I repeat it? A real self-check with a feedback signal.
structural: Loop claim then a test: would you repeat this indefinitely? That tests the previous line. Rare real seam in the appendix.
satirist: The loop claim becomes a test: would I repeat this unchanged forever? Passes the bar test. The one mantra here that makes me do something.
mythmaker: Loop is picked up and turned into a question. Real hand-off, but it deepens rather than adds a cost.

P1059>P1060.label: A. The Mantras, Prayers, and Meditations — Full Text
P1059>P1060.desc: the seam from paragraph [P1059] to paragraph [P1060] (chapter "A. The Mantras, Prayers, and Meditations — Full Text")

modeler: Individual loop audit to group origin chant. Cross-references pile up; no handoff. Different register and scale.
skeptic: Solo question to group chant; Iterations cited, not shown. 'Someone who noticed: you' hands me an identity by cadence. Give the chain a reason.
clinician: Personal question to group cosmogony cold. 'From difference, a shape... someone who noticed: you' is a cadence asserting a causal chain and an identity.
habit: Personal loop question to group origin chant. Different mode and cross-references. Put group mantras in their own list.
contemplative: From a personal question to a group chant, with cross-references that interrupt breath. Keep references out of the spoken text.
stress: Private self-audit to group Iterations chant. Scale and cross-references change with no bridge.
gamedesigner: From solo loop audit to group Iterations chant, with cross-references to far chapters. New context, no handoff.
structural: Individual loop-check to group Iterations chant. Scale and register shift, with cross-references standing in for a link.
satirist: From a personal audit question to cosmogony ('from difference, a shape') for a room. Altitude leap with no handoff. Busy, busy, busy.
mythmaker: Solo question to group chant with a chain of coined steps and chapter cross-refs. Cold start and heavy.

modeler: Individual loop question jumps to group origin cosmology cold. 'The loop I just named' points at nothing on the page. Unearned scale leap.
skeptic: Personal loop-audit question jumps to a cosmic origin chant and a room. 'The loop I just named' presumes the previous line; the reader just met a different one.
clinician: A personal inventory jumps to a cosmic origin chant. 'The loop I just named' is borrowed, but the hurt is never touched. Needs a bridge.
habit: One question to carry, then a cosmic origin chant. Altitude jumps, 'the loop I just named' isn't in P1059. Nothing to do.
contemplative: 'The loop I just named' carries the question into the group. But a cosmic origin story leaps in at once. Needs a step between.
stress: 'The loop I just named' does reach back, but the swing from a personal audit to cosmic genesis is unprepared. Cross-reference clutter.
gamedesigner: Individual loop-audit to group origin chant: cross-references stack, 'the loop I just named' doesn't match anything in 1059. Jump of scale and register. Lost the player.
structural: Personal loop jumps to a cosmic origin chain ending in 'you, and everyone in this room'. The chain is asserted, not earned, and the scale leap skips any bridge. Add one.
satirist: Personal audit questions abruptly become a group origin chant. 'The loop I just named' was never named. Stage prop.
mythmaker: 'The loop I just named' is a true handoff. But it leaps from a personal check to a cosmic origin story with no acknowledgement of the person holding the loop.

modeler: The loop question gets an origin and agency answer, and 'however heavy' nods at the hurt. But the difference-to-noticer chain is asserted, and the scale leap needs one step.
skeptic: 'Loop' carries over and 'however heavy' nods at the hurt. Then comes a cosmic sequence stated as fact, ending in a claim about who 'you, and everyone in this room' are.
clinician: 'However heavy' nods to hurt, but the leap from loop-question to cosmic origin to 'you' is fluent assertion, not link. Bridge it plainly.
habit: Personal self-question to group cosmic origin story, cold start. Different register and no handoff. Group version needs its own single question.
contemplative: The 'loop' is carried across, and 'however heavy' acknowledges the hurt. But a cosmic origin story after a plain question jars. Shorten it.
stress: Personal audit question jumps to a group origin chant. Neat cadence, hindsight story with no luck or cost in it. Needs a bridge.
gamedesigner: Group version picks up 'loop' but swaps my test question for a cosmic origin chant. Hard altitude jump, no check I can run.
structural: 'Loop' carries over, but cosmic derivation chain lands on 'however heavy' with one nod to the hurt. Origin story doesn't back the adjust-today test; pattern becomes identity ('you').
satirist: 'However heavy' nods at the hurt, but then comes a cosmic chain from difference to 'you and everyone in this room'. Rhythm does the persuading; no claim survives.
mythmaker: Solo question flips to group chant with 'you, and everyone in this room.' The room appears from nowhere, no hurt acknowledged. Give the group a face.

P1060>P1061.label: A. The Mantras, Prayers, and Meditations — Full Text
P1060>P1061.desc: the seam from paragraph [P1060] to paragraph [P1061] (chapter "A. The Mantras, Prayers, and Meditations — Full Text")

modeler: 'Together' and 'beginning now' carry across, but P1061 only restates the group frame. Worth repeating is asserted, not tested.
skeptic: 'Together' carries across, and the register holds. But 'will do again' is a vow rather than a claim, so nothing is tested between them.
clinician: 'Together' carries across, and the table brings it down to earth. But dropping from cosmic to table is unprepared. Soften with the hurt in the room.
habit: Both group chants about the room. 'Do it again, together' ends it. Warm, but 'again and again' could name a cue.
contemplative: Both are for the group. The second is plain and repeatable, though it only echoes the first. Good to say aloud.
stress: Group voice carries across ('together'), but both are cadence. Neither names a cost or a condition.
gamedesigner: Two group chants that share a register. 'Together, beginning now' and 'this table' are close, but neither tests or extends the other.
structural: Two group chants, similar cadence. Second restates 'together, again'. No lever, no owner.
satirist: Cosmic ladder lands on 'this table, these people', prepared by 'everyone in this room'. A fair landing, though the two mantras restate each other.
mythmaker: Together carries over, and the table finally appears, which I like. Still a restatement, not a turn.

modeler: Origin chain ends in 'beginning now'; second picks up the table. Warmer and continuous, but repeating a commitment adds no cost or test.
skeptic: 'Beginning now, at this table' carries the group and the 'building together' across. Hard days are admitted. Still a parallel pair; no new claim between them.
clinician: Cosmic origin lands on 'at this table', with 'hard days too' naming the difficulty. A group commitment small enough to keep.
habit: Origin chant lands on a commitment: do it again, hard days too. Group cue is the table. Concrete enough, and it names the cost.
contemplative: 'Beginning now, at this table' hands the room across cleanly and the register holds. Still two lines saying one thing; no new content.
stress: 'Beginning now' hands the cosmic arc into a concrete commitment, now admitting 'hard days too'. Cost named; the best seam here.
gamedesigner: Group chant ends on 'beginning now', and the pledge picks up 'at this table' with the cost of hard days. Commitment follows the origin story; gives a real moment of action.
structural: Origin story ends in 'together, beginning now', and the vow picks it up at 'this table', naming 'hard days too'. A commitment, not a claim, so the scale change is prepared.
satirist: Origin story lands in a commitment: 'beginning now' carries across, and the vow gets cost with 'hard days too'. Earns its hush.
mythmaker: 'Beginning now, at this table' turns the origin into a vow, and 'hard days too' admits cost. The room, not the abstraction, finally holds the loop.

C000.label: How to Read a Recursive Book
C000.desc: chapter "How to Read a Recursive Book" (FRONT MATTER; paragraphs [P0001] to [P0020])

modeler: Reading routes are clear and each earns its place. It ends on a slogan, not a built landing, and offers no test of the reading.
skeptic: Aim is clear, but reading routes and path lists say the same job twice, and the ending is a slogan. Test the slogan before landing on it.
clinician: Clear, kind route map that lets a tired reader choose a path. But it names no test of whether a path is working. Add one.
habit: Reading routes are clear, but arcs-theory padding precedes them and it ends on a slogan. 'Notice the feeling' has no cue. Name a first page and a time.
contemplative: Aim splits: reading guide, three paths, a warning on method. Paragraphs stack caveats. The sentence at the end lands gently. Offer one path, one first small act.
stress: Aim is clear: how to enter. P0017 names its own trap, good. But route paragraphs stack, and it ends on a slogan, not a storm-tested test.
gamedesigner: Aim is clear (how to read). But the path-list is a rulebook up front, the closing sentence lands big, and no tiny test or check.
structural: Aim is plain: how to enter a circular book. Lands on the one sentence. But nothing to test; 'notice the feeling' has no sign of working.
satirist: A plain map with three routes; good. But 'notice the second reading' is a test nothing could fail. Give a checkable sign.
mythmaker: Aim is clear, but it's all instructions with nobody standing in it. Give me one reader on a second pass, then return to them at the close.

modeler: Job stated (get you to page one), Maya returns, test has a falsifier. But the reading-order list and the three doors do the same routing job twice; merge them.
skeptic: Two jobs: route-finder and thesis delivery. Three doors restate the order paragraphs; the book sentence is asserted, not supported. The phone test with a stated failure is usable.
clinician: Aim is stated (get you to page one) and tonight's phone test can fail. But reading order and the doors overlap, and Part names go unexplained. Fold one into the other.
habit: Aim ('one job: your first page') appears only at P0005. Reading order and three doors do the same routing twice. Merge them. Ending tests the sentence tonight, falsifiably.
contemplative: Aim is stated plainly and ends on a testable sentence with Maya returning. But P0003, P0009-P0011 run long and repeat the return-to-Part-One idea. Trim to one breath each.
stress: Test tonight with a stated failure condition is good. But the sources caution and one-sentence thesis detour from 'get to your first page', and Loop, Third Thing and Standing Thirds are used untaught.
gamedesigner: Tutorial has one stated job, but warning, arcs, six reading rules, doors and caution compete. Rules P0006-P0011 duplicate the doors. Cut to doors plus tonight's test.
structural: Aim is stated (P0005), but two routing schemes, a source caution and a book-in-a-sentence compete for it. Merge the path lists; who benefits from the order?
satirist: One job is stated, then the doors repeat the paths twice over. Maya cites the 'Third Thing' before it's taught. Phone test with a failure clause is good. Merge the duplicate route lists.
mythmaker: Maya gives the warning a face, then vanishes until the last lines. Route paragraphs and the order paragraphs do one job twice. Keep Maya standing through the doors.

modeler: Aim (get you to your first page) is clear and the tonight test is checkable. But the doors, caution and sentence setup overlap; trim, and name a stock somewhere.
skeptic: Aim (get you to a first page) is clear and Maya helps, but the thesis sentence and caveat bolt on late; the closing test at least names its own failure.
clinician: Aim (get you to a first page) is clear and kind. But routes, sources caution and slogan pile up; the long reading list is pure reception. Cut P0009/P0017 duplication.
habit: Good: a door, a tonight test with a fail condition. But the circle point repeats across P0002-4 and the caution; trim to one pass.
contemplative: Its one job is clear, and the sentence test is small. But warning, orders, doors, caveat all stack. Keep the doors; fold the rest into fewer breaths.
stress: Aim is clear and the 'count against the book' test has teeth. But order, doors and one-sentence pitch overlap; the Maya return is nice, pitch less so. Trim.
gamedesigner: Aim is clear and the three doors give a choice. But Loop Tongue and Standing Thirds are front-loaded jargon, and the caution paragraph delays play.
structural: Aim is getting you to a first page; Maya planted at open and paid off at the close. Test tonight has a failure sign. Solid scaffold.
satirist: Aim is plain: get you to page one. But Maya, the second-reading promise and the 'scaffolding' line say the same thing three times. Merge them.
mythmaker: Maya in her sister quarrel is a face, and June pays off. But P0003 and P0017 run on abstractions with nobody in them.

C001.label: PART ONE — WHY THIS MATTERS (opener)
C001.desc: chapter "PART ONE — WHY THIS MATTERS (opener)" (PART ONE — WHY THIS MATTERS; paragraphs [P0021] to [P0023])

modeler: Crisp three-line opener that does its job. It promises the loop will be seen but names no stock or flow, and gives no test.
skeptic: Honest signpost, three lines, no padding. But it promises a 'shift in seeing' with nothing testable, and a promise is not a landing.
clinician: Three italic signposts, not a chapter. Honest about being a shift in seeing, but nothing to try and no payoff. Merge into Chapter 1.
habit: Three lines say what the part is for and give a route. No landing, no action; fine as a signpost, but it equips nobody.
contemplative: Three plain lines say what the part is for. Honest and short. Yet it asks nothing of me; add one thing to notice today.
stress: Honest about being a shift in seeing, with an exit. But three promissory italics: no break condition, no test to run yet.
gamedesigner: Part opener works as a quest briefing, but three italic paragraphs only announce rewards later; nothing to try or test here.
structural: Three italic promises, no build. It forecasts the Third Thing before it is taught, then hands off. Fine as signage, not a Skein.
satirist: Three italic blurbs. It uses 'Third Thing' before anyone taught it and promises a 'shift in seeing'. Busy, busy. Nothing to try.
mythmaker: Three italic promises, no person. The phone, die and coastline are named, not lived. Put one face in the opener and pay it off.

modeler: Phone test is small, with a failure condition. P0023 repeats the practice-path routing from front matter at equal strength; cut it to a pointer.
skeptic: Aim is stated, and the cue test names what counts against it. But the routing line repeats the practice path, and the three-line opener promises more than it shows.
clinician: Maya's 6:40 reach gives it a person, and a missed cue counts against the claim. It ends on a pointer, not a landing, and P0022 stacks three terms.
habit: Short, one job, and the closing test is tiny: catch the cue before the hand moves, with a stated way to fail. Third Thing is named a bit early.
contemplative: Clear purpose and a small test for tomorrow. P0022 packs loop, Third Thing, marriage and workplace into one sentence. Give it one image and let the rest wait.
stress: Maya's morning test can fail and costs nothing. But it ends on a pointer to Chapter 3, not a landing, and Third Thing arrives undefined.
gamedesigner: Clear goal, and the phone test is a real move with a fail condition. But P0022 front-loads Third Thing and repeats the route advice. Ends on a pointer, not payoff.
structural: Clear purpose and a falsifiable first test. It stops on a pointer to Chapter 3's unexplained 'four beats' instead of landing. Close on Maya.
satirist: Aim is plain and the Maya test can fail, which I respect. But P0022 stacks loop, marriage and Third Thing in one breath. Unpack it into one idea.
mythmaker: Maya's 6:40 reach is a real scene, but the second blurb stacks loop, Third Thing and marriage with nobody in them. It ends on a pointer, not a landing.

C002.label: 1. What You Already Know
C002.desc: chapter "1. What You Already Know" (PART ONE — WHY THIS MATTERS; paragraphs [P0024] to [P0030])

modeler: Aim is clear and the order builds. P0028 repeats P0027. 'Ask what holds it there' names no stock, delay, or sign of success.
skeptic: Lovely, and I have no reason to believe it. Anecdotes stand in as evidence, P0028 restates P0027, and 'what keeps it there?' is rumination without a check.
clinician: Gentle, blame-free opening and a clean aim. Ending question is a small step, but it asks for self-inspection with no sign of whether it worked.
habit: Ends on one good question, the kind I'd carry all day. But no cue, no time, no sign it worked. Attach it to a moment, like the next fridge visit.
contemplative: Short, calm, one aim. The closing question is something I can do in my kitchen. Only the claim 'weather' is asserted, not shown.
stress: 'Nothing large was built large' is unbreakable; P0028 repeats P0027. Closing question is self-scrutiny with no sign of working. Name a case where it fails.
gamedesigner: Tight hook, one claim, ends on a doable question: what keeps this solid thing happening? Needs a sign that it worked.
structural: Lawn shortcut is planted then dropped. Ending is a question, not a return. 'What keeps it there?' has no outcome to check.
satirist: P0028 restates P0027 at lower volume. Lawn path, phone, fern are nice. Closing question has no sign of success. Add one measurable thing.
mythmaker: Lovely thought, who's holding it? Lawn, fern, phone: images used once and dropped. End on an instruction, not a person. Give one person a worn path.

modeler: Lawn path is a real local-rule case with a footstep to catch. P0027, P0028 and P0029 restate one claim; also name what stops a path growing.
skeptic: Aim is clear and the footstep test can fail. But it tells readers what they have felt without support, and it closes on 'the rest of the book falls out', which is oversold.
clinician: The lawn path returns at the close, which is a good landing. But P0028 and P0029 restate P0027. 'Find your footstep' on Sunday dread hints the dread is your doing. Pick a neutral example.
habit: Test one solid thing, find the footstep, catch it once today; a failure condition is stated. Lawn opening returns at the close with weight. Fine.
contemplative: The lawn path opens and closes it, and the check is small and falsifiable. P0028 repeats P0027 and P0029 repeats P0028. Keep one, and say it once.
stress: Good: the bridge exception names a break condition, and the 'can't find a repeating act, the claim failed' test is real. But P0028 restates P0025 and P0027 at equal strength; merge them.
gamedesigner: Strong hook: the lawn path returns as a footstep test with a fail state. P0027 and P0028 state the same claim twice; merge them.
structural: One test, one aim, and the lawn footstep returns at the close. But P0028 restates P0027 at equal strength, and 'worn path' ignores who paved it.
satirist: The lawn path is a real image and the test can fail. But the fern is a tangent, 'built small' is said three times, and 'the rest of the book falls out' is Bokonon-grade overreach.
mythmaker: The lawn path and the footstep return nicely. But 'built small', 'weather' and the claim restate one point three times. Give the Sunday dread a face.

C003.label: 2. The Third Thing
C003.desc: chapter "2. The Third Thing" (PART ONE — WHY THIS MATTERS; paragraphs [P0031] to [P0049])

modeler: Coastline, die, thresholds, chairs, bees, essentialism: many aims, with tangents and a landing. Needs splitting. Third Thing still lacks a named stock or loop.
skeptic: Emergence, forces, essentialism, two senses of 'real': four aims. Analogy is asserted as ontology. Split the chapter; keep the die, which can actually be checked.
clinician: Emergence, symphysical, thresholds, essentialism and two senses of real, all in one chapter. Bee and force pairs are tangents. Split it; give the marriage a face.
habit: Emergence, symphysical, two senses of real, essentialism: concept pile-up, bee tangent. The end exercise is fine but unanchored. Cut to one idea, one Monday-morning test.
contemplative: Beautiful pieces, too many: coastline, die, chair, bee, essentialism. 'Real' stretched thin. One idea, one practice would breathe. The closing Try this works.
stress: Third Thing, emergence, threshold, force pairs, essentialism, two senses of real: a pile. Bee tangent. Admits 'argument by likeness' yet never breaks it. Split it.
gamedesigner: Overloaded: die game, emergence, threshold, chair, bee, two senses of real, essentialism. Three concepts at once; split it. Try-this is good.
structural: Emergence, symphysical, thresholds, forces, two senses of real, essentialism: a list of topics. Bee and chair pairs repeat. Split it; give one case a face.

satirist: Phone calls, radios, lifeguards, icebergs, night nurses: five metaphors for one claim. 'What else?' twice is a real move. Prune metaphors.
mythmaker: The quiet friend, night nurse and lifeguard give it blood, and the ending pays off 'whether you were.' The game and radio images get used once and dropped.

modeler: Good: conversation as a balancing loop with delays, plus the friend-goes-quiet payoff. But wavelength, voicemail, lifeguard and iceberg metaphors pile up where one mechanism would carry it.
skeptic: One habit promised, yet the body runs thirty-odd paragraphs of models, wavelengths, lifeguards, four moves. Ending says material 'was always there', contradicting 'not available a moment earlier'. Prune and reconcile.
clinician: The 'hold your read, ask what else' aim is clear and the try-this is safe on a bad day. But thirty-five paragraphs repeat themselves, with game, radio and phone tangents. Trim to one image per idea.
habit: The 'hold your read, ask what else twice' habit is real, but 35 paragraphs bury it. Game, radio, walk, voicemail stack up as images; reduce to one.
contemplative: Aim is clear and the 'ask what else' practice is real. But game, phone, radio, walk, nurse and iceberg images crowd it. One image, fewer breaths of theory.
stress: Hold your read, ask what else twice is breakable and small. But thirty-odd paragraphs: game, voicemail, radio, walk, lifeguard, iceberg. Pick one image per claim; the ending overreaches.
gamedesigner: Aim is clear and the 'what else' twice test works. But the middle is a long cutscene: games, wavelength, feeling-for, lifeguard. Cut or give each a move to try.
structural: The 'ask what else' aim is clear from the opening. But the long middle (model, wavelength, balancing loop, empathy, nurse) has overlapping paragraphs and a conceptual pile-up. Try-this is small, with a null case.
satirist: Phone call, game, wavelength, iceberg, lifeguard, night nurse: a metaphor per paragraph, promoted to mechanism. The 'ask what else twice' step is plain and checkable; build the chapter on it.
mythmaker: The quiet friend and the night nurse carry real weight, and 'ask what else' works. Game, wavelength and radio pages are lectures with nobody in them; cut to one scene.

modeler: Aim is stated, then wanders through models, wavelength, bandwidth, empathy, cost and bias. Cut to the loop of two models updating; the what-else test is good.
skeptic: Aim is stated: hold your read, ask what else twice. But game, radio, walk and lifeguard images overlap, and iceberg is flagged only as an image. Try this admits its own failure cases.
clinician: Quiet friend returns at the end and 'ask what else twice' is small, testable, forgiving. But flinch-from-your-own-grief and respect-as-space paragraphs diagnose the reader; the bias section runs long.
habit: Hold your read, ask 'what else' twice: perfect rep, with a falsifier. But thirty paragraphs of models, wavelength and bias delay the verbs; trim the middle.
contemplative: A beautiful stance, but thirty-odd paragraphs of models, wavelength, cost, verbs and warnings. It is too much. Keep one habit: hold the read, ask what else twice.
stress: Aim stated early; closes on the friend who went quiet, with failure outcomes named. But game, wavelength and walking-in-step passages repeat one point, and four verbs plus cost sprawl.
gamedesigner: Strong hook and a good 'ask what else twice' move with a feedback signal. But thirty-odd paragraphs of cutscene: models, radio, lifeguard, bias. Trim; the stool has no controller until the end.
structural: Aim is stated, then thirty paragraphs of wavelength, feeling-for, fatigue, bias, iceberg pile on. Radio and falling-into-step pairs repeat. Try this is usable and falsifiable; the body needs trimming.
satirist: Aim is stated, and the quiet friend pays off at the end. But phone call, radio, walk and lifeguard stack metaphors, and the four verbs pad. Pick one image.
mythmaker: 'Ask what else twice' is a clear aim and the quiet friend returns at the end. But game, radio, walk, lifeguard and iceberg stack up, and the middle sits idle, unpeopled.

C032.label: 17. Receiving
C032.desc: chapter "17. Receiving" (PART TWO — HOW TO PRACTICE; paragraphs [P0506] to [P0526])

modeler: Six responses, vote caveat, stable standoff, stuck argument: no single aim. The standoff test (who pays to move) is a real payoff structure. Split chapters.
skeptic: Six responses, stable standoffs, and loop-breaking are three chapters. 'Break it in weeks' has no evidence. The table's two columns are testable.
clinician: Six responses, vote caution, standoffs, stuck arguments: no single aim. Try-this asks the reader to audit their own habit, which risks self-blame. Split it, give one step.
habit: Six responses, standoff test, stuck-loop exit: three chapters. The 'which of six is yours' try-this is usable; the rest is a lecture.
contemplative: Six responses, a standoff test, a stuck argument: three chapters in one. Naming which response is yours is a true, small practice. Let that carry it.
stress: Good honesty that the other person gets a vote. But vote, six-response table, stalemates and the stuck argument are four chapters. No single aim.
gamedesigner: Caution, six-response table, standoff test, deadlock exit: four levels in one. Table-guessing and 'which is yours' is a real playable move; the rest is sprawl.
structural: Vote caveat, six-response table, standoffs, stuck arguments: four chapters. Table with no ranking is good. Ending names the response you lack, not a landing.
satirist: Caution, six-response table, standoffs, dish-fight deadlocks: three chapters in a coat. Table is fun and falsifiable-ish. Split it.
mythmaker: Caution, six-response table, standoffs and stuck arguments: four chapters. Table is rich but nobody lives in it until the Try this. Pick one fight.

modeler: Standoff test (who pays for moving) is a real structure. But four of six responses stay a bare table, so the landing outruns the body. Develop each or narrow it.
skeptic: Six responses is a clear aim. The martial-arts aside, the caseless table and the 'second lock' dodge the aim. Ending asserts a payoff unshown; the task is self-scrutiny.
clinician: Six responses are promised, but only two get deep treatment while the martial-arts and 'other person votes' paragraphs drift. The noticing step is gentle and checkable. Balance the six or narrow the aim.
habit: Six-ways aim is clear. But only 'doing nothing' gets depth, and the deadlock exit isn't one of the six. Table lands before explanation. Develop all six or trim.
contemplative: The six-response table is the heart and the guess-first move works. The vote caution and martial-arts aside restate Part Five. Trim those; the locks earn their place.
stress: Table lists six with no ranking, which is honest, and the Dad's-drinking test can be broken. But the second lock is not one of the six. The chapter is stitched; align it.
gamedesigner: Guess-then-read-the-table is real play, and dinner criticism returns in Try this. The 'other gets a vote' caution and standoff tangents blur the six-responses aim.
structural: Six responses is a clear aim and the table earns its place. The caution and the two locks drift from the table, so it lands on a self-diagnostic with a weak sign. Tighten the ending.
satirist: Six responses, a table, a deadlock lock, a leader picking a fight abroad: sprawling. Aim is a list of options. 'Name which of six you used' is usable but light.
mythmaker: Dinner criticism and the dishes-fight couple live. Table, stable-standoff and deadlock sections sprawl past 'six ways'; the siblings and corner shops are cameos. Name a protagonist.

C033.label: MOVEMENT III — SKEIN (opener)
C033.desc: chapter "MOVEMENT III — SKEIN (opener)" (PART TWO — HOW TO PRACTICE; paragraphs [P0527] to [P0528])

modeler: Many threads versus one thread: nice load-sharing point. Nothing to test, and no stock of kindness named. Fine as opener only.
skeptic: Short and pleasant; the closing prompt is a small noticing. 'Many threads hold' is metaphor with nothing behind it yet.
clinician: Warm, short, aim is clear. 'Think of the last one you gave' is a pleasant noticing, not an action or test.
habit: Lovely image and a tiny prompt ('last one you gave'). But no cue, no step, no sign. A lead-in, not equipment.
contemplative: Short, warm, true. Many threads hold a group. The closing invitation to remember an unlogged kindness is lovely but not yet a step or a test.
stress: Small and honest, and it hands the reader a real person to recall. Nothing to do or test, though.
gamedesigner: Nice image, tight. Closing prompt to remember the unlogged kindness is a gesture, not a move, with no feedback signal.
structural: Tight opener; the unlogged kindness image sets up the Skein. 'Think of the last one' is reflection, not a step. Nothing here about whose rules shape groups.
satirist: Short, warm, and ends on the reader's own uncounted casserole. Earns its landing. Not a task, but it doesn't pretend to be.
mythmaker: Lovely image and the unlogged meal gives a human. But it stops on an invitation, not a landing the body earned.

C034.label: 18. Group Practice
C034.desc: chapter "18. Group Practice" (PART TWO — HOW TO PRACTICE; paragraphs [P0529] to [P0537])

modeler: Four steps you can run Saturday; saying it aloud to witnesses is a causal account. Leverage-ladder paragraph is a detour. Add what shows it failing.
skeptic: Four steps you can run this month. 'Does most of the work' is unsupported, and the leverage ladder paragraph is a detour. No sign it failed.
clinician: Four-step kitchen-table format is concrete and kind. The leverage-ladder paragraph is dense and off-tempo. Rework it into the sharing step.
habit: Four steps around a kitchen table: runnable, with a cue. The leverage-ladder paragraph is a detour; give it a person or move it.
contemplative: A kitchen table, four steps I could do this month. The leverage-ladder paragraph is a lecture inside a gathering. Shorten it to one sentence.
stress: Clear four-step format anyone can run. The leverage ladder digression drifts, and the corny-closing payoff is asserted, not shown. No sign it worked.
gamedesigner: Four-step kitchen-table game is exactly a playable tutorial. The leverage-ladder paragraph is a rulebook insert; rework into one concrete group story.
structural: Four runnable steps and a clear aim. The leverage-ladder paragraph is a tangent from Chapter 14 repeated. Cut it or make it a group lever.
satirist: Four kitchen-table steps, a card, a corny prayer that knows it's corny. The leverage ladder detour is a lecture in the middle of a potluck.
mythmaker: Kitchen table, gym-door friend and the corny prayer have charm; the closing line lands. The leverage-ladder paragraph is a lecture from another chapter.

C035.label: 19. The Skein
C035.desc: chapter "19. The Skein" (PART TWO — HOW TO PRACTICE; paragraphs [P0538] to [P0565])

modeler: Skein, Banner, Braid, four-factor check, Rohn, ledger: too many. Five-versus-one-plus-four critique is good structure thinking. The nod test is usable. Split.
skeptic: Skein, Banner, Braid, four tests, Rohn, kindness: far too many aims. Brain-imaging gets 'suggests', good. The four questions are usable; cut the rest.
clinician: Skein, Banner, Braid, four questions, Rohn, belonging neuroscience, kindness ledger. 'Would I believe this if leaving cost nothing?' may invite rumination. Four-questions test is usable.
habit: Four noticing questions and a nod test are usable. Around them: Rohn, Braid, brain imaging, currency. Twenty-eight paragraphs, many aims. Split it.
contemplative: Twenty-eight paragraphs, many voices: Vonnegut, Rohn, proverbs, brain imaging. Much is wise, too much is said. The four noticing questions are the practice; clear the rest.
stress: Skein, Banner, Braid, four tests, Rohn critique, kindness ledger, belonging science. A pile of topics. The label-disappears test is good; the rest needs splitting.
gamedesigner: Skein, Banner, Braid, karass, four tests, Rohn, kindness ledger: five chapters in one. The four-question noticing and label-vanishes test are usable; split the chapter.
structural: Twenty-eight paragraphs: karass, Banner, belonging science, Rohn, Braid, kindness ledger. Four-question noticing is usable. Split into two chapters; lever is missing.
satirist: Skein, Banner, Braid, karass, Rohn, four questions, ledger: a conceptual pile-up. Label-vanishing test is good, the vermilion line charming. Break into three.
mythmaker: Twenty-eight paragraphs of Banner, Braid, Rohn and belonging science. The lion is dropped after the opening. The six people at the end is earned only late. Split.

modeler: Test, four noticings, Rohn, Braid, ledger, formalizing: a pile of lists. No stock of contact or delay named. Pick one; the weekly four-line check is usable.
skeptic: Promised test plus four noticings plus thickening, then Rohn, Braid and kindness currency wander in. Lovely closing return to the empty chair. Today's four-question check has a stated miss condition.
clinician: Test, four noticings, belonging science, Rohn, ledger, Braid, formalizing: a list of topics. Closing 'six people turn up' outruns the evidence. Today's one-person four-line check is safe and usable.

contemplative: The four noticings are lived and the ending returns to the empty chair. Rohn, Braid, ledger and belonging science are extra words. Say one thing, plainly.
stress: Test, four noticings, thickening: three jobs, plus Rohn, Braid, belonging neuroscience and ledger tangents. Shuffleable. Today's four-question exercise with a month recheck is testable.
gamedesigner: Four-question noticing test is playable with a one-month recheck. Around it, Rohn, ledger, Braid, formalizing pile up: too many mini-games. Aim blurs; cut to test, then thicken.
structural: Test, four noticings, Rohn, kindness ledger, Braid and formalizing: four chapters in one. Closing 'six people turn up' outruns the evidence. Four-question check today is concrete and usable.

mythmaker: Test, four noticings, Rohn, kindness ledger, Braid, belonging science: one aim cannot hold them. Saturday runners and the six who turn up are lovely; too few faces, too much sprawl.

C036.label: 20. Closing the Loop
C036.desc: chapter "20. Closing the Loop" (PART TWO — HOW TO PRACTICE; paragraphs [P0566] to [P0580])

modeler: Dana's lap is a genuine closed loop across scales. Then sprouts, compost, canopy, tide: metaphors with no stocks. Keep Dana, trim botany. Last step is small.
skeptic: Dana is a constructed story doing the work of evidence; 'hope is a loop' is asserted. Canopy passage hedges well. Ending action has no sign of working.
clinician: Dana helps and the final step, one first word in a chosen tone, is bad-day safe. Canopy, compost, hope and suffering crowd the landing. Cut to one thread.
habit: Dana's lap earns the landing and the closing step is concrete: first word, chosen tone. Planting and canopy paragraphs stack metaphors; trim.
contemplative: It ends well: the first word, said on purpose, in a chosen tone. But soil, canopy, compost and sprouts pile up. One image would be enough.
stress: Dana's lap earns the closing and hedges honestly ('rarely runs this cleanly'). Planting, canopy, compost, tide: too many images where Dana's case alone would hold.
gamedesigner: Dana's lap lands the loop nicely. But planting, canopy, compost and shade stack up, and the ending move has no check on whether it worked.

C037.label: PART THREE — THE LOOP TONGUE (opener)
C037.desc: chapter "PART THREE — THE LOOP TONGUE (opener)" (PART THREE — THE LOOP TONGUE; paragraphs [P0581] to [P0585])

modeler: Tells me what the part buys and where to start. Opener only; the second-time conflict claim is untested here. Fine.

clinician: Clear purpose and 'not whose fault' removes blame. Names one tonight step, the Second Pass. Honest about being unsettled. Good.

contemplative: It tells me to try the Second Pass in my next argument, which is good. Three italic paragraphs say the same thing in different clothes. Reduce to one.
stress: Modest and testable: try it in your next argument, and breakage counts as correction. Best risk-taking on the page.
gamedesigner: Good game-manual opener: goal, payoff, fastest route (Chapter 5, try in next argument). Honest about being unsettled. This is how to onboard.
structural: Opener states aim, payoff and fastest route. Try it tonight, and breaking counts as correction. Honest about being unsettled.

mythmaker: Promises a concrete ability and a fastest route, in plain voice. Stops at instructions; no one is shown mid-argument to make the promise felt.

C038.label: 1. Why Lines Break Loops
C038.desc: chapter "1. Why Lines Break Loops" (PART THREE — THE LOOP TONGUE; paragraphs [P0586] to [P0596])

modeler: Best at this scale: phone sentence shows the missing feedback arc, each check speeds tomorrow's anxiety. Line, loop, tree is learnable. Wants an explicit delay and failure sign.

clinician: Phone-morning exercise is concrete, nonjudgmental, causal. Line, loop, tree land three at once. Slow that, and show what the new sentence changes.

contemplative: Beginning with my own sentence aloud is right. Then line, loop and tree arrive together, and the ending only restates. Stop after the phone example.
stress: Phone sentence demonstrates the failure on the reader. But line, loop and tree arrive at once near the end, and it just stops.
gamedesigner: Great hook: I write the phone sentence and watch it fail. Last paragraphs rush line/loop/tree and fade out instead of landing.
structural: The phone sentence shows the line-loop gap well. The ending is a thin aside, not a landing, and nothing says how to tell the exercise worked.

mythmaker: Reader's own phone sentence is the person; the chapter turns it into a loop and back. Missing a step to try and a sign it failed.

C039.label: 2. The Grammar of Pattern
C039.desc: chapter "2. The Grammar of Pattern" (PART THREE — THE LOOP TONGUE; paragraphs [P0597] to [P0615])

modeler: Nine-word glossary, Tree transfer, Go proverb, fern history, Word versus Label: five aims. Predictiveness test for names is actionable and checkable. Cut to vocabulary plus test.
skeptic: Nine terms, Go proverb, fern history, Word/Label test: too many things at once. The 'does a plain phrase do the job' test is falsifiable. Split it.
clinician: Nine terms plus Go, fern, Tywin, pilot's licence. 'Say I think we're in a Loop tonight' is a good small step with a visible response. Cut tangents.
habit: Nine-word glossary, then Go, fern, Word-versus-Label. 'Say I think we're in a Loop tonight' is a real rep; the second half is a different chapter.
contemplative: Nine words, a Go proverb, a fern, a king, a pilot's licence: clever and crowded. 'I think we're in a Loop' tonight is the practice. Trim to that.
stress: Nine-word glossary, then Go proverb, fern history, Word/Label and pilot's licence. Too many aims. 'Does the phrase do the job?' is a real test; keep it, split the rest.
gamedesigner: Nine terms front-loaded is a rulebook nobody reads, then Go, ferns, Word/Label pile on. 'Say I think we're in a Loop tonight' is the playable bit.
structural: Nine-word glossary, then Tree transfer, Go proverb, fern, Word versus Label: three chapters. Trying 'Loop' tonight is usable; the end is a caveat. Split.
satirist: Nine capitalized words, a Go proverb, Mandelbrot, Tywin Lannister: glossary plus lecture. Fern history is real Bryson. 'We're in a Loop' is usable tonight.
mythmaker: Nine definitions, then fern, Go and Tywin. Reads as a glossary with anecdotes bolted on; too many concepts at once. The proverb landed.

modeler: Nine words, Tree, transfer, Go proverb, fern, king and pilot overload one chapter. Lake house return and the predict-the-lap test are good. Cut, and teach three words at a time.
skeptic: The lake-house return and 'can they finish the lap' test make a checkable landing. Go proverb ('measurably worse') and fern history are asserted tangents; nine definitions arrive as one dump.
clinician: The aim is two things, words plus a test. Transfer, Go and fern paragraphs each pull a different way. The lake-house return and 'finish the lap' test land well. Rework or merge the tangents.
habit: Two aims (words, plus a test). Nine words, then Tree, Word, Label, Go, fern: terms pile up. Lake-house return works; the finish-the-lap test is checkable. Split the chapter.
contemplative: Lake house return lands well and the tonight-test is checkable. Go proverb, fern history, Tywin and pilot licence pile on one test. Keep one illustration.
stress: Lake-house return is earned and the phone-lap test can fail. But it has two aims, and Go, fern and pilot's-licence detours pad it. Cut to one test, one case.
gamedesigner: Six definitions in a row is a rulebook dump, then Go, fern, king, pilot tangents. Lake house return plus 'finish the lap' test is a good playtest signal.
structural: Aim is stated and the lake house return pays off. But Go proverb, fern history, Tree and transfer paragraphs sprawl and could be reordered; the Word/Label test is usable and falsifiable. Prune the tangents.
satirist: Nine words plus a Word/Label test is two aims. Tywin's king line passes the bar test and the lake-house return lands. Cut the Tree detour; jargon is critiquing jargon.
mythmaker: Lake house returns nicely at the close. But nine definitions in a row, then Go, ferns and Tywin as sideshows; no one is standing in them. Teach three words, with a face.

modeler: Nine words land at once, then Tree, Go, fern, Word/Label. Padding and a spike. Predict-or-not test and finish-the-lap check are crisp. Trim.
skeptic: Nine words dumped at once, then Tree, Go proverb, fern and Tywin as support: vivid, not evidence. Closing test, can they finish the lap, is checkable. Cut the pile.
clinician: Aim is two things (words and a test). Tree, Go, fern, Tywin and pilot's licence overlap and nine definitions arrive densely. The lake-house return and 'can they finish the lap' check earn the ending.
habit: 'I think we're in a Loop' tonight, and the finished lap is the sign. But aim is words plus test, nine definitions stack at once, and Go, fern and king drift.
contemplative: Nine words, Tree, Go, fern, king, pilot's licence: the mind agitates. The lake-house return is lovely and 'try one tonight' is usable. Fewer images, more breath.
stress: Aim is words and a test, so 'and also'. Go, fern, king, pilot stack up where one would carry it. Lake-house return and 'can they finish the lap' check are earned.
gamedesigner: Nine words dumped as a rulebook, then Tree, Go, fern, king, pilot. Two aims: words and a word-test. 'Finish the lap' check is a good playtest signal; move the test earlier.
structural: Aim is words plus a test, which is two aims. Go, fern, Tywin and pilot detours cluster. Lake house return lands modestly and honestly; tonight's Loop test is checkable.
satirist: Nine capitalized words arrive in one dump, then Go, ferns, Tywin and pilots argue for them. Lake-house test is good. Teach three words, earn the rest.
mythmaker: Nine definitions in a row, then Go, fern, Tywin and pilot. Aim is words and a test. The lake-house return rhymes nicely, but the body is a glossary; give each word someone.

C040.label: 3. Sketching a Loop
C040.desc: chapter "3. Sketching a Loop" (PART THREE — THE LOOP TONGUE; paragraphs [P0616] to [P0624])

modeler: Sign-counting gives a real mechanism: even minuses reinforce, odd balance. But no delays or limits, and the close merely restates the notation.
skeptic: Notation plus a countable sign rule is checkable. Phone-loop causes ('relief teaches you to need it') are asserted, not shown, but the napkin ending is earned.

stress: Rare chapter that can be tested: the sign-count settles ↻ versus ⤸ with a worked phone case. Honest skip clause. Ending is a touch tidy.

structural: Clear aim, a countable sign test, a phone example. Still no lever: whose market? Name who builds the checking loop.
satirist: Four marks plus a sign-count you can verify with the phone loop. Bryson-grade: you can count it. Opening throat-clearing aside, this earns its napkin.
mythmaker: The anxiety-and-phone napkin has a face and a countable sign test. Lovely. The kitchen-table close returns to the napkin and pays it off.

gamedesigner: Name-your-scale is a clean move, then it drifts into three kinds of knowing and 'nothing is running'. Cosmos appears unprompted. Split the back half.
