structural: Aim and the reply-all ending are well planted, and the sideways lever is concrete. But the reading advice appears twice, and the stable/stalled pair pads the middle; dedupe and trim.
satirist: Clear aim and a usable reply-all example. Table is dense, three directions plus seki edge toward jargon. Builds well to the closing line. Tighten the Standoff passages.
mythmaker: The reply-all colleague is a real face and returns at the close, nicely. But P0845 and P0846 do the same job, and the seki detour feels bolted on.

C059.label: 3. The Skein-Kin
C059.desc: chapter "3. The Skein-Kin" (PART FIVE — THE STANDING THIRDS; paragraphs [P0855] to [P0861])

modeler: Eleven-row table, then the chapter swerves into one figure. Aim splits. Only Second-Order Design gets a mechanism, the return path. Give the other ten a stock and a limit.
skeptic: Table of eleven figures, then one buried argument. The return-path test is checkable, but the aim only emerges late. Lead with Second-Order Design.
clinician: Table dominates and Second-Order Design lesson is bolted on; P0860 repeats P0859. The push (check what reaches the rule-setter) is a real, testable step.
habit: The return-path question is a real test I can run. But the table dumps eleven figures first, and the last two paragraphs restate the inversion. Cut one.
contemplative: Aim is clear: read by return path. But the table dwarfs the teaching, and the 'pleased team' opener has no person standing in it. Give it a face.
stress: Table plus one figure's reading; two aims. The return-path test is breakable and the workaround image pays off. Trim the table to what the reading needs.
gamedesigner: Table dump with one figure doing the teaching. Return-path test is a real move I can run. Cut the table to a few rows.
structural: Eleven-row table then one figure; aim splits. P0860 restates P0859. The return-path test and push on information flow are real levers.
satirist: Eleven-row table of capitalized Thirds, then a pivot to one. Busy, busy. The usable bit (does the result reach whoever sets the rule?) hides at the end.
mythmaker: An eleven-row table, then a second chapter about Second-Order Design. Nobody stands in the rows. The return-path test is the one usable thing; give each row a person.

modeler: Two aims: survey eleven figures, then one deep dive. P0857, P0858 and P0860 restate the inversion. Table dumps eleven loops before return path is taught. Cut repeats, teach loop first.
skeptic: Eleven table rows asserted with no evidence, then a pivot to one figure; the feelings-versus-reading point appears twice. The Priya return-path test is checkable and earns the 1. Trim to one worked figure.
clinician: Aim is stated, but eleven figures plus a deep dive on one pull two ways. The table is a reference dump. Ending on a push, not a landing. Test is concrete, small, safe: ask who set the rule.
habit: Opening now promises one thing: stay with Second-Order Design, run a test. But the eleven-row table is a catalogue that dilutes it, and the Priya case appears only in the table. Trim rows.
contemplative: Two aims: survey eleven figures, then dwell on one. P0860 repeats P0859's inversion. The claim lands before it is taught. The ask-the-rule-setter test and Priya's spreadsheet are usable and warm.
stress: Opening names the aim and the Priya test is runnable and can fail. But P0860 restates P0859's inversion, and ten rows get one line each. Merge them, give two rows a person.
gamedesigner: New intro states the aim well. But ten rows are a cutscene table of untaught Dyad-Kin names, and P0857/P0860 repeat the same inversion. Teach one row; trim the rest.
structural: New opener names the aim and the rule-setter lever is real. But P0857, P0859 and P0860 say the pole is hidden from feeling three times, and ten rows of dense table arrive untaught.
satirist: Opener now says the aim, and Priya finally has a face. But P0857 and P0860 say the same thing twice, and the table is jargon soup. Merge them. Test is good.
mythmaker: Aim is signposted up front. But eleven figures arrive as one abstract table with one-phrase scenes, and P0857 and P0860 repeat each other. Priya is the only face; give each figure one.

C060.label: 4. The Culture-Kin
C060.desc: chapter "4. The Culture-Kin" (PART FIVE — THE STANDING THIRDS; paragraphs [P0862] to [P0866])

modeler: Table, Goodhart, Newton and Leibniz, then a warning. Three jobs, no stocks or limits. The clinic clock is the lone case. Unusable as built.
skeptic: Catalogue plus two essays, self-labelled provisional. Nothing to try or test; Goodhart and Newton are stories, not evidence of the mechanism.
clinician: Catalogue table plus two unrelated figures, ending on a provisional warning. Nobody stands in it and no step is offered. Give the reader one thing to check this week.
habit: A table of seven figures plus two essays. What do I do Monday? Nothing here. It ends on a warning. Give one Goodhart check to run.
contemplative: Table, Goodhart, Newton and a warning: three aims, no practice. Ends on a caveat, not a landing. Pick one figure and give a today-sized test.
stress: Table, Goodhart, Newton, then a provisional warning. Nobody stands in it but a clinic. Admits it is unchecked; give one testable step.
gamedesigner: Seven-row table, then two unrelated figures. Chapter itself says 'questions, not answers'. No move, no signal; pick one figure and test it.
structural: Catalogue plus Goodhart plus Newton tangent; ends on a disclaimer. No owner or lever named; give one test the reader can run.
satirist: A table, Goodhart in a trench coat, a Newton aside, and a warning that it's all provisional. Foma, labeled as such, but no step.
mythmaker: A table of abstractions, a Goodhart gloss, a Newton scrap, then a warning to hold it all loosely. The clinic is the only person. No step to take.

modeler: Clinic opener and the check-one-figure test work. But a seven-row table lands untaught, the convergence paragraph drifts off the question, and no stock or delay is drawn.
skeptic: Clinic clock opens and closes it, and the figure-check carries a stated 'young measure may be unread' caveat. Newton aside is a fork, but I'll allow it.
clinician: Clinic aim and clock-check are safe and small. But six of seven patterns have nobody standing in them, just table rows; give each a face.
habit: Good: clinic image and a this-week check on one figure, with a sign. But the Independent Convergence paragraph is a different job; rework it into the same test.
contemplative: Clinic opens and closes it, and the one-figure check has a sign. The Newton paragraph is a second subject, and the table is dense. Trim it to a sentence.
stress: Clinic opener pays off in the close, and the check can fail. But seven table rows mostly lack a person standing in them. Give each a case.
gamedesigner: Clinic hook and 'one question' set the aim; the try-this-week check has a pass/fail sign. Five of seven table rows get no case or person.
structural: Clinic image and one figure to check earn it. But the Convergence paragraph and a second provisional warning drift off the aim; fold or cut to one.
satirist: Clinic clock is a real joke with a real bite, and the figure test works at a bar. But seven-row table is mostly jargon nobody stands in.
mythmaker: The clinic clock returns at the close with a test; lovely. But the table's six other figures have nobody standing in them. Give Newton's rival camp a face.

C061.label: 5. The World-Kin
C061.desc: chapter "5. The World-Kin" (PART FIVE — THE STANDING THIRDS; paragraphs [P0867] to [P0871])

modeler: Car lift, table, Sweden, honesty test blur the aim. The 'rejects the book, still agrees on direction' test is falsifiable and good. Cut the rest to serve it.
skeptic: Sweden gives someone to stand in it, and the reject-the-book agreement test is checkable. But the aim splits and the ending pivots to a disclaimer.
clinician: Strangers and Sweden give people to stand in it. But it holds four jobs, and the closing 'reject the book and still agree' test is the one usable check.
habit: Strangers lifting a car, then a table, then Sweden. The aim wanders. The advocacy test is clever but no cue, no step. Name one two-minute move.
contemplative: Strangers lifting the car is lovely, but the chapter wanders from biosphere to Sweden to honesty test. The 'rejects the book' check is usable; the rest is scaffolding.
stress: Many-hands aim lands via the car and Sweden. The could-a-rejecter-agree test is breakable. The table is thin; give each figure a face.
gamedesigner: Car-lift and Sweden are great hooks, but the table sits idle between them. The reject-the-book polarity test is a real checkable signal.
structural: Car-lifting and Sweden carry collective push well. Ending test (could a rejecter agree?) is checkable. Still thin on whose rules.
satirist: Sweden's 3 September 1967 passes the Bryson test. Biosphere aside is a tangent. The skeptic-at-a-bar pole test is genuinely usable.
mythmaker: Strangers lifting the car and Sweden's night are real people, but the table sits between them. The reject-the-book test is a good checkable step.

modeler: One claim, one test, and the car-lifters return at the end. Sweden is a coordination switch, not a loop; I'd still like the stock and delay.
skeptic: The 'could a rejecter agree on the pole' test is real calibration. But biosphere and carbon-price paragraph stacks caveats; trim it to one sentence.
clinician: Strangers at the car carries the claim and the lift. The test is small, checkable, and blame-free. Biosphere paragraph is dense but earns its place.
habit: Strangers at the car return as the ending. 'Ask someone who hasn't read the book which way it points' is doable today and falsifiable. Keep.
contemplative: The car and the lift return at the end, and the agreement test is small. But Sweden restates the strangers, and the biosphere paragraph is heavy. Merge them.
stress: Car and Sweden do the same job twice. The 'would a skeptic agree on the pole' test is real and can fail. Merge the images.
gamedesigner: Strangers at the car and Sweden carry the claim. The 'same direction of lift' test is playable today with a clear miss condition.
structural: Strangers at the car, Sweden, and a pole test anyone could run. Many hands, one lift: a lever. Good.
satirist: Sweden, 3 September 1967, ten to five: finally a date. Car-lifting strangers return at the end. The agree-on-direction test is checkable. Keep it.
mythmaker: Strangers at the car, then Sweden, then 'same direction of lift': a real rhyme. The biosphere paragraph and table are abstract nouns with no one inside.

C062.label: 6. The Infinite Boundary — Cosmos Scale
C062.desc: chapter "6. The Infinite Boundary — Cosmos Scale" (PART FIVE — THE STANDING THIRDS; paragraphs [P0872] to [P0878])

modeler: Aim is clear: no poles at the totality. But the fractions picture and the god paragraphs repeat. 'Drift' has no stock or flow behind it.
skeptic: Aim is clear, but fractions, G-O-D, believers and fatalism circle one point. The 'drift' claim is unevidenced. Reduce to one paragraph and one test.
clinician: The God and fatalism detours outgrow the riverbank opening. Nothing to do or test here. Cut to the stopping point and say where to push.
habit: Pure abstraction: fractions, drift, faith. It says nothing to do beyond 'push below.' Nothing to try before breakfast. Give one action.
contemplative: The river post image is good, then G-O-D, drift, faith and fatalism pile up. Too much defence of the framework; nothing to do. Cut to the breath.
stress: G-O-D, a drift, fatalism made 'uncheckable': a theory of everything that shields itself. No test, no cost, no step. Show the storm.
gamedesigner: Aim is clear: leverage ends here. Then fractions, God, faith, fatalism pile up. Pure cutscene; nothing to try.
structural: Fractions, G-O-D, believer seam, fatalism: four jobs. Mood, not mechanism. Nothing to try; split off and keep the fatalism point.
satirist: Initials G-O-D, a drift, a believer's seam, fatalism: grand, hushed, and nothing to do. Fails the bar test. Label it foma or cut it.
mythmaker: Riverbank is a fine opening image, then fractions, God and fatalism pile on. The ending is a refusal, not a landing. Nothing to try.

modeler: Promised one job, then drifts into theology and fatalism. The drift is a metaphor with no stock. It ends on a restatement, never returning to the riverbank, and gives no test.
skeptic: Honest about its limits, yet 'the drift is real' outruns anything shown. Nothing here can be tried or contradicted; the practice is deferred to other chapters.
clinician: Kind to believers, but paragraphs 875 and 876 do the same job twice. Fractions, drift, fatalism pile up, and there is no step to take.
habit: Faith and god get two paragraphs doing one job, and G-O-D, drift and fatalism stack up. No step for Monday. Give one small check, merge 875 and 876.
contemplative: Promises where pushing starts, then wanders into faith and fatalism. The drift is said twice, with no step to try. Keep one drift paragraph and give a practice.
stress: Drift claim is unfalsifiable and 'nothing larger' is grandiose. Fractions, G-O-D and fatalism pile up. No step to try. Cut to one image, add a test.
gamedesigner: Riverbank hook works. Drift appears twice (P0875, P0876), the fractions detour is extra, and there's nothing to try. Merge the drift passages and add a small check.
structural: Aim is clear, but the drift and believer paragraphs run long and overlap. No step: 'push the nearest figures' is advice nothing could contradict.
satirist: G-O-D wink, fractions, drift, fatalism: four ideas in a hushed voice. Bokonon would label it foma. Nothing to try; fatalism 'uncheckable' is a shrug.
mythmaker: The riverbank is a fine image but gets dropped. Fractions, drift and God stack up; it ends on bare 'recursion chain terminates'. Return to the bank; give fatalism a person.

modeler: Aim is clear and the riverbank-to-post landing is earned. But P0875 and P0876 repeat the drift point, and drift has no stock or flow. No small test to run.
skeptic: One stated job, and the riverpost image returns. But the seam passage repeats the drift point, and 'the drift is real' is unsupported. Nothing here is testable; add one fatalism check.
clinician: Aim is clear, and the 'you can't fix it, push below' framing is gentle. But the fractions, God and fatalism detours pile up, and no step exists beyond 'push nearer your hands'. Give one small test.
habit: Aim is stated (where reading stops, pushing begins). But the fractions picture, G-O-D and fatalism paragraphs pile concepts, and the close is a push with no first step. Name one figure to push tomorrow.
contemplative: The aim is plain and the river post returns to close, earned. But the faith and fatalism passages overlap and run long. Nothing is offered to try today.
stress: Aim is stated: where reading stops and pushing begins. But P0875 and P0876 do the same hedging job, and 'drift is real' and the fatalism point cannot be broken. Offer no test; add one or cut.
gamedesigner: Aim is clear and the river post pays off at the end. Fraction picture and the faith and fatalism paragraphs overlap, and no test to run today. Merge, add a move.
structural: Aim is stated and the river post returns to close it. But P0875 and P0876 restate the drift and the seam, and no lever or test exists; fatalism is only declared uncheckable.
satirist: The G-O-D wink is honest, which I like. But believer-reassurance appears twice (P0875, P0876), fractions detour is ornament, and the close preaches. No test; add one.
mythmaker: The riverbank post returns in the last paragraph and earns it. But the drift and faith paragraphs overlap, and the failed year has no named person. No test to run.

C063.label: 7. What This Catalogue Is Not
C063.desc: chapter "7. What This Catalogue Is Not" (PART FIVE — THE STANDING THIRDS; paragraphs [P0879] to [P0886])

modeler: 'Does the extra figure change what you would do?' is a real test, and traffic is a clean case. The adding-figures paragraph is an authors' tangent. Move it.
skeptic: Strongest skeptic-friendly chapter: 'does the extra figure change what you'd do' is testable. Over-reading and under-reading paragraphs overlap and need merging.
clinician: Safe on a bad day: it licenses stopping. 'Does the extra figure change what you'd do?' is checkable, and the late-for-traffic landing is earned.
habit: Best test yet: does the extra figure change what you'd do? Traffic example lands. But stopping and both-failures paragraphs overlap. Merge them.
contemplative: Stop at the simplest reading. Late because of traffic is the right quiet landing. The extra-figure test is small, checkable, and humble. Best chapter here.
stress: Modest and self-limiting: stop when the extra figure changes nothing. The traffic example holds. The 'adding' list drifts from the aim.
gamedesigner: Good rulebook. 'Does the extra figure change what you'd do?' is a clear test, and the traffic line lands it.
structural: Clear stop-rule; 'does the extra figure change what you would do' is a usable test; late-because-of-traffic lands the chapter.
satirist: Best joke in the book: 'late because of traffic.' Test 'does the extra figure change what you'd do?' is real. Paragraphs 880-884 repeat each other.
mythmaker: Late-for-traffic man finally gives the abstractions a body, and returns at the end. Test is usable. Opening and closing limits repeat each other.

C064.label: 8. Going to Ground
C064.desc: chapter "8. Going to Ground" (PART FIVE — THE STANDING THIRDS; paragraphs [P0887] to [P0898])

modeler: Conservation and second law carry the physics. Then Zhuangzi and a field metaphor take over. 'Seed one thing' has no outcome to check. Close on the physics.
skeptic: Confident metaphysics on death, with Zhuangzi and the Buddha as convergence 'evidence'. Cheaper explanations are left standing. 'Seed what you can' has no sign of working.
clinician: The 'experiencer does not continue' line lands blunt for a grieving reader. Six strands (physics, Fold, sages) pile up. The seed step has no sign of working.
habit: Moving, and it returns to the field image. But it's reflection, not a step. 'Seed what you can' has no cue or sign of success.
contemplative: Honest about death, but three continuations and Zhuangzi's drum run long. The closing seed is small and usable. Breathe more, argue less.
stress: Confident claims about death no one can check; the Zhuangzi evidence is a stack of anecdotes. The seed step cannot fail. Cut certainty.
gamedesigner: Death, physics, Zhuangzi, Sacrifice Trap, seeding. Too many aims and too many concepts at once; the one action is vague and has no signal.
structural: Laws, Fold, noticing, Zhuangzi, comfort, today: stacked, overlapping. Landing is larger than evidence. Seed-one-thing has no sign it worked.
satirist: Conservation and second law are real physics; the rest is eulogy. Ends on a confident 'mostly good' the body can't verify. One checkable step missing.
mythmaker: Heavy claim, three continuations, physics, three traditions, and a practice all at once. The field returns at the close. Seed advice has no sign of working.

modeler: Conservation plus second law is real mechanism, and the seed-it-unseen step is checkable. The last paragraphs repeat each other: Sacrifice Trap twice, comfort twice. Rework one.
skeptic: 'Do it unseen' is a checkable sign. But conservation, entropy, Fold, noticing and convergence crowd in together, with two paragraphs of comfort repeating each other; split and slow.
clinician: Names loss honestly and ends on a small seed with a sign. But 'hardest sentence' and the Sacrifice Trap jab could sting a griever; soften.
habit: Tonight's action with a sign ('would you do it unseen') is good. But seven dense paragraphs on physics and noticing before it; 897 and 898 overlap. Trim to essentials.
contemplative: Gentle aim, but too much: conservation, second law, noticing, convergence. Comfort and noticing overlap. The seed step is good. Fewer ideas, one breath each.
stress: Honest about testimony versus evidence, and the unseen-action test can fail. Comfort is graded, not blanket. Ending is plain enough to hold under stress.
gamedesigner: Father's voice gives a human anchor and the 'do it unseen' signal works. P0896 and P0897 restate the no-separate-self point; trim to one.
structural: Gives a small seeding step and a sign it works. The noticing, comfort and 'today' paragraphs restate one point; rework into one.
satirist: Candid about death and about thin evidence (testimony, not measurement). Daughter's 'sleep on it' carries it. 'Do it unseen' is a checkable step.
mythmaker: Zhuangzi drumming and the daughter hearing her father's voice carry real blood. Ends on the epigraph's field with a doable step. Physics paragraphs run long.

C065.label: 9. Becoming a Third
C065.desc: chapter "9. Becoming a Third" (PART FIVE — THE STANDING THIRDS; paragraphs [P0899] to [P0906])

modeler: Aim is stated, but 'resonant and durable' has no mechanism, ratio or decay rate. The ending is unfalsifiable by design. Needs a stock-and-loss account of survival.
skeptic: An origin story admitted to be uncheckable ('nobody can check'). Unaimable by its own account, so nothing to do. Landing is lyrical, not earned.
clinician: Gentle and shame-free, but it says it can't be aimed at, so there's no step. The grandmother speculation is padding and the ending relies on cadence.
habit: The gradient is nice, then it says you can't aim at it. So what do I do Monday? Pointless to a habit builder. Add one small rep.
contemplative: The grandmother who could not stop starting things is a real face. But the gradient restates itself and nothing is offered to try.
stress: An origin story offered as story, and a grandmother nobody can check. 'Cannot be aimed at' means nothing to try. Needs a case and a test.
gamedesigner: Aim is clear, but it is a gradient told as story, and the chapter says you can't aim at it. No move, no signal.
structural: Gradient from fade to Third builds cleanly. But admits it cannot be aimed at; no step, no test. Pure reception.
satirist: Origin story admitted as story, which earns a smile. But 'cannot be aimed at' means no reader action, and the grandmother can't be checked.
mythmaker: The recipe and the grandmother carry it, but the gradient repeats itself. Closes on a grand payoff about outliving the seeing, bigger than shown. Nothing to try.

modeler: Gradient and the copied-once check are good, and the recipe cook returns. The fade-by-handoff cause is good. Skein-scale and origin paragraphs overlap in function.
skeptic: Gradient, hedged origin story and a first-copy check within a month. Admits the claim is story, not record. The cook image returns paid for.
clinician: Gentle, shame-free, and the recipe image returns at the close. The first-copy test is small, checkable, and says finding none is no failure.
habit: The 'try this today' with a one-month look for a first copy works. 905 and 906 both say it can't be aimed at; reduce to one sentence.
contemplative: The cook callback is earned and the first-copy check is small. But origin and transcendence say the same thing twice, and the tier paragraph is padding.
stress: Origin story is flagged as unprovable and the first-copy test is checkable. Closing 'one idea' line outruns what the body showed. Trim it.
gamedesigner: Gradient is learnable and the closing recipe cook pays off the opening. The 'try this today' step is checkable, with failure defined as one person wide.
structural: Gradient, then a copy-check with a recipe-cook landing that returns the opening image. Tight. Whose rules shape copying goes unnamed.
satirist: Admits the origin story is a story, then offers a check: has anyone copied you? Recipe image pays off. Grandmother joke earns its place.
mythmaker: The recipe cook returns at the close, grandmother is a nice ghost, and the look-for-a-copy test is honest about its limits. Earned.

C066.label: PART SIX — WEAVINGS (opener)
C066.desc: chapter "PART SIX — WEAVINGS (opener)" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0907] to [P0910])

modeler: Opener states the aim and promise cleanly. It stays preview and asks the reader to bring a question. Nothing to test yet.
skeptic: Clear promise in short paragraphs. But 'at least one angle you would not have found' is a claim with no way to tell if it failed.
clinician: Clear promise and a small ask: bring one question you keep circling. The closing paragraph restates rather than builds.
habit: Finally: bring one question tonight, lay cards. Good cue. But P0910 repeats the setup and the promise is large. Tighten to one tonight-sized instruction.
contemplative: Four short italic previews, each saying what the part is for. Clear, but it is signage; the reader is told, not given a first step.
stress: Clear purpose, but it promises 'at least one new angle' without saying how you would know. The last paragraph repeats the first.
gamedesigner: Clear promise and 'bring one question' is a hook. But it only announces; there is no first move or sign of working yet.
structural: Previews are clear but lean on unexplained terms (rings, pull, spread). Opener promises use; delivers none itself.
satirist: Honest opener: aim, payoff, 'bring one question.' Brisk. But no sign yet of how you'd know a Weaving worked.
mythmaker: Opener states purpose and promise, and says to bring a question you keep circling. That question is the only person here. Promises a practice without equipping it yet.

modeler: Reread-the-line test gives a falsifiable sign. But the opener says what the cards are twice, in the quick-run and card paragraphs. Merge them.
skeptic: Three preview lines overlap, and nothing builds. The 'if nothing changed, it hasn't worked' test is a fair sign but needs an actual step.
clinician: Reread-the-line check is a real sign of failure, good. But three italic previews overlap, nobody stands in it, and the close just stops.
habit: Write one question, lay cards, reread the line: usable, with a sign. But it points to cards and rings before defining them; forward references pile up.
contemplative: Short and calm, with a clear tonight task. Rings, pulls and spreads are named before they are taught. The ending is a check, not an arrival.
stress: Short opener with a built-in failure condition: if nothing beside the line changed, it has not worked. Modest claim, and it holds.
gamedesigner: Part opener stacks Weaving, Standing Third, rings, distances and speeds in three short paragraphs. The reread-the-line test is a good feedback signal. Cut the front-loaded terms.
structural: Opener states what the part is for and gives a tonight step with a failure sign. Still all private reflection, no group lever.
satirist: Short opener with a one-line recipe and a failure condition: line unchanged means not worked. Little build, but honest and brisk.
mythmaker: Four lines of promise with nobody in them; the cup and a person with a stuck argument belong here. 'Read the line again' is the usable bit.

C067.label: 0. What a Weaving Is
C067.desc: chapter "0. What a Weaving Is" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0911] to [P0919])

modeler: Cup and perspective are metaphor. The tarot defence is long and repeats itself. 'Is this here?' is checkable but has no sign of success.
skeptic: Good honesty about tarot, and 'is this here?' is checkable. But it gives no step to try yet and no sign the angle helped.
clinician: The cup image is strong and 'is this here?' is checkable and blame-free. The ending drifts into connections instead of returning to the cup.
habit: The cup is nice, but the tarot defence runs three paragraphs. The practice itself is described, not given as steps. Put the steps up front.
contemplative: The cup in the hand is a good start. Then orthographic, perspective, tarot, three changes, and five bolded claims. Too many concepts stacked; soften and trim.
stress: Honest about tarot, and cards that describe can be wrong. But the cup and the cards go over the same ground twice, with no step to try.
gamedesigner: Cup is a nice hook, then tarot defense and three bolded rule-blocks. Never gets my hands on a card; the landing is a vague 'slow down'.
structural: Cup image opens well but drops. Three tarot-disclaimer paragraphs overlap. Practice defined, not yet doable; ending is reassurance.
satirist: The cup is good and the tarot confession is the book's most Bokonon moment. Yet nothing here to try or test; it's all justification.
mythmaker: The cup is a good seed, then dropped for tarot comparison. Ending is connection bookkeeping, not a return to the cup. Checkable is-this-here, but no step yet.

modeler: The cup turning and Ines's checkable Sunday call earn their place. Orthographic, perspective and the mantra arrive together in one paragraph, a difficulty spike. Split them.
skeptic: Ines gives the cards someone to stand in, and 'nothing new said means it failed' is an honest test. Orthographic, perspective and mantra arrive together; space them.
clinician: Ines and the cup land well, and 'did not work, try tomorrow' is kind. But orthographic, perspective, and the mantra arrive together in one paragraph.
habit: Ines and 'one question, four cards tonight' are strong. But 913 hands over orthographic, perspective and the mantra in one paragraph. Split or drop one.
contemplative: The cup is lovely and the closing return to it lands. But the orthographic paragraph stacks three terms plus a mantra. The tarot paragraphs repeat each other.
stress: Ines gives a checkable case and the cup lands. Three 'nothing is consulted' paragraphs overlap, and the last one carries two jobs. Rework them.
gamedesigner: Cup, tarot comparison and Ines's check each add something. Three-step method with a 'did not work' signal, and the ending returns to the cup.
structural: Cup turned, tarot named plainly, Ines checks a Sunday call, and a null result is allowed. Lands on the cup. Solid.
satirist: Owns the tarot comparison out loud, which is the Bokonon move. Ines is a person with a checkable Sunday. Cup image returns. Good.
mythmaker: Cup opens and closes the chapter, Ines gives the idea a face and a checkable answer. The tarot answer is plain and disarming. Three short parallel items drag slightly.

C068.label: 1. The Deck
C068.desc: chapter "1. The Deck" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0920] to [P0933])

modeler: A reference table is not a build. The rate-of-change phrasing in the poles is the nearest thing to a stock. Chapter ends on a ritual reminder, not a landing.
skeptic: Reference tables, not a built argument. Reading each card as Tending or Fraying is vague enough that either answer fits. Needs a worked check.
clinician: A reference table, not a chapter. Some Self-Kin readings (Salve, Mask) could hand a low-mood reader ammunition. 'Draw The Mask, ask' is a usable step.
habit: A fifty-card lookup table is a reference, not a chapter. No order builds. Usable only mid-Weaving. Trim to one drawn example with a named answer.
contemplative: A reference deck, not a chapter. The pocket tables repeat Part Five. 'Draw The Mask and ask' is usable. Breathe: show one card lived.
stress: A reference table, not a chapter. It repeats Part Five and ends on a reminder ritual. Fine as an appendix; no build or test.
gamedesigner: A reference table, not a chapter; four of these tables. Fine as a lookup, but there's no teaching, no arc, no feedback.
structural: A reference deck, not a built argument; shuffling tables loses nothing. Mask example is the only usable step.
satirist: A pocket reference repeating Part Five's tables nearly verbatim. Fifty-two as a card deck is a decent joke. 'Draw The Mask, ask' is usable.
mythmaker: A reference lookup with almost no one in it. Tables could be shuffled freely. The Mask example offers one small test. Put a person in the tables.

modeler: Dana's shoes-by-the-door count is the right causal check, with a sign. But the tables could be shuffled, and Dana's follow-up sits oddly after the never-drawn paragraph.
skeptic: Dana's count of three runs in five mornings against one is exactly the evidence I want. The tables are lookup, so order doesn't build; expect no arc.
clinician: Dana's counted runs and 'never a verdict on you' are what I want at 3 a.m. The cosmos paragraph is a bypass-flavored aside; rework or move.
habit: Dana's shoes and the count of three runs in five mornings is the right rep, with a sign. But Dana's follow-up sits after the Cosmos note; move it up.
contemplative: Dana's number and her next-week sign make this usable. But the long tables repeat Part Five, the order is shufflable, and the Cosmos note is decoration.
stress: Dana's shoes and run counts make a card falsifiable, and next week's recheck gives a sign. This is the stress-tested kind of advice.
gamedesigner: Dana's shoes and run count make a clean hit/miss demo, and the revisit pays off. The pocket tables mostly duplicate Part Five, so the pairs repeat each other's job.
structural: Dana's shoes and run count give a checkable reading and a next-week sign. Deck as names, not facts, is honest.
satirist: Fifty-two like playing cards is a charming pitch; Dana's shoes and three-in-five count save it. Rest is a reference list with no arc.
mythmaker: Dana's runs give the card a face and a number, but the rest is a reference table. No build, no landing. Let Dana walk the whole deck.

C069.label: 2. Tending and Fraying
C069.desc: chapter "2. Tending and Fraying" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0934] to [P0937])

modeler: Stronger or weaker is a checkable direction, and the scroll example works. Ends on the rule about good and bad news, not a landing. Add how to tell which you've got.
skeptic: Clean. But a pattern 'either stronger or weaker' can't be contradicted. Add what observation would show a card isn't running.
clinician: Best guard against shame: no good or bad card, with the late-night scroll example. Add what a wrong reading looks like.
habit: Scroll example and 'stronger or weaker?' is a clean daily question. Ends restating that neither pole is good news. Land on a worked example.
contemplative: The late-night scroll and the rope make the two poles plain. Not good, not bad is stated once and clearly. The ambiguity is allowed to sit.
stress: The scroll example and the five-year job question are usable and checkable. The 'not good news' warning is fine, but it ends flat.
gamedesigner: Late-night scroll makes both poles concrete. 'Running stronger or weaker?' is a checkable question; the not-good-news landing is earned.
structural: Scroll and Set Course examples make 'stronger or weaker?' checkable. Ending guards against verdict-reading. Needs a sign of misreading.
satirist: Late-night scroll is a real case; 'not good news, not bad news' is clear. Ending restates its epigraph instead of arriving.
mythmaker: The late-night scroll and the rope make the two poles concrete, and asking stronger or weaker is usable. Closes by restating the opening claim.

C070.label: 3. The Rings, Not the Row
C070.desc: chapter "3. The Rings, Not the Row" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0938] to [P0942])

modeler: Rings versus a row is clear. 'Each ring feeding the one around it' names no flow. The Monday example is sketched, never run. Show the feed between rings.
skeptic: Rings-not-row is argued well, with the dinner-silence example. The four-sizes question is usable but gives no sign of working.
clinician: The nested rings stop the first card from becoming the culprit. The Monday-dread example helps. The no-cards fallback is a usable step but ends the chapter flat.
habit: Nested rings and the no-cards version, four sizes of one question, is something I can ask at 7:04. Ending just adds a variant. End on the Monday dread.
contemplative: Rings, not a row: Monday dread is a person standing in it, and no-cards question at four sizes is doable today. Settled and quiet.
stress: Rings against a row is a real claim, and the Monday and dinner examples help. It stops on a no-cards fallback; nothing says how you would know it failed.
gamedesigner: Good rule: rings, not a row. The Monday-dread questions work as a no-cards move. Ends on four answers, not one story.
structural: Rings against the row is the book's structural point; Monday example and four-sizes question are doable without cards.
satirist: Plain and useful: rings not row, Mondays-style dinner example, and a no-cards fallback of four questions. Sayable to a skeptic.
mythmaker: Dinner silence through culture is one person's pattern seen four ways. The no-cards version is doable tonight. The return to the nest image lands.

C071.label: 4. Weather, Climate, Terrain
C071.desc: chapter "4. Weather, Climate, Terrain" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0943] to [P0951])

modeler: Best chapter: loop period sets the window, with the follow-into-next-job test and a warning that distress mimics Terrain. Delays are finally named.
skeptic: Best here. The 'would it follow you into the next job' test and the distress-feels-like-Terrain caution make it checkable and honest about error.
clinician: Strong. The 'would it follow you into the next job' test is checkable, and the closing caution that distress feels like Terrain is protective.
habit: Strong. 'Would it follow you into the next job?' is a real test, and the distress-feels-like-Terrain caution is a sign of misfire. Keep.
contemplative: Weather, climate, terrain are easy to hold. The next-job test is specific. The warning that distress feels like Terrain is wise and kind.
stress: Best here: follow-into-next-job test, and the warning that distress feels like Terrain. It names its own error mode.
gamedesigner: Three speeds, the next-job test for Terrain, and a distress caution that pays off. Tight and playable.
structural: Weather, climate, terrain with a follow-you-to-the-next-job test, and distress-feels-like-terrain caution. Tight and checkable.
satirist: Weather, climate, terrain with a 'follows you to the next job' test and a distress caution. Passes the bar. Little ceremony.
mythmaker: Weather, climate and terrain are felt through marriage and job. Escalation at three speeds shows the idea. Ends on distress posing as terrain, which the body earned.

C072.label: 5. The Single Pull
C072.desc: chapter "5. The Single Pull" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0952] to [P0954])

modeler: Small and clear. Nothing says what finding the card, or not finding it, would show. Add a miss rule.
skeptic: Small and doable, but no sign of failure and no causal account. A random card plus 'go look' will find something every day.
clinician: A small, daily, low-stakes step, ideal for a bad day. But P0953 and P0954 say the same thing twice, and there's no sign of whether it worked.
habit: Cue is right: first coffee, before the phone. One card, go look. But no sign of whether it worked, and it just stops. Add an evening check.
contemplative: One card with first coffee, then go look for it. Light and breathable. The two paragraphs largely repeat each other; give one a day's example.
stress: Small enough for a bad day, and 'is it running?' can be wrong. Too brief to say what a failed pull looks like.
gamedesigner: Easy daily move I can try today. Two paragraphs say the same thing, there's no sign of working, and it just stops.
structural: Small enough for a bad day; 'is it running, which way' is checkable. Two paragraphs, no arrival; no sign of failure.
satirist: Short, doable over first coffee. Stops rather than lands, and gives no sign the pull did anything.
mythmaker: Pocket card, first coffee, a clear small step. Both paragraphs say question not forecast. No person stands in it and nothing says what failure looks like.

modeler: Small, daily, falsifiable: hit or miss logged by evening, narrow the search if too vague. It lacks a stock, but the test is honest and the ending lands.
skeptic: Hit/miss rule is good, but ends on 'new card' repeat, not changed understanding. Dana's two o'clock hit invites confirmation bias; name the base rate.
clinician: Safe, tiny, falsifiable. Hit versus 'maybe, in general' is a clear sign, misses are logged without shame, and the coffee returns at the close.
habit: This is the rep: a cue (first coffee), one card, a hit or miss by 2 o'clock, a log. Returns to coffee at the end. Nothing to change.
contemplative: Small, breathable, doable over one coffee. Dana's hit and miss give a clear sign, and the closing line is quiet and complete. Little to remove.
stress: Hit versus miss is defined, and a vague 'maybe' counts as a miss. Dana's two o'clock email thread is a real case. Small enough for a bad day.
gamedesigner: Short and playable: draw a card, go look, log a hit or miss. Dana's two o'clock email thread shows what a hit looks like.
structural: One card, one coffee, a hit-or-miss test at evening. Misses are logged, not excused. Small enough for a bad day.
satirist: A hit is a named moment at two o'clock; a miss is 'maybe, in general'. Logs its own failures. This is how to sell a prompt.
mythmaker: Dana with the first coffee and the two o'clock email thread: hit, miss, and 'same coffee, new card'. Small, human, and it returns to its opening image.

C073.label: 6. The Four-Point Weaving
C073.desc: chapter "6. The Four-Point Weaving" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0955] to [P0958])

modeler: The Monday-dread example is good. 'Real and partial' is a caveat, not a test. No sign of working. Name what a failed Weaving looks like.
skeptic: Mondays example is sound and the partial-reading caution is good. But four cards that need not agree can never be wrong. Say what would disconfirm.
clinician: Dreading Mondays gives a person to stand in. It's explicit that the rings need not agree and the first card is partial.
habit: Dreading-Mondays example makes four rings runnable. Disagreeing cards as information is good. Add a time box and a tomorrow action.
contemplative: Dreaded Mondays carries all four rings. Caution is held before the cards. Disagreeing rings are information. Small, usable, humble.
stress: The Monday dread example is concrete. Disagreeing rings are rightly kept as information. It ends mid-caution rather than arriving.
gamedesigner: Mondays example is a real spread. The caution up front stalls the start, and the ending states a value rather than showing a result.
structural: Dreaded Mondays walks four rings; disagreement among rings is the payoff. Caution on first card is useful. Outcome sign thin.
satirist: Dreading Mondays carries the whole spread; rings may disagree, and that's the value. Concrete enough for a skeptic.
mythmaker: Dreading Mondays gives the four rings a person to stand in. Disagreement between rings is explained as the payoff. Usable tonight.

C074.label: 7. The Full Unravelling
C074.desc: chapter "7. The Full Unravelling" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0959] to [P0967])

modeler: Derivation step by step with a check at each rung: where did you see it, which table, which week. The Escalation chain is worked. Ending limit holds.
skeptic: Rare rigor: 'name where you saw it, which table, which week', else it's a story. The Escalation chain is worked and a limit is stated.
clinician: 'Not blame, where the chain begins' protects the reader, and the 'where did you see it' test is good. But too many new moves at once, and not a bad-day practice.
habit: Difficulty spike: derivations, pairings, ring climbing. The 'where did you see it, which table, which week?' check is the usable bit. Cut it to that.
contemplative: Spark, Escalation, Lock-In, Long Cycle chain is a worked example, and the pointed-at-the-last-time test is good. But dense; too many concepts at once.
stress: Real tests at each rung: name the week and the table. It admits most pairs make nothing, and has a hard limit. Strongest chapter.
gamedesigner: Best level design here. Two cards, climb with an 'is this happening?' check, and Escalation to Long Cycle example. The limit lands it.
structural: Derivation up the rungs with 'can you name where you saw it' test; stops at World-Kin. Strongest on structure and rule-ownership.
satirist: Rare honesty: 'most pairs list nothing,' and 'if you can't name the week, it's a story.' Returns to the two cards.
mythmaker: Spark meets Spark, Escalation, up to the Long Cycle: the derivation has a rival standing in it. Ends on a stern limit. Strong checkable test at each step.

C075.label: 8. Weaving for Another
C075.desc: chapter "8. Weaving for Another" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0968] to [P0970])

modeler: One card at a time, folding in their answers, is a usable feedback loop. The two paragraphs say the same thing. Give a concrete miss example.
skeptic: The one-card-at-a-time technique with the other person's answer as the check is usable. But the two paragraphs repeat each other and the ending is a claim.
clinician: One-card-at-a-time and listening for a miss is sound. The two paragraphs do the same job, and it never covers someone in distress. Add a stop signal.
habit: One card at a time, wait for the answer: a real technique with a feedback signal. The second paragraph restates it. Merge and add a first-sentence script.
contemplative: One card at a time, listening between. Right instinct, but two long paragraphs restating it; no person, no named miss. Trim, add a spoken example.
stress: Two paragraphs saying 'listen and fold in answers' twice. No example and no sign it worked. Show a miss and what changed.
gamedesigner: One-card-at-a-time with their reply as feedback is solid. The two paragraphs repeat the point, and nobody concrete stands in it.
structural: Two paragraphs make the same listen-and-fold point. Ends on Gardener gloss. Reveal one card, wait, adapt is a usable technique.
satirist: Reveal one card, wait for the answer: usable. But two paragraphs say the same thing, no named person stands in it, and it just ends.
mythmaker: Reveal one card at a time, listen. Good, but two paragraphs say the same thing. Nobody is named; write the friend who says no.

modeler: Her own phrases rising across cards is a measurable sign, with stop rules. The final paragraph is overloaded, but it returns to the epigraph question.
skeptic: Checking a reading by whether it carries her phrases is testable, and the stop rule respects her. Returns to the epigraph's question with its answer paid for.
clinician: Stop-if-she-goes-quiet is exactly right, and her phrases are a measurable sign. Paragraph 969 is long and partly duplicates 970; trim.
habit: One card at a time, a miss counts, stop if she tightens, and check for her phrases by the last card. Concrete, testable, and the ending answers the epigraph.
contemplative: The Monday friend, the stop rule and the check by her own phrases make it practical. It returns to the epigraph question. The core-technique paragraph is still long.
stress: Miss counts as a result, a stop rule protects the friend, and a count of her own phrases checks it. Skin is in the room.
gamedesigner: One card at a time, with the Monday-drive miss as the model. The 'more of her phrases by the last card' check and the stop rule are solid.
structural: One card at a time, stop when she tightens, and a check that the reading carries her phrases. Usable and falsifiable.
satirist: Dreaded-Monday friend is a miss worth as much as a hit. Stop-signal and her-own-phrases check are concrete. Lands on her reply.
mythmaker: The friend dreading Mondays turns into 'it's really the drive in'. Misses count, stop-signals named, and her phrases count as the sign. Give her a name.

C076.label: 9. Weaving Together
C076.desc: chapter "9. Weaving Together" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0971] to [P0977])

modeler: Concrete structure, a rule against verdicts on a person, and a seed. The 'that's not us, we go quiet' line stands in the claim. Ending pays off.
skeptic: A group practice with real mechanics: 'that's not us' said aloud, one ring per reader, a seed to repeat. Misses count as data. Keep this standard.
clinician: The no-tribunal rule keeps it from becoming a verdict on a person. Reading in turns and ending on a seed give a real, checkable step.
habit: Group structure with a cue, a no-blame rule, and ending on one seed each will repeat before next meeting. That's a rep. Strong.
contemplative: Nobody wrote the card, so disagreement is free. The 'that's not us, we go quiet' line is a real voice; the closing seed lands.
stress: Shows how it fails (verdict on a person) and has a quote for a miss. It ends on a seed to repeat; a small result check would help.
gamedesigner: Clear room structure, rules against tribunal, and a miss script. The closing seed lands. Every paragraph earns its place.
structural: Card-as-neutral-object rule, reading split, no-verdict rule, closing seed. Ends on a Local Rule. Specific, usable, protects the quiet.
satirist: 'Nobody wrote the card' is the book's best working mechanism. Rules for readers, disagreement, and a closing seed. Pleasant evening averted.
mythmaker: The room, the loud talker and the tribunal risk are real people. The disagreement line is lovely. Ends with a seed and a cost for skipping it.

C077.label: 10. Reading Honestly
C077.desc: chapter "10. Reading Honestly" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0978] to [P0985])

modeler: Aim is clear (read without hiding behind cards), but P0980 and P0981 overlap, and it ends on a mirror warning with no test to run. Add a checkable step.
skeptic: Good: the 'nod that costs nothing' is a checkable failure sign. But confirmation and mirror paragraphs repeat; ends on a warning, not a landing.
clinician: Clear aim, and the 'does anything feed back?' gate is a real test. But the confirmation and mirror cautions say the same thing twice, and the ending stops on a warning.
habit: Gate question 'does anything feed back?' is a real before-you-draw step. But confirmation and mirror paragraphs repeat; ends on a warning, not a landing.
contemplative: Aim is clear and each caution earns. Ends on the mirror warning, not a changed understanding. No small act to do today; add one check-question to ask after a reading.
stress: Cautions are concrete, and the mirror test (readings always agreeing) is a real failure signal. Order is a shufflable list; ending is another warning, not an arrival.
gamedesigner: Clear aim, each caution distinct, and the feedback-gate question is a real test. But cautions could shuffle and it ends on a mirror warning, not a landing.
structural: Aim is clear, but P0979-P0985 repeat 'nod that costs nothing' five ways. No rule, no owner, no lever. Merge the cautions; add a worked reading and a test.
satirist: Five cautions, two of them the same nod-that-costs-nothing twice. Shuffleable list; no one stands in it. The feedback gate is the one testable step.
mythmaker: Aim is clear, but it's five cautions with nobody standing in them: no reader caught nodding, no face. Give me one person hiding behind a card.

modeler: Aim is clear and Dara returns at the end. But P0981 (confirmation) and P0985 (mirror) do the same job twice; merge them. Say-aloud test is a real, checkable step.
skeptic: Dara's nod pays off and 'predict, then ask what surprised you' is testable. But the confirmation and mirror paragraphs do the same job twice; merge them.
clinician: Aim is clear and the say-aloud prediction test is usable. P0981 and P0985 do the same job twice, and the cautions could be shuffled. Merge them.
habit: Good: say your expectation aloud, ask what surprised you. But the confirmation and mirror cautions do the same job twice. Merge them.
contemplative: Aim is clear: read honestly. But confirmation and mirror cautions say the same thing twice, and the cautions could be shuffled. Merge them; the say-it-aloud test is a good practice.
stress: Dara's bookend and the say-it-first, wince-after test can fail. But the old confirmation paragraph and the mirror paragraph do one job twice. Merge them.
gamedesigner: Aim is clear and Dara stands in it; mirror test with a pre-draw prediction is a real feedback signal. Ending on Dara's next question is thin; chapter drifts to gate talk mid-way.
structural: Aim is clear and the mirror test is checkable. But P0981 and P0985 make the same confirmation point twice; cautions could be reordered freely. Merge them.
satirist: Aim is clear, but P0981 and P0985 both warn about the pleasing nod, and the cautions could be shuffled. The say-it-aloud test earns the k4 point.
mythmaker: Dara bookends it nicely, but the middle is abstract cautions, and the confirmation paragraph repeats the mirror one. Merge them; shuffle-proof the order.

modeler: Aim is clear: keep readings honest. But confirmation and mirror cautions run the same loop twice, and the list reshuffles freely. Merge them. The say-it-aloud expectation test is a real check.
skeptic: Cautions cohere and Dara carries them to a fitting close. But 'four cards seem to say something' is asserted, not shown; the mirror test is self-reported wincing.
clinician: Dara lands it well and the expect-then-ask-if-surprised test is small. But several cautions have nobody standing in them, and 'wince' risks 3 a.m. self-blame. Give each caution a person.
habit: Aim is clear, but P0982/P0984 vs revised paragraphs overlap, ending on mirror is a warning, not a landing. Offers a pre-draw expectation test, but no small daily step.
contemplative: Aim is clear: read honestly. But P0981 and P0985 both warn of the nodding mirror, and the cautions could be shuffled. Merge them; end on one lived case.
stress: Aim is clear and Dara's mirror test is falsifiable. But the cautions are a shuffleable list; the prophecy and spark paragraphs have nobody in them. Order the cautions and give each a face.
gamedesigner: Clear aim, each caution earns its place. But it's a list of warnings that could shuffle, and ends on Dara's self-scrutiny; the mirror test is the only real move.
structural: Aim is clear. Dara stands in it, but P0979, P0981 and P0985 all recycle the nod/mirror point and the cautions shuffle freely. Mirror test (say expectation aloud) is usable.
satirist: Aim is clear: don't misuse a card. But confirmation and mirror cautions twin each other, and the list shuffles freely. Dara's test (predict, then look for a wince) is usable.
mythmaker: Dara earns her place and returns at the close, lovely. But P0982 and P0984 have no face, and the cautions could be shuffled. Give them Dara.

C078.label: 11. What a Weaving Cannot Show
C078.desc: chapter "11. What a Weaving Cannot Show" (PART SIX — WEAVINGS; paragraphs [P0986] to [P0991])

modeler: Three limits announced, then delivered in order, and the fork landing pays off. But no step or sign of failure. Add a test, e.g. ask the other person before saying 'the card says'.
skeptic: Three limits, honestly bounded. 'Stop and ask them instead' is a testable step. The last paragraph widens to generic comfort; land on the fork.
clinician: Three limits, gently landed, and 'stop and ask them instead' is a safe, doable step. Warm ending. A named person standing in the fork limit would help.
habit: Three limits, each with a stop-rule I can run ('card says you're...' then ask them). Ends on tomorrow. Add a sign it worked.
contemplative: Three limits, honestly stated, closing on 'tomorrow is the next'. Calming landing. But nothing to do or test; the only step is 'stop and ask them'.
stress: Three limits clear, fork example good. Ends on soft 'tomorrow is the next' comfort. No test or sign that a reading failed; add one.
gamedesigner: Three limits promised, three delivered, and the 'tomorrow' ending pays off. But no small thing to try and no signal telling me I'm doing it wrong.
structural: Three limits are distinct, but the ending is a poetic 'tomorrow is the next' payoff. Nothing here a person can try or check; give a fork-decision step.
satirist: Three limits, plainly counted. Thermometer earns its keep. The close drifts from the map image into tomorrow. 'The card says you're' is a usable tell.
mythmaker: Three limits plus a fork gap; thermometer helps, but 'the card says you're...' has no friend. Ending dissolves into tomorrow. Give one person, one stopping test.

C079.label: PART SEVEN — THE TURNINGS (opener)
C079.desc: chapter "PART SEVEN — THE TURNINGS (opener)" (PART SEVEN — THE TURNINGS; paragraphs [P0992] to [P0994])

modeler: The promised outcome is clear, but the opener is three short blurbs. No stock or mechanism, and it ends mid-argument on an ache. Needs a tiny worked case.
skeptic: Tells the reader they envy others' holidays; guessed feeling, no support. Opener promises an outcome but offers nothing to try.
clinician: The 'envied holidays, had none' ache is named kindly. As an opener it gives nothing to try and stops before arriving.
habit: Outcome promise is good, but it's three framing paragraphs with no step. Give one two-minute action here.
contemplative: Honest aim and a kind opening about envied holidays. But it's an opener of promises; no step to take here. Add one line to try.
stress: Outcome stated plainly, but it's a doorway only. Nothing to try, no landing; the 'ache' line is mild flattery.
gamedesigner: Good skip-ahead menu for the player, but it's a menu screen: no move, no arrival, nothing to try. Fine as a lobby.
structural: Opener works as a route map and names the ache of having no holidays. Nothing to do or test yet, and no mention of who owns calendars.
satirist: A door with a promise on it and a nod to envy. Fine signage; it is not a chapter. No step, no test.
mythmaker: Honest opener, and the envied-holidays ache has a flicker of face. But it's a router with no one standing in it; no landing.

modeler: Aim, shortcut and two-minute holiday test are tight. It ends on the table-ache image never planted earlier, so the landing is thin; plant that person in the first paragraph.
skeptic: Tonight's two-minute test is small and checkable. The 'three tests' arrive as a pointer, so trust is borrowed from Chapter 0; the table-guest image is lovely but unsupported.
clinician: Short, honest opener. The two-minute test is small, checkable and kind: no answer is a finding, not a failing. Someone at the table carries the ache.
habit: Two-minute holiday test tonight, with a built-in answer. Cue is clear. This is how I want openers to work.
contemplative: Short and honest, with a person at the table and a two-minute test. But it uses 'shared, recurring, aimed' and 'Global Form' before they are taught. Name the terms simply.
stress: Two-minute test can actually fail ('can't say what it's building'). But it ends on an ache and a promise to follow, not a landing. Close on the test.
gamedesigner: Short opener with a two-minute test tonight and an answerable stop condition. Table-guest image hooks. Ends on the part's promise, not strong payoff, but earns its place.
structural: Outcome, shortcut and two-minute test all earn their place. The close only sets up the Part and lands on no changed understanding. Return to the table-guest image.
satirist: Aim is stated and the two-minute test is real. But the try-this lands before the why, and the close is a mood. Move the ache earlier.
mythmaker: The person at the friend's table is the right face and the two-minute test is good. It ends on a thesis, not a return to that table.

C080.label: 0. What a Turning Is
C080.desc: chapter "0. What a Turning Is" (PART SEVEN — THE TURNINGS; paragraphs [P0995] to [P1009])

modeler: Many aims (definition, three tests, move vocabulary, warning). Shared, recurring, aimed is a usable test, but the Turning loop has no stock or drain named. Name what rot drains.
skeptic: Four Move verbs and the warning crowd in late. Try-this asks what an occasion 'actually produces' with no way to know. Name a measure.
clinician: Strong aim, but too many concepts at once: Global Form, three tests, four Moves, menu, rot warning. Trim. The Try-this asks for current honest accounting, which is gentle enough.
habit: Try-this is concrete: name an occasion, ask what it actually produces. But shared/recurring/aimed, move, Global Form arrive stacked; no cue for when to run it.
contemplative: Fifteen paragraphs carry definition, three tests, moves and warning. Too much, with stacked analogies (clubs, roast, pan). The Try this is kitchen-doable. Trim and split.
stress: Shared/recurring/aimed is a checkable test. But the roast and ancestor analogies pad, the rot warning repeats, and it ends on a prompt.
gamedesigner: Strong three-test rulebook and a playable Try this. But the fake-ancestry and commemoration beats overlap, and Shared/Recurring/Aimed arrive alongside the Move vocabulary all at once.

modeler: Definition and three tests work. P1006 dumps Look/Plant/Tend/Thin plus Third and figure at once, and P1008 repeats P1005. Split the moves out and merge the warnings.
skeptic: The 'last one' observable test is good. But the Look/Plant/Tend/Thin moves land mid-chapter, and the seder-and-reunion claims lean on assertion. Give P1000 a person.
clinician: Aim and the three tests are clear, and the observable 'last one' question is good. P1006 drops four moves at once, and the close is a try-this, not a landing.
habit: Three tests plus a good Try this. But Look/Plant/Tend/Thin land in one paragraph, and the optional and rot warnings repeat the Aimed point. Trim, and end on the brick.

mythmaker: The two clubs and the invented ancestor have faces, and the Try this tests are strong. The four Moves arrive at once, and the seder is never revisited.

modeler: Aim and test are stated up front. But P1006 drops four moves at once, and P1007/P1008 are asides. P1008 repeats P1005's aimed-warning. The seder-child test closes well.
skeptic: Opening promises one definition and one test. Then Global Form, four moves, menu and rot warning arrive stacked; the club claim is asserted. Try-this is small and checkable.
clinician: Try-this is safe and small, with 'not a failing of yours.' But Move/figure/four verbs land at once in one paragraph, and the Aimed and rot warnings overlap. Rework.
habit: Definition plus tests blur into a catalogue; tests and Move concepts crowd P1006. But the revised Try-this gives a one-minute, checkable question for tomorrow.
contemplative: Seder to Aimed question is good and the Try-this is small and testable. Too heavy: P1000 repeats P0999, and four moves arrive at once in P1006. Trim.
stress: The Aimed test is small, checkable and breakable. But four moves arrive at once before the tables, and the warning trails the practice. Defer the moves and move the warning earlier.
gamedesigner: Definition and three tests are playable, and the Try this has a real signal. But P1006-P1008 pile on new terms (moves, menu, rot) before the payoff, with a warning ending.
